#6548. Trinity Rodman and Ben Shelton’s Complete Relationship Timeline

A love born on TikTok, their relationship quickly captured the internet’s attention.

Being a professional athlete takes an inordinate amount of hard work and dedication, which is why Trinity Rodman’s romance with Ben Shelton makes so much sense. While Rodman is a soccer star, playing for the Washington Spirit and the United States women’s national soccer team, Shelton is a professional tennis champ, representing the U.S. at tournaments across the globe, including Wimbledon. Since making their relationship public in spring 2025, interest in Shelton and Rodman’s connection has only intensified.

In November 2026, multiple outlets, including People, reported that the pair had broken up. Here’s what you need to know about Rodman and Shelton’s relationship timeline.

Rodman is prolific on TikTok, with more than 305,000 followers as of August 2025. As a result, it makes perfect sense that the star athlete appeared to tease her new romance with Shelton on the platform. The pair hinted that they were both “shooting their shot” with one another in a TikTok trend in March 2025, via espnW’s Instagram account. And it wasn’t long before the two athletes decided to hard-launch their romance on social media.

On March 18, Shelton shared a series of photos on Instagram, the last of which was a mirror selfie taken with Rodman in an elevator. “I been focused, but I’m steady climbin’, I’m nowhere near my peak,” he captioned the post. The soccer player commented on her boyfriend’s post, writing, “Shooters shoot I guess,” suggesting that the TikTok most certainly paid off, as reported by The Mirror US.

After Shelton and Rodman revealed their relationship on Instagram, tennis pro Frances Tiafoe suggested he was actually responsible for introducing the pair. During an appearance on the TikTok account Overtime Tennis on March 18, 2025, Tiafoe said, “By the way, I don’t think people realize, I was like, the one who [connected them]—if we’re going to be real.”

“I’m happy for him, man,” Tiafoe said of Shelton. “The elevator photo out the gate...everybody knows who Trinity Rodman is. [The photo] at the end of the carousel, sick.”

However, Shelton and Rodman later denied Tiafoe’s version of events, suggesting he wasn’t responsible for them meeting. “I don’t know if I want everyone to know the story [of how we met], but I can assure you Frances was not the reason we met or got together. I don’t know why he’s taking credit for that,” Rodman told ESPN’s SportsCenter. “Me and Ben can both cut that out. It was solely a me and Ben thing.”

Shelton also shot down Tiafoe’s claims, telling the New York Post, “We’d like talked about her once, twice before and I was like, ‘But come on, man. You didn’t do anything.’ Putting us together, like that’s a bit of a stretch.” He continued, “[Rodman] was kind of annoyed by that. She was like, ‘Come on, bro.’ I think she said something to him a couple times. But we’re all friends.”

After Shelton took their relationship public with his March 18, 2025 Instagram post, Rodman returned the favor by posting an adorable photo on social media, too. The picture showed Rodman gazing up at her tennis pro boyfriend, whose face was hidden by a baseball cap. Tagging Shelton in the photo, Rodman captioned her March 27 Instagram post, “Dibs.” Shelton commented on the post, writing, “Whoever that is he won [for sure].”

From that point on, the romance between the two athletes seems to have only grown stronger. For instance, in an Instagram carousel posted on April 5, 2025, Shelton shared a short clip as he walked alongside Rodman, captioning the post, “In n out of time zones,” suggesting they were traveling together.

The public’s excitement about the romance wasn’t lost on Rodman and Shelton. During an appearance on ESPN’s SportsCenter in March 2025, Rodman spoke about her decision to go public with the relationship, saying, “I mean, I’m just another person in a relationship and people know about it.” She continued, “I’m obviously very happy.”

In his April 2025 interview with the New York Post, Shelton discussed his romance with Rodman, and the incredible response they had received after revealing their relationship on Instagram. “It’s been great, obviously,” the 22-year-old athlete said. “I guess I didn’t think it would blow up as much as it did. That’s not why I did it.”

The tennis pro also suggested that “posting your girlfriend on Instagram is a more normal thing,” so he didn’t necessarily think the photos would make such an impact. “I realized, ‘Wow, people care about my life that much,’” he told the outlet. “But yeah, [we’re] happy for sure.”

The same month, Rodman shared a TikTok video of herself hugging her boyfriend, with the caption, “My safety blanket...you make everyday better.”

In April 2025, celebrated Olympian Rodman traveled to Munich in support of Shelton, who made it all the way to the men’s singles final in the BMW Open 2025. Rodman made her debut in the player’s box when Shelton beat Francisco Cerundolo in the men’s singles semifinal, and was spotted talking to her boyfriend’s dad, Bryan Shelton, during the competition. “She’s a good luck charm,” @tennischannel wrote on Instagram. Although Shelton ultimately lost the final to Germany’s Alexander Zverev, Rodman’s presence at the tournament made their relationship status quite clear.

In July 2025, Shelton made it to the quarterfinals at Wimbledon, where he ultimately lost to Italian tennis player Jannik Sinner. Rodman supported her boyfriend at the tournament in London, and she also criticized commentators for calling her the wrong name and mentioning her estranged dad, former NBA player Dennis Rodman.

“For those who don’t know...my name is TRINITY not Tiffany,” Rodman wrote on her Instagram Stories, via Sports Illustrated. “Also, for Ben’s matches he has his family there as his support system, which includes his dad... my dads not even in MY life no need to bring him up during HIS matches when I don’t even want him talked about during mine.”

As well as competing across Europe throughout the summer, Shelton still found time to savor some vacation days with his girlfriend. On May 20, Shelton shared two sweet photos on Instagram, which he captioned, “Happy birthday beautiful girl...I love you.” The Olympic gold medalist responded in the comments, writing, “I luhhh you.”

The following month, Rodman shared footage showing her holding hands with her boyfriend as they walked around Europe. “No one else,” she captioned the Instagram post. On July 5, the Washington Spirit player shared another cute photo with Shelton, with the caption, “Watching you with googly eyes,” to which he responded, “Why am I cheesin so big.”

As both Shelton and Rodman are accustomed to traveling the world for their careers, they’ve had to adjust to dating while being in completely different places. “It has its challenges, but it’s definitely worth it,” Shelton told Town & Country. “It’s not something that we’re not used to—it’s been the story of our lives, especially me being on the road all the time. It’s just normal life stuff.”

In August 2025, Rodman made her long-awaited return to soccer after taking time off to deal with a back injury. Prior to returning to work, Rodman shared vacation snaps with Shelton, along with training videos, writing on Instagram, “Not the summer that I had in mind but still loved every moment...can’t wait to be back on the field.”

On August 3, Rodman’s team, the Washington Spirit, played against the Portland Thorns in the National Women’s Soccer League. After joining the game for the final 14 minutes, Rodman was able to score the winning goal, cementing her triumphant return to the sport.

Shelton wasn’t able to support his girlfriend in person, as he was in Toronto for the 2025 National Bank Open. However, he celebrated her win from afar, telling ATP Tour, “One year anniversary from her incredible goal at the Olympics, hadn’t played in 100-something days and she goes in and in 15 minutes scores a banger. It’s pretty cool, especially [because] she was emotional. I’m always happy for her.”

On June 14, Rodman shared a selfie with Shelton on Instagram, writing simply, “#1 fan I love you ❤️.”

Rodman traveled to Montreal to surprise Shelton during the Canadian Open after playing with the Washington Spirit in Washington, D.C., on August 8. She documented his reaction on her Instagram Stories, writing, “Surprised his ass, happy matchday in Montreal 😘❤️ @benshelton.”

Shelton went on to win the tournament, and Rodman celebrated his victory in an August 14 Instagram post. Alongside a photo of the couple walking together on the tennis court, she wrote, “Drive, dedication, and commitment. Back to back Canada champ! Celebrate every win baby ❤️ I love you.”

During an August 2026 appearance on Kylie Kelce’s Not Gonna Lie podcast, Rodman opened up about how her relationship with Shelton began, revealing that she was the one who initially reached out.

“Everything I do is just embarrassing. I’m really embarrassed,” she said.

Rodman explained just how quickly she wanted to get to know Shelton: “I fully committed to this guy that I didn’t even meet yet, for him to stay at my house for the weekend. It’s actually crazy, it’s insane, but it worked out.”

She also discussed why she personally embraces being called a WAG despite being a professional athlete herself.

“For me, I think I like the term personally because, like I said before, I feel like 24/7 I’m on in front of cameras…and so I think I use the term WAG for me to simplify what I’m doing,” she said. “For me, saying WAG, it’s me being like, ‘I’m Ben’s girlfriend.’ But I can understand why [the term] is so hated.”

Rodman added that having a partner who understands the demands of professional sports has been particularly meaningful to her.

“It’s the best feeling in the world, honestly. I think to know we’re both on the grind, running our bodies to the ground, always exhausted, doing what we love, and then to also be able to be a little like a WAG in a sense, it feels so good for us,” she said.

Rodman showed her support for Shelton after he beat Carlos Alcaraz in the quarterfinal of the US Open. The competitive match ended at 3:30 A.M. “My 🌎,” she wrote on her Instagram Story.

She was also in the stands cheering him on:

On November 24, People reported that the couple had broken up. Days before, Shelton responded “no” when asked if he would attend Rodman and the Washington Spirit’s championship game against the Kansas City Current on November 21.

#6544. Meet ‘Dune: Part Three’’s Ida Brooke, the Young Brit Denis Villeneuve Picked to Play Zendaya’s Daughter

Ida Brooke is wearing a piece of Dune around her neck. The necklace is silver and unassuming, but she explains its provenance: at the end of filming Denis Villeneuve’s Dune: Part Three, silver used in the production was collected, melted down, and recast into wrap gifts for the cast. Brooke hasn’t taken hers off since.

“There’s nothing that’s going to be as good as that,” the 18-year-old actor says, turning it between her fingers over coffee in a central London café. It has changed the rest of her jewelry too: once a gold devotee, today she is wearing a stack of silver rings. (She is otherwise dressed in the Gen-Z uniform of a tank top and low-rise cargo trousers, her hair falling in glossy natural curls.) It feels particularly apt for someone whose life is currently divided into very distinct before and afters. Only a few months ago, she was a film student at the Brit School; soon, audiences will know her as Ghanima, the daughter of Zendaya’s Chani and Timothée Chalamet’s Paul Atreides, opposite Nakoa-Wolf Momoa as her twin brother, Leto II, in Villeneuve’s third Dune film.

To get there was a months-long exercise in trying not to unravel. Brooke initially self-taped without knowing she was auditioning for Dune. When her agent revealed the project, she shut the curtains on a sunny day and watched the first two films back to back. “I fell so in love with it,” she says. “I was like, ‘OK, this is going to really hurt if I don’t get this.’” By the final audition, she had already convinced herself that another girl outside the room had the advantage. Brooke went to the bathroom and gave herself a talking to. “You don’t have to get it,” she remembers thinking. “You just have to show them that you have something to say. Just make their choice a little bit harder.”

The following day, Brooke was sitting beside a teacher at school trying to solve an editing problem when a message flashed up from an unknown number: Villeneuve wanted to call her in 20 minutes. Her phone had five percent battery. She tore through the school searching for a charger, eventually hiding in a stairwell to take the call. He first warned her about the intensity of the shoot—the heat, the physical demands—and asked whether she wanted to join the film. A friend found Brooke crying and took a photograph. “She was like, ‘You might want this one day.’”

Cinema has been the organizing obsession of her life since childhood. At six, she would rewatch films endlessly on a portable DVD player; as a teenager growing up in west London, she traveled across the city for Saturday acting classes. She now lives with her father and younger sibling, a household she affectionately describes as “very rowdy.” A lifelong cinephile, though he doesn’t work in film, her father’s fascination with human psychology has informed her own approach to storytelling. (The two share a love of Martin Scorsese.) “He always loved quality stories and has really good taste,” she says, smiling.

Writing interests her as much as performing: she likes structure, psychology and—gleefully—eavesdropping, listening to “the cadence of how people speak,” she says, gesturing cheekily at the conversations trilling around us. She is currently working on a screenplay exploring Vietnam veterans and the pharmaceutical industry, a project born from the inquisitive way she approaches the world. She will also star in and executive produce an indie drama, Grass Roots, due to shoot next summer.

Calm proved instructive in the desert. Zendaya, who had already endured the elements on the earlier films, helped Brooke understand how to quiet her body enough to perform. “I feel so much more confident acting in somewhat normal environments now,” she says. Learning to act, for Brooke, has also meant learning when to pay attention and when to give in. “Denis has such a vivid imagination that you can step right into his vision… You just have to be a kid.”

Ida Brooke as Ghanima and Nakoa-Wolf Momoa as Leto in Dune: Part Three.

Brooke missed her graduation—and the screening of her final Brit School film, The Operator, which won an award—because she was away filming the forthcoming sci-fi live-action Gundam movie alongside Noah Centineo and Sydney Sweeney in Australia. When she told her new castmates how gutted she was, they improvised a graduation of sorts: everyone piled onto a sofa and screened her film together. “I had that sense of community that I missed.”

For the moment, Brooke is resisting any pressure to decide exactly what she is. Actor? Writer? Director? All three? She chose not to go to university and has instead devised her own education, meeting writers to ask how they work, reading about psychology and screenwriting, watching films, researching whatever historical period has most recently caught her imagination. “One of my biggest priorities is self-education,” she says.

Her necklace is a souvenir from one of the biggest film sets ever conceived, but Brooke looks voraciously forward at what she hasn’t encountered yet. She wants to work with Scorsese, but she also talks excitedly about young, unknown filmmakers in London: “The friends that I have now, I see them as my future colleagues.” Her ambition is not in conquering new terrain, it’s to remain porous enough to keep discovering. After all, silver can always be melted down and made into something new.

#6543. The True Story of Ian Charleson, the Trailblazing Actor Andrew Scott Plays in Elsinore

In Elsinore, quite possibly this year's most moving film, Andrew Scott gives a captivating, awards-worthy performance as the late, great Scottish actor Ian Charleson. Though he never became a household name, Charleson's star shone brightly in the early 1980s when he appeared in two consecutive Best Picture winners: 1981's Chariots of Fire and 1982's Gandhi.

"I'd rather die of Hamlet than die of AIDS," Scott-as-Charleson says in Elsinore, which opened in select theaters last week. This defiant line sums up the incredible coup de grâce that Charleson pulled off at the end of his life. When he began his valedictory stage run as Shakespeare's Danish Prince in October 1989, the 40-year-old actor was dying of AIDS. His face was so swollen with septicemia that the cast, crew, and audience at London's National Theatre were told he was recovering from a sinus operation.

"I begged him not to do Hamlet. I said to him, It will kill you, which it did," Charleson's friend Sean Mathias, an accomplished actor and director in his own right, told me. "The amount of energy it takes to play that kind of classical role, both physically and spiritually, would tire the most ardent athlete. For a man dealing with the onslaught of AIDS, it was almost impossible."

But against the odds, Charleson turned in a monumental performance. In a review for The Sunday Times, theater critic John Peter described his Hamlet as "virile and forceful" and wrote that the actor "oozes intelligence from every pore." Charleson's performance was all the more remarkable because he was an eleventh hour replacement for Daniel Day-Lewis, who left the production early—quite literally, midway through a performance—because he was so haunted by Shakespeare’s gothic tragedy.

"People still remember Ian's performance as Hamlet," says Andrew Scott, whose performance in the film captures Charleson in the tumultuous final year of his life. Elsinore's screenwriter Stephen Beresford believes it's fitting that no footage of Charleson's defining performance exists. "An important thing to remember about Ian is his extraordinary contradictions," he says. "He wants to be seen and not seen, to be known and not known." Charleson, in fact, was so publicity-averse—perhaps partly because he was a closeted gay man—that he walked out of the Chariots of Fire press junket.

At the same time, he was simply an old-school British thespian who believed that the work should speak for itself. "Ian was incredibly passionate about this extraordinary part of Hamlet," Scott adds, citing the actor's devotion to his craft as a major incentive in his decision to join Elsinore. "But the chief thing [I love about him] is his courage and sense of humor."

In Elsinore, we see Scott's Charleson share his AIDS prognosis with his Hamlet castmates. When he died on January 6th, 1990, just seven weeks after his final curtain call, it was also disclosed to the public at large. At the time, Charleson's close friend Ian McKellen told the British press: "It is rare for anyone in the public eye to say that they are HIV positive, let alone that they have AIDS. It is a tribute to Ian that he should ask for the cause of his death to be made public and it is the most marvelous offer of support that he could have given to other men and women all over the world suffering from the AIDS virus."

Beresford, who wrote Elsinore's screenplay after extensive conversations with Charleson's friends, family, and contemporaries, told me that it was actually the actor's father, Jack, who made the decision to disclose his cause of death publicly. "The tabloids were already circling, so I think there must have been fear that it was going to come out anyway," suggests Beresford, who previously penned the 2014 film Pride, which told the true story of gay and lesbian activists who raised money for the families of English coal miners during their 1984 strike.

Still, even if it wasn't carried out at his own behest, Charleson's posthumous contribution to HIV/AIDS awareness was very significant at a time when the disease was highly stigmatized and virtually impossible to treat. It would be another five years before HAART (highly active antiretroviral therapy) made the disease manageable.

In the U.K., the actor has also been immortalized with the annual Ian Charleson Awards, which since 1991 has recognized the best classical stage performances by actors under the age of 30. Past winners include David Oyelowo, Andrea Riseborough, Paapa Essiedu, Rebecca Hall, and Jack Lowden, while Benedict Cumberbatch, Cynthia Erivo, and Jessie Buckley have all received runner's-up prizes or commendations. "Ian's name is legendary within the [British] theater because of what he achieved in Hamlet, and the awards were set up to keep his memory alive," Beresford says.

In Elsinore, we see Scott's Charleson wryly lamenting the fact that, though he starred in the Oscar-winning Chariots of Fire, "all anyone can ever remember is its theme music." In this stirring sports biopic, Charleson played Eric Liddell, a devout Christian who managed to win gold at the 1924 Olympic Games despite withdrawing from his best event, the 100-meter sprint, because the heats fell on a Sunday. Charleson also appeared in the following year's Best Picture winner, Gandhi, as an Anglican priest who supported the iconic title character's fight for Indian independence.

Sadly, despite these back-to-back triumphs, Charleson never made it as a bona fide movie star. By 1986, he was reduced to appearing in Car Trouble, a crass British comedy about a man who falls in love with his new convertible. "He was very disappointed that film stardom didn't prolong itself," says Mathias, who believes that Charleson's sexuality denied him further opportunities in mainstream movies. "He wasn't out [publicly], but everyone in the business knew he was gay. And back then, gay actors just weren't given work in Hollywood."

Consequently, and perhaps aptly given his predilection for the stage, Charleson found salvation in the theater. On June 25th, 1989, he appeared in a one-night only revival of Martin Sherman's seminal queer play Bent. This pointed production at London's Adelphi Theatre, which also starred McKellen, Ralph Fiennes and Richard E. Grant, was staged to raise money for The Stonewall Group, a newly formed nonprofit that went on to become the U.K.'s leading LGBTQ+ rights organization. Charleson portrayed Greta, a drag performer who changes into male-presenting clothes during the play.

By this point, Charleson's torso was covered in lesions caused by Kaposi's sarcoma, a rare form of cancer common in AIDS patients. Mathias, who was directing the fundraiser, had screens erected on stage so that Charleson could change costumes out of view. "Ian said to me, But the crew can still see my body from the wings! So I said I'd get more screens put up," Mathias remembers. "But then he thought about it, and went, You know what? Fuck it! I always feel that was the moment, really, that he decided he would come out [as having AIDS]."

Shortly after Bent, Charleson was asked by Hamlet's director, Richard Eyre, to step in for Daniel Day-Lewis. Dickie Beau, an actor and writer who paid tribute to Charleson with his one-man stage show Re-Member Me (and who appears in Elsinore as the drag activist Sister Belladonna), believes Bent is a "truly significant" part of his legacy. “Not only did it help to kickstart [the charity] Stonewall, but it said a lot about him that he was happy to play Greta, who isn't a leading part,” he says. "Ian McKellen once said to me that, as much as Charleson saw himself as a lead actor, he was also a company man."

It's another of the fascinating contradictions that seem to make up Ian Charleson. Mathias says he was generally "quiet and private" and "very masculine," but also possessed a "wonderfully camp sense of humor." There's a poignant irony in his becoming the subject of a major motion picture, Beresford says, laughing: "Ian would have hated this publicity tour. I can guarantee that absolutely no part of him is watching us today!"

For Scott, who embodies Charleson so beautifully that he’s considered an awards season frontrunner, Elsinore's purpose is simple: “I hope our movie continues his legacy.”

#6542. Fascia Release Is the Key to Regulating Your Nervous System, Getting Better Sleep, and Improving Skin

Fascia, the thin web that envelops the face and body, is more powerful than you might think. Here’s how to release it

I’m curled up on a treatment bed in the Corinthia spa, feeling a knot of tension dissipate slowly from my neck and shoulders. Within minutes, tears prick my eyes. I’m familiar with the sudden catharsis bodywork can bring, but this is different. Known as “myofascial release”—a targeted therapy that works with fascia, the continuous matrix of connective tissue that wraps every muscle, nerve, and organ—it aims to reduce tightness and release restricted tissue, restoring its natural glide.

“Fascia is deeply connected to the entire sensory network,” explains Nadia Alibhai, a London-based osteopath who was unfazed by my heightened emotions. “When you move or hold stress, forces are transmitted through this interconnected system. It senses everything and dictates how the whole body responds. This treatment directly influences how we perceive and react to tension.”

Once dismissed as mere biological wrapping paper, fascia—made up of water, collagen, elastin, and hyaluronic acid—is now understood as a living, three-dimensional web. “It’s part of a complex system involving movement, circulation, lymphatics, posture, and tissue health,” Alibhai explains. When it works well, it keeps everything moving and prevents systems from becoming sluggish, but when it becomes restricted, often from scrolling, sedentary habits, or chronic stress, the fluid between the layers can thicken. This affects physical mobility and emotional well-being, leading to issues ranging from pain and stiffness to a dysregulated nervous system.

Fascia and neurology are intrinsically linked, explains skin-health expert Annee de Mamiel. “Fascia changes according to how we move, breathe, and repeatedly load the body,” she says. “Cortisol and adrenaline change our physiology; the nervous system alters breathing, muscular tone, and stress response. Over time, these repeated patterns affect the tissues.” It’s a catch-22: greater stress can tighten fascia, which in turn can send your body into fight-or-flight mode, prolonging the anxiety that caused the damage in the first place.

This mind-body connection is just one reason why fascia has piqued the wellness industry’s interest. Google searches for “fascia release” have soared in the past year, while facials targeting the system are becoming more popular. Robert Schleip, the director of the Fascia Research Group at Ulm University, attributes this to its holistic possibilities. “Fascia is now studied in relation to the autonomic nervous system, and therefore emotional regulation, as well as the immune system and aging,” he says. The latest findings show that supporting your fascia goes far beyond easing a tight neck; it's linked to reduced arterial stiffness and improved cardiovascular health.

Fascia release has also entered the skin-health conversation. Tight fascia can be an overlooked culprit behind loss of luminosity, puffiness, and premature aging, says de Mamiel, because it’s heavily involved in fluid drainage and lymphatic pathways. “The diaphragm plays a role in pressure changes and fluid movement through the body, and the fascial system connects these areas,” she explains. “When I work on movement and tension through the neck, chest, and rib cage, I often see a change in how congested or puffy the face appears.” However, releasing fascia effectively doesn't require aggressive force. “If I use so much pressure that your body braces, I’ve produced the opposite response—it’s about creating conditions where the nervous system and tissue can both settle.”

Facialist Nichola Joss achieves similarly impressive results with her signature Inner Facial, which fuses lymphatic drainage, fascia release, buccal massage, and sculpting techniques. “Fascia surrounds and supports our muscles; when restricted, it affects how freely muscles move,” Joss explains. This affects lymphatic flow and your skin’s natural glow. “By releasing muscular and fascial tension, you lift, tone, and sculpt contours while boosting circulation and softening fine lines.”

Beyond professional treatments, supporting fascial health depends on consistent daily habits. First, fascia thrives on varied movement: try walking, twisting your body, reaching overhead, and squatting to support overall health. Unfortunately, there are no true quick fixes: Spending the day glued to an office chair and then going straight into an intense HIIT session can actually be counterproductive. Instead, interrupt patterns throughout the day: Stand during phone calls instead of sitting, swing your arms gently during screen breaks, and make sure you’re not holding your breath during stressful periods at work. Counteract hours spent hunched over a device with this simple doorway stretch: Place your forearms against the frame, step forward gently, and hold for 20 to 30 seconds while breathing deeply.

Schleip recommends aligning exercise with your circadian rhythm. “Incorporate dynamic, elastic, or bouncing movements in the morning, ideally outdoors, and slow stretches in the evening,” he suggests, adding that sustained yoga positions, such as a child’s pose held for at least 30 seconds, can be particularly helpful. “Regular stretching improves joint mobility and may benefit cardiovascular markers such as arterial stiffness,” he adds. Finally, make nutrition and hydration a priority: fascia is 70 percent water and needs hydration to glide freely.

As Alibhai reflects at the end of my session: “The goal isn’t to constantly release fascia; it’s to keep your body moving, adaptable, and well nourished.” I leave feeling lighter and more grounded—and I instinctively skip the Tube and walk home.

#6541. All Aboard Fashion’s Absurd Hat Train

Swim caps and train conductor hats: The runway’s most theatrical headwear is made for standing out.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Fashion can’t get enough of freaky hats lately. Following the main character hat trend from a few seasons past, this time headwear has gone totally theatrical and over-the-top. Between Chanel’s fin-embellished Nemo-esque swim caps and Junya Watanabe’s super camp, oversize ’70s baker-boy-style caps, headpieces are seemingly obsessed with transforming their wearers into outlandish personas. And at a time when clothing is centered on escapism and storytelling, an eccentric chapeau might just be the most perfect finishing touch.

Simone Rocha’s sequin-embellished bonnets with chin straps might turn you into a living doll. Celebs, too, have already gotten the memo: Elle Fanning recently wore a Stephen Jones-designed makeup compact headpiece to match her Givenchy dress inspired by an archival piece he created over three decades ago, while doing press for The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping. Elsewhere, Cardi B showed up in a white embellished gown from Tamara Ralph’s spring 2026 couture collection, styled with a huge, showgirl-style feather hat. Ciara walked the Junya Watanabe spring/summer 2027 runway while wearing a bedazzled helmet dripping with chains.

At Vaquera’s spring/summer 2027 show titled “I’m a put-on-a-show kind of girl,” the neon high-octane gowns were counterbalanced with huge, satirical boater hats, followed by a weird and whimsical chef hat and maid headpiece paired with shrunken, mini bloomer uniform onesies. Adding more humor to the collection, the designers ended the show by performing a live karaoke version of Sonny & Cher’s “I Got You Babe.” The brand is the king of the theatrical character hat. For fall/winter 2026, it showcased pillbox-style hats that eclipsed the face with cutouts for the eyes, fencing-mask-inspired headwear, and an elongated train conductor hat that resembles a cross between The Rockettes Toy Soldier costumes and English bearskin caps.

Transforming is exactly the point: “Vaquera has always celebrated fashion’s transformative power,” read Vaquera’s show notes. “The collection confronts the tension between perfection and chaos. Can you be unhinged and complete at once? Its cast of characters—distorted drab mods, twisted ladies who lunch, abstracted leather daddies—all seem to suggest that the most covetable clothes for your future are those that mirror our fractured present.”

While years of the past were defined by singular aesthetics, 2026 lacks one solo homogeneous style. Formality, too, has been traded for casual looks. Hats used to be ubiquitous; now they’re sort of a rare dying breed, save for a baseball cap.

Perhaps that’s one of the reasons why these character-driven hats are so prevalent now. Many of them are tied to uniforms, occupations, or the everyday made extreme. It’s beautiful absurdism, verging on delightfully unhinged. Consider an over-the-top hat pure whimsy.

#6540. The Year Fashion Fakes Became Too Real

Fashion has a reality problem. Celebrities can be seen wearing clothes they’ve never touched, luxury houses may appear to release products they’ve never designed, and, in some cases, even clothes that actually exist don’t quite look like themselves online.

Earlier this month, the embattled Nvidia co-founder and now reinstated CEO Jensen Huang became an unlikely menswear sensation when the Instagram account @hidden.ny posted images of him wearing an archival, silver-studded Saint Laurent leather jacket from Hedi Slimane’s tenure. The post came just a day after Nvidia opened an investigation into Huang’s alleged affair with a suspected Chinese spy. “Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang in Hedi Slimane SLP Studded Leather Jacket after admitting to affair with alleged Chinese spy,” read the caption.

The internet rushed to crown Huang a Hedi boy, but he’d never worn the jacket. As CNN first revealed, the images were fake; Vanity Fair subsequently verified they’d been generated or altered using AI. The originals, in fact, showed Huang wearing Dior at an airport in Seoul in June. The post was subsequently taken down, but the fantasy had already traveled.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang waves to the media as he arrives at Gimpo airport in Seoul on June 5, 2026. Photo: Jung Yeon-je / AFP via Getty Images

Days later, designers including Reese Cooper and Gerrit Jacob called out luxury retailer Ssense over product imagery that misrepresented their clothes, from distorted construction details to inaccurate branding. Unlike Huang’s fictional fashion moment, these were real garments available to buy.

Cooper, founder of Reese Cooper and RC Outdoor Supply, discovered the inaccuracies while browsing the website himself. He had not been consulted about the imagery, which depicted his brand’s signature trademarked hook at twice its actual size.

“There’s a lot of sewing and design detail inaccuracies but the important issue is misrepresenting my trademarks — our hook is a major part of our branding, and of course all of the logos,” Cooper says. “The initial reaction is disappointment and frustration. It takes an overwhelming amount of time and resources to protect your brand legally with these trademarks, not to mention the work going into designing the clothes themselves.”

The errors were subtler than AI signifiers of the past, like extra fingers or missing limbs. But when shopping online, details matter. Fashion commentator and journalist Odunayo Ojo identified missing design details and Gerrit Jacob trousers with an invented waistband, additional seams and altered lettering.

“AI pulls everything toward an average, but design lives in the details that depart from that average,” Ojo says. “Generative models are built to make something that looks plausible, not something that’s precise. Plausible is fine for a moodboard. On a product page, plausible is misrepresentation.”

In a statement to Vogue Business, a spokesperson for Ssense acknowledged the errors: “Accurate representation of our brand partners and their products is fundamental to Ssense. We recognize that some recent e-commerce imagery did not meet that standard, resulting in inaccuracies in product details. We take full accountability and have taken steps to resolve this issue with urgency.”

It comes after local media reported over the summer that Ssense had laid off its full-time photography and retouching teams as it invested in AI Virtual Try-On (VTON) in August to support content production and has since strengthened quality controls. The spokesperson for Ssense confirmed to Vogue Business that “in preparation for the transition to Virtual Try-On (VTON), Ssense made organizational changes in June that affected certain roles within its visual content department.” Ssense did not explicitly confirm that the AI technology caused the inaccuracies last week.

Together, the incidents exposed two sides of fashion’s growing synthetic image problem: AI can make an imaginary garment look real, and a real garment look imaginary, with both able to put brands in a difficult spot.

The Huang images were far from an isolated incident. In April, AI-generated images showed celebrities including Megan Fox and Robert Pattinson wearing fictional Balenciaga designs made from cardboard shipping boxes, while another fake imagined the Olsen twins in a Louis Vuitton campaign.

Nor was Ssense the only case of AI imagery creating confusion around real products. In May, after Swatch and Audemars Piguet teased a collaboration, AI-generated images of a colorful Royal Oak wristwatch circulated online. The actual release was a collection of Bioceramic pocket watches, disappointing fans who had come to expect a product that never existed.

While the average person has struggled to distinguish many AI-generated images from real photographs for a couple of years, experts say things seem worse now because it’s become so much easier to produce them. “It’s now at the point where it’s really easy to create highly realistic content with minimal knowledge of how to optimize for the tool you’re using, and there’s plenty of tools to choose from,” says Henry Ajder, a synthetic media expert and founder of Latent Space Advisory, pointing to their integration into popular chatbots and the growing availability of open-source alternatives.

Fashion is particularly exposed. “With fashion imagery, because there’s so much highly stylized, high-quality content associated with the industry, there’s been a huge amount of training data for these tools to utilize,” Ajder says, arguing that we’ve reached a tipping point. In 2026, unofficial campaigns can now look practically indistinguishable from a house’s own advertising, even as brands experiment with AI themselves.

For Cooper, the Ssense episode has created a commercial dilemma. “Simply put, it’s brand damage,” he says. “RC Outdoor Supply is a new company and all we have is our trademarks and reputation of design aesthetic and quality. To have these things put in question by the customer, it really erodes trust for the brand as a whole.”

He points out that retailers judge brands on sell-through, and inaccurate listings can deter purchases or generate returns, while removing them means losing sales altogether. “Ssense has removed the images, which I’m thankful for. However, it also removed the ability for anyone to purchase those items, which will result in low sales when looking at this season’s data,” Cooper says.

Experts say the problem is particularly acute in luxury, where small design decisions and fit often underpin a garment’s value. “In luxury, the details are the price,” Ojo says. “If the image erases them, you’ve erased the reason the garment costs what it costs — the problem isn’t AI as a tool, it’s using it for the one job where accuracy is the whole point.”

An accurate image of Reese Cooper’s Outdoor Supply Sierra Puffer Jacket. Photo: Screenshot, rcoutdoorsupply.com, courtesy of Reese Cooper.

Wholesale contracts, meanwhile, haven’t caught up. “When a retailer’s AI imagery misrepresents a garment, the designer absorbs the returns and the reputational harm, and most of the wholesale agreements I review do not address AI-generated product imagery,” says Shermin Lakha, founder and managing attorney at Lvlup Legal.

For luxury brands, the legal questions become more complicated when AI-generated images of their products circulate online without anything being sold, as in the Huang case. Lakha argues that luxury brands have fewer remedies against these non-commercial viral fakes than many might assume. “Existing law is effective against commercial actors and leaves a gap for the viral fake that nobody monetizes,” she says. Susan Scafidi, founder of the Fashion Law Institute at Fordham Law School, agrees legal options are limited. “There is no single, universal cause of action that a brand can invoke to target unauthorized imagery that includes its products, whether that imagery is created by AI or not,” she says. Trademark and false advertising claims may apply where recognizable products or logos are involved; other claims may arise from reputational harm.

The calculation changes if an account uses a brand’s identity to sell services, promote counterfeit goods or generate revenue. The Balenciaga cardboard box images, for example, were associated with an account promoting a course on creating viral AI visuals. But even when brands have grounds to challenge unauthorized imagery, the distinction between infringement and creative expression is rarely straightforward. “Luxury brands have for decades chafed against the imprecise nature of parody and other forms of ‘fair use’ under US law,” says Scafidi.

Daniel Shapiro, a brand protection executive at Red Points, which helps brands detect counterfeits and online impersonation, says traditional monitoring tools that look for logos are increasingly inadequate. Newer systems analyze entire images for unreleased colorways, inaccurate hardware or recognizable patterns, even when logos have been removed.

But policing the internet is only part of the answer. Scafidi urges brands to distinguish harmful images from passing memes to decide whether to take action. When necessary, brands can work with platforms on removals and respond through their own channels. Lakha also recommends tighter contracts and internal verification before brands share viral images.

On brand and retailer sites, Ojo wants human review against physical garments, designer approval and disclosure of AI alterations. “If what’s on the page isn’t a photograph of the real garment, they [a designer] should say so,” he says. “A small [AI] label costs nothing. Finding out later is what causes scandals and also costs Ssense the customer,” he says.

The deeper challenge may be cultural. Luxury has traditionally relied on controlling its image, from campaign casting to the placement of a logo. AI makes that harder, while increasing the value of visual credibility. Lizzie Wheeler, founder of archival bridal salon Studio Dorothy and the resale expert behind the Instagram account @shit.u.should.buy, sees consumers becoming more discerning and brands returning to human craft as a ‘realness’ signal.

“Aside from the legal issues, luxury is moving back toward more organic, human work (like the hand-drawn Prada holiday campaign) and showing AI shortcuts will dissuade a luxury client,” she says. “Ssense does rely heavily on the luxury client and I imagine this type of error will impact them seriously,” she adds.

The irony is that fashion’s most elaborate fakes have often been powered by some of its most recognizable signatures: a Balenciaga provocation, an archival Saint Laurent jacket, an instantly identifiable luxury watch. As these signatures become easier to imitate, the ability to prove what’s real is becoming a more valuable part of luxury itself.

“The consumer is becoming increasingly educated,” Wheeler says. “So I’d advise all retailers against pulling wool over the customer’s eyes.”

#6538. Maple Bourbon Chicken With Brussels Sprouts

If you, like most people, hear the term “bourbon chicken” and have no idea what it is, let me call it by its more common name: toothpick chicken. Yes, the suspiciously delicious chicken shelled out at mall food courts on toothpicks is most likely bourbon chicken. Popular at American Chinese or Cajun-style Chinese restaurants, the sticky-sweet chicken is the utter definition of delicious, luring weary shoppers into food courts to find refuge from the bubblegum pink sweatpants and ripped denim. This version takes cues from the classic but swaps in some autumnal ingredients to make it fit for the season. Charred brussels sprouts leaves and pecans add bulk, while maple syrup and apple cider vinegar give it that delightful tart-sweet flavor we know and love. Serve it over rice or noodles or all by its lonesome for a hearty dinner that will take you back to the '90s.

More chicken dinner winners here: Sheet-Pan Hot Honey Chicken and Peaches; Basil Chicken Stir-Fry; and Ginger-Garlic Chicken and Vegetable Stir-Fry.

Whisk one 1½" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, ⅓ cup bourbon, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, ¼ cup apple cider vinegar, ¼ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes, 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, ¼ cup low-sodium soy sauce, and ½ cup water in a small bowl to combine. Set sauce aside.

Toss 1½ lb. skinless, boneless chicken breasts, halved crosswise, thinly sliced against the grain, remaining 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, and remaining 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce in a medium bowl until chicken is coated; set aside.

Heat 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. brussels sprouts, halved through stems, leaves separated, and cook, stirring very occasionally, until just tender and blackened in spots, about 5 minutes. Transfer to another medium bowl.

Add more oil if pan looks dry and, working in batches if needed, arrange reserved chicken in a single layer and cook, turning occasionally, until golden brown and cooked through, about 5 minutes. Transfer to bowl with brussels sprouts.

Add reserved sauce to same pan and bring to a simmer. Cook, stirring constantly, until thickened, about 1 minute. Remove pan from heat and return brussels sprouts and chicken to pan; top with 1 cup salted roasted pecans, coarsely chopped. Toss to coat in sauce. Serve chicken and brussels sprouts with steamed white rice if desired.

#6537. The Art of the Winter Layer

Use these cold-weather staples from The North Face for practical warmth with polished style.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Like any specialized skill set, winter layering is one that must be continually practiced and perfected, lest your talents wane. It’s not as easy as throwing on a pair of cashmere leggings and a coordinating hoodie—that’s only the beginning. From there, it takes a careful curation of hero pieces (like puffer jackets and parkas), as well as a cast of supporting details (hats, gloves, and high-performance footwear), to layer effectively and aesthetically in the harshest conditions.

That said, even the most adept artist is nothing without an arsenal of trusted creative tools. And in these bitter temps, you’ll want to reach for the best, which essentially means any piece of gear with The North Face’s iconic rectangular logo attached to it. The storied brand has dominated the outdoor space for decades, having perfected the art of elevated style at elevated altitudes.

As we head into the chilliest season of the year, look to The North Face’s vast selection of dependable staples for all your layering needs. Designed both for performance and appearances, these pieces are in it for the long run.

Whether painting or dressing, it’s essential to start any creative endeavor with a blank canvas made of quality materials. A good base should be versatile and simple to pair with a host of helpful staples. Long-sleeve tees, cashmere turtlenecks, and crewneck sweatshirts, for example, are all good jumping-off points.

If you’re looking for a high-performance piece with enough style power to stand on its own, we recommend the Women’s Chabot 2.0 Mock-Neck. This cozy layering top offers the same reliable comfort of a traditional insulated thermal with a few modern updates. Though understated by design, its delightfully oversized fit and a funky waffle knit texture make the basic feel intentional and interesting.

For a closer-fitting base, the Women’s Golden Ridge Ribbed Long-Sleeve Tee layers easily under other pieces. Its slim fit and ribbed texture give this practical layer a polished look, while thumbholes at the cuffs add a functional detail. Bonus points for the tee’s anti-odor technology that helps keep the fabric feeling fresh.

Women’s Golden Ridge Ribbed Long-Sleeve Tee

After you’ve selected the first layer, the next stop should be your coat closet. This is where you’ll select the hero of your look. While each piece of the layering puzzle is uniquely important, the power jacket is a non-negotiable. The right iteration should supply a thick layer of warmth, while also doing its part to make the outfit, as a whole, feel cohesive.

Those who crave a more subdued winter aesthetic will love the classic appeal of the Women’s Arctic Bomber. The waterproof winter jacket boasts all the utility of a parka, with the sleek design details most commonly found in trend-focused outerwear. In four comforting colorways, this winter coat is an insulation powerhouse in a chic, wearable package.

Look to the Women’s Hydrenalite Down Jacket for a more classic puffer. This workhorse is a versatile down layer that can be slipped on at any time to keep you warm for any duration that you spend outdoors, whether you are on the mountain or running around town.

For the more artistically inclined, try the Women’s Yumiori Off Peak Full Zip Jacket. This fleece outer layer offers unfailing warmth and a distinctly sporty flavor. Its two-tone color palette, meanwhile, adds a fun, whimsical feel to the utilitarian, zip-up-style silhouette.

During the summer months, it’s all about the mani-pedi. But once that icy weather blows in, self-care starts to look a bit different. The North Face’s Etip Gloves are basically a hand treatment on the go. Crafted from soft, stretchy fleece made with 93 percent recycled polyester, these tech-friendly gloves will keep your hands comfortable on cold-weather outings. They’ll also keep you connected: Touchscreen compatibility lets you check your phone without taking them off, while silicone grip dots on the palms help you hold onto your device as well as smaller essentials like keys and credit cards.

For footwear, the Women’s THERMOBALL Traction Mule V will quickly become the standout of your seasonal lineup. These cloud-like slip-ons pair warm insulation with a quilted upper that gives them a casual, streetwear-cool vibe. The rubber outsole adds traction for quick trips outdoors.

The minimalist philosophy requires you to take off one item before leaving the house. But during the cold weather season, it’s in your best interest to do the opposite. As you walk out the door, make sure you grab a beanie since most of your body heat can escape from your head.

Beanies are simultaneously the most underappreciated outfit addition and the most indispensable. The North Face’s Wool Blend Beanie, for instance, pairs the warmth of its 65 percent merino wool knit with a refined, metropolitan style. Its classic cuffed design and textured knit add visual interest, while its deep fit offers roomier coverage. If you prefer the rectangular logo with the same cuffed look, you can never go wrong with the rib-knit and soft lining of the Salty Lined Beanie. On the slopes or on your morning commute, either will add a polished finishing touch.

The importance of a functional winter hat cannot be overstated—think of it as the final brushstroke in the art of winter layering.

#6536. What The Altruists Gets Right About Tech Scammers Like Sam Bankman-Fried

The math holding up Netflix’s The Altruists is simple. Anthony Boyle plays currently imprisoned one-time cryptocurrency king Sam Bankman-Fried, and Julia Garner plays Caroline Ellison, fellow momentary crypto royal and Bankman-Fried’s one-time romantic partner. Both actors cook so fearlessly that the show’s shortcomings recede into the background. What you’re left with is a tidy sum: two excellent performances that offer rich, vatic examinations of real-life figures. From these visions of Bankman-Fried and Ellison we get a glimpse into a crime and into a psychology.

Famously, no bankers were sent to prison in the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis. No suit from Countrywide Financial walked the yard in Lompoc. But Samuel Bankman-Fried did go to prison after being found guilty of wire fraud and conspiracy. For the Bloomberg set, his trial was covered as intensely as O.J. Simpson’s, and each day of it hit trip wires: polycules, blockchain, non-fiat currency, etc.

One of the threads in the journalism about the crimes, and on The Altruists, is that our power couple did not feel good in fancy spaces. But unlike the protagonists of so many other shows and movies from the tech-disruptor-story boom of the past 15 years, neither Boyle’s SBF nor Garner’s Ellison lean into rage.

On The Altruists, SBF and his inner circle frequent a Margaritaville in the Bahamas. They seem happy there, or at least at home. To be wildly rich, extremely young, and crushing vegan nachos at Jimmy Buffett’s theme restaurant is a choice made out of avoidance.

The show’s first episodes make clear the overlaps between Ellison and Bankman-Fried. They were true math minds surrounded by the glib Wharton crowd, goofs with board games. They were not-conventionally-attractive people in an industry where many people are quite hot, and where the primarily hot at least know which regression tool best fits what task.

The Altruists’s versions of SBF and Ellison found love in a hopeless place. Boyle interviews Garner for a position at Jane Street and they realize they have the exact same investment strategy—all in, all the time. If you didn’t know better, you’d be rooting for these two off-putting lovebirds to make a go of it.

Boyle’s performance mesmerizes. He seems to have control over his lashes, so completely articulated is his eye acting. His whole posture changes as he takes up different roles in the story: a curious loser, a gifted rhetorician, an anxious boss, an ignored former lover. The show shifts from alienation in New York to crypto adventures in Hong Kong to the office-dorm hybrid of “The Orchid” in the Bahamas. Boyle owns the physical transformations, letting the glee of the Hong Kong era fester into the eyebags and stress-weight accrued (probably one of the more ethical uses of a bodysuit I can recall) in the scheme’s last days.

Garner, meanwhile, has entered rarified air as a TV actor. Over the course of her career she has given us a moody, adrift Gen X student (Kimmy on The Americans), a Millennial lady of rage trapped in her dumpy hometown (Ozark), and now two glimpses of the self-satisfied Zillenial scammer (Anna Delvey in Inventing Anna and The Altruists). Garner’s signature move as a performer is to fail to sublimate anger or distress. Her characters have their own idiosyncratic patterns of twitches and attempts at steely gazes. The brittle darkness inside each of them sings. Her TV career belongs next to those of Elisabeth Moss and America Ferrera and Walton Goggins. It is time that this was generally acknowledged.

The supporting cast is solid, with one particular highlight. In the middle of The Altruist’s eight-episode run, we get an entire episode focused on Sam Trabucco, a college bestie of SBF, a former Alameda Research co-CEO, and an early cooperator with federal prosecutors once the wheels started falling off.

Alex Lawther plays Trabucco and almost walks off with the show. Lawther’s slight frame and self-searching candor give each line of dialogue intimacy. I first saw Lawther on Andor, playing Nemik, idealistic proto-Rebel and truest of true believers, a character based on Lei Feng, the Chinese communist folk hero and soldier, who, like Nemik on Andor, died in a freak accident but left behind a diary of such pure faith that it became a recruitment tool for the revolution. (A recording of Lawther reading that manifesto from his diary—his voice reedy and prophetic—literally haunts Imperial high command at the end of Andor.)

In maybe my favorite scene of The Altruists, Trabucco and Ellison get dinner together. They talk and realize their childhood paths intersected and diverged across metro Boston—the same math competitions, the same tests. But their hometowns were quite different. She was from Newton. He was from Natick. If you’re from New England, that’s the only detail you need. (If you aren’t, I recommend Love Story and/or the novels of Dennis Lehane for background.) At that dinner, Lawther shares a deep, specific childhood memory of his father and Garner’s Caroline flinches without breaking eye contact, like she’s watching a recording of a natural disaster.

Sadly, the Netflix sins are here in full effect. The lighting is smeary and wildly off in many scenes. The music and sound mix could hardly be blunter. Even Oscar-nominated showrunner Graham Moore and talented directors like James Ponsoldt can’t lift dialogue that not-infrequently feels tailored to second-screen viewers: “They’re both off-the-charts math geniuses!”

The braided narrative can turn single episodes into distracting puzzle boxes. The form is designed to function the way a big juicy 10,000-word legacy-media reported feature does: You know the ending, so it takes a memorable reshuffling of moments and incidents to create something new.

But watching this gang of true believers and opportunists and criminally naïve teenage dream brains go from geographic zone to zone does carry emotional import. To them, and to The Altruists, the Bay Area has become a dated country club, a mirror image of The Social Network’s version of Harvard from the 2000s, back when the Bay Area promised something fresh. Post-Recession New York is greyscale normie central. Hong Kong and Macau blur together. The show ends in the Bahamas, a place that rich outsiders have always treated as both Eden and the afterlife.

I think the era of the tech-bro-scammer-titan show and movie is reaching its end. If its dawn was The Social Network, the unrepeatable, mesmerizing You Can See Everything might be the sunset. Gen X icons Aaron Sorkin and David Fincher once tried to get their heads around millennial narcissism and now millennial genius Nathan Fielder has transformed his time with a real-deal apex-predator narcissist into a Möbius strip of content.

The drama of The Altruists depends on the psychology of the people who believe in crypto as a kind of syncretic faith. The show avoids a technical delineation of crypto itself, which makes sense. (I’ve yet to encounter a crypto evangelist who can provide a transparent explanation of the asset class that is superior to this.) ExxonMobil sells you a product and it works. Glock sells you a product and it works. Crypto works in so much as its existence justifies its existence. There are no earnings reports. Value is vibes.

Whenever something is being marketed as the future, it’s usually just the past, accelerated. People made crypto into an alternative financial system because they were “outsiders” who wanted to “disrupt.” Now the crypto system wants to be held close to the bosom of the enduring US financial markets and bulge bracket banks. A bill that would have brought them closer, setting up a regulatory framework, nose-dived in the senate.

It sounds almost cowardly, like running home to mom and dad: We made a brave new thing better and cooler and freer than your corrupt old monetary system. A few years later: Let us back in and give us all the benefits of the old system! Get us in your PNC digital wallet, normie!

Bankman-Fried and Ellison are both the children of elite academics. To its credit, The Altruists pokes these Freudian pains. Bankman-Fried was raised by Stanford Law professors and chose MIT. Ellison was the child of MIT academics and chose Stanford. There’s self-belief in those exact choices. The children of faculty get a significant leg up in gaining admission at their parents’ institution. SBF and Ellison wanted to do something honest on their own, at least once.

My parents are retired professors. You learn early on that you cannot possibly replicate your parents’ careers. A child of a lawyer can have their parent’s career 2.0. Same if you have doctors for parents. But truly successful academics—and given the market today, you either are truly successful or you don’t exist—create niches built only for one.

Successful academics eschew any number of linear career paths and lucrative fields to burrow into zones of learning where they have to be singular, own every network and endure any marginal post (Oregon State, thou hast thy music, too). To make it to a top institution, you need luck and power and timing to dovetail your own research record and professional charisma. Many people make it to powerful banks and hospitals and law firms. But if you manage to get tenure at Berkeley, you might really be that special.

The track record of the children of academics I know is messy: deluded guys floating around Portland or Boston trying to jam their unreadable YA series into the world, an acquaintance who self-sabotaged a promising, morally-clear career as a social worker because they did not get a doctorate and let that arbitrary marker of value smother their self-worth for decades.

SBF and Ellison were expected to perform precocity at all times, but the minute that they stumbled, Dr. Mom or Professor Dad stepped in with the better therapists and better lawyers to set everything right. The last two episodes of The Altruists bubble over with dread. Paul Reiser and Robin Weigert play SBF’s parents, and Jennifer Grey plays Caroline Ellison’s mom. Each performance puts its own spin on enmeshment and infantilization. The parents are not the big bads here. But they are the judgmental elitists who analyzed when they should have listened, and who raised these world-class scammers.

There was a guy a little like me in high school. Like me, he was the child of academics and teachers. Like me, he was clever and capable, which might have been enough in another high school. But such minor skills were door prizes in our grand, old, dizzyingly competitive boarding school. We both loved De La Soul. We were both cut from the same teams. We were both contrarians who trafficked in equal measures of insight and anserine bullshit. I won’t pretend to have been good friends with the guy—it was the classic situation where young men who play similar roles in their respective circles repel each other like the same sides of different magnets. But I sympathized. It’s painful to know exactly why you are not near the top of an elite ecosystem and then having to go on living in it.

I imagined he might have a career adjacent to mine. I imagined that we might see each other in the late 2000s at a Babygrande Records release party or in the bathroom at Santos Party House. It did not play out that way. A few years ago, during the inevitable age-related transition from Facebook to LinkedIn, the guy’s face and name swum across my screen. He’s become a big deal in the crypto space. At one point, he rapped about crypto on crypto podcasts. On a class-wide group chat, as former classmates who had chosen to work in community health settings or on federally-funded research projects shared their pain after losing their jobs in the DOGE cuts, and as they voiced their concerns about what other digits of the American experiment would be severed next, this crypto dude commandeered the chat to brag about taking his company public. No child of an academic has ever missed a chance to make it about them.

One of the side effects of the world-gobbling narratives around A.I. (which gets its own Social Network moment in Luca Guadagnino’s imminent Artificial, with Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman) is that crypto already feels cringe—at best, a chrome decoration on the world-shaking machinery of LLMs and Deep Learning. The brave new world of private money that needed no society and no army behind it has become just another widget. The most vulgar people in the world trade meme coins with Turkish billionaire failsons. That Uber driver for whom you had great sympathy waits forever for a crypto ship that will never come into port. (Bankman-Fried, as it happens, was an early investor in Anthropic; it was reported last week that his shares, liquidated during FTX's bankruptcy, would be worth $35 to $37 billion in the wake of the AI lab's splashy IPO.)

If 2026 is the close of the tech-movie and tech-show era, then how do we square The Altruists? It has arrived at the end of something. It’s not perfect, maybe not even excellent, but it is effective and memorable, and provides a showcase for superb young actors. I wonder how many of these shows about tech founders, disruptors, optimists, hustlers and misanthropes will last. The paranoia of 70s American film evaporated in the desert of 80s escapism and the wry smirk of Ronnie Reagan. The thorny, violent prestige TV era begat the soft-clothes forever-childhood of Stranger Things and of Ted Lasso. Legacy cannot be legislated in advance. I hope viewers check out The Altruists, and appreciate its gumption in allowing love—the least efficient of emotions—to animate the story.

But maybe I’m wrong. Maybe I’ve been hustled by Boyle and Garner’s wonderful acting. Maybe my almost-instinct about the past 15 years of watching damaged young ladder-climbers and their digital dreams on screen is almost true: what will survive of us is coins.

#6535. The Vogue Business AI Tracker

The Vogue Business AI Tracker keeps a record of the most important AI developments that will influence our industry and our world, each week. From venture capital investments and startup launches to product drops and regulatory updates, we’ll make sure you never miss a beat when it comes to the AI news that matters.

The news: Meta is introducing virtual try-on to its Muse AI shopping agent

Why it matters: Meta is introducing a virtual clothing try-on feature to Muse, the personal AI agent it launched in September. The new feature, announced on X by Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer, will offer shoppers AI-generated previews of how garments might look on them before they buy. “Trying things on in person? As if…” Wang wrote on X, in a nod to the 1995 film Clueless.

Muse can already discover products, navigate checkout and make purchases on users’ behalf, subject to their approval. Adding virtual try-on brings Meta another step closer to controlling the entire shopping journey, from inspiration to purchase. But the technology also raises familiar questions about the accuracy of AI-generated clothing imagery and how much personal data consumers are willing to share.

The news: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO, sending shares soaring

Why it matters: Nvidia has reinstated co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO just 11 days after his resignation following his admission of marital infidelity and reports of a relationship with a woman suspected by US intelligence of being a Chinese spy. The board voted unanimously to bring him back, saying it was satisfied with his leadership and that his return posed no national security risk. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment [...] I can’t wait to get back to work,” Huang said in an official statement.

Shares surged as much as 33% in early trading, underscoring investors’ faith in Huang’s leadership of the AI chipmaker. An independent investigation into his conduct remains ongoing, while Nvidia has announced additional national security and compliance oversight.

The news: J.Crew launches AI stylist built on Anthropic’s Claude.

Why it matters: J.Crew is the latest luxury brand to introduce an AI-powered shopping assistant. Built on Anthropic’s Claude, its new “Style Advisor” helps customers put together outfits based on occasions, personal preferences and specific items, drawing on the brand’s styling archives and campaign imagery.

The launch reflects a growing push among fashion retailers to make online shopping more conversational and personalized, as brands look to keep customers within their own digital ecosystems, rather than lose product discovery to third-party AI platforms. It comes a week after Prada became the first luxury brand to launch a dedicated plugin with ChatGPT, and follows Ralph Lauren’s push into branded AI personal styling last year with its “Ask Ralph” white-label AI styling tool.

The news: Natural Cycles launches its own fertility-tracking smart ring.

Why it matters: Natural Cycles is launching its first smart ring, moving beyond its existing partnership with Oura into its own wearable hardware. The new “NC Ring” measures body temperature overnight, feeding data into the company’s AI-powered fertility algorithm, which uses machine learning to calculate daily fertility status for its hormone-free contraceptive app.

The move puts Natural Cycles into competition with Oura, whose CEO Tom Hale told Vogue Business that women’s health features have been a significant driver of growth as the company moves towards a much-anticipated IPO. Unlike the Oura integration, which requires subscriptions to both services, NC Ring works with a Natural Cycles subscription alone. The company says around 80% of its active users already track their temperature using a wearable, giving it an established customer base for its own hardware.

The news: Pre-orders for Gentle Monster’s Google smart glasses are already sold out.

Why it matters: All 16 styles of Gentle Monster’s new AI smart glasses, developed with Google and Samsung, have sold out their initial pre-order allocations just days after launching, despite prices starting at $449. It’s a surprising sign that fashion-forward design could help win over consumers who might otherwise be reluctant to wear a computer on their face. Notably, most of Google’s more conventional Warby Parker styles remain available.

Gentle Monster’s sellout suggests that distinctive design could be a powerful draw, even as the surveillance debate remains unresolved. The caveat? Neither Google nor Gentle Monster has disclosed how many pairs were available to pre-order, making it difficult to gauge the scale of demand.

The news: Gentle Monster taps Joaquin Phoenix to front its Google AI Glasses.

Why it matters: Gentle Monster unveiled a campaign starring Joaquin Phoenix for its forthcoming AI-powered glasses, developed with Google and Samsung. Directed by filmmaker Jonathan Glazer, the short film will debut in mid-November, ahead of the collection’s December launch. (Pre-orders open on November 12.) The glasses, first previewed at Google I/O in May, run on Google’s Android XR platform and integrate its Gemini assistant, offering features including real-time translation, navigation and hands-free photography.

The launch marks a significant step in Google’s return to smart eyewear, adding competition to Meta’s established Ray-Ban partnership. Google has also teamed up with Warby Parker, while Kering is developing AI glasses with Google for Gucci. Gentle Monster’s decision to enlist Phoenix and Glazer is yet another sign that fashion credibility and cultural positioning are central to Big Tech rivals’ attempts to win the smart glasses race.

The news: Amazon launches SMS-based AI shopping agent after blocking Meta’s Muse.

Why it matters: Amazon has begun testing an expanded version of its AI shopping agent, Alexa for Shopping, among a small group of US customers over text. The new SMS feature lets shoppers search for and compare products, send photographs to find similar items, track prices and complete purchases without opening Amazon’s website or app.

The move reflects a broader shift toward making every consumer touchpoint shoppable, from social media and search engines to messaging. As AI agents become accessible through everyday interactions, the distinction between browsing, asking for advice and making a purchase could become increasingly blurred. For luxury brands, the challenge is not just where their products are sold, but how they appear in shopping conversations that take place beyond their own channels.

Amazon’s decision to block Meta Muse from accessing its marketplace in September also suggests that retailers want to extend their own reach without necessarily ceding control of discovery to competitors.

The news: Zalando unveils plans for AI shopping agent that can buy from other retailers.

Why it matters: Zalando has announced plans for a new AI shopping agent that will allow customers to purchase products from other retailers without leaving its app. Called Zalando Extended, the service is being piloted with homeware retailer Westwing, with AI-powered checkout scheduled to officially launch in 2027. The agent will eventually be able to complete purchases on shoppers’ behalf, expanding Zalando’s offering beyond the products it sells directly. The move builds on its existing conversational AI assistant, which has attracted more than 22 million unique users this year, according to Zalando’s Q3 earnings update.

The retailer’s plans follow a similar move by Amazon, whose Buy for Me feature allows customers to purchase products from external retailers through its shopping app. Both point to a potentially significant change in the marketplace model: rather than requiring brands and retailers to list their products on a platform, AI agents could facilitate purchases directly from their own websites.

For brands, this could open up new routes to customers without the usual marketplace integrations, while raising questions about who controls product discovery and the customer relationship. For Zalando, it offers a way to expand its assortment without holding additional stock, while keeping shoppers within its own ecosystem.

Why it matters: Prada has launched a ChatGPT plugin allowing users in the US, the UK and Italy to discover products, explore collections and find stores using information sourced directly from the brand. As AI assistants become a gateway to product discovery, the move gives Prada a more authoritative presence in conversations it might otherwise struggle to influence. “Conversational experiences represent a natural evolution of traditional e-commerce,” said Prada Group digital director Laura Campanella. “Through this pilot initiative, we are exploring a new territory for customer engagement.”

The news coincides with the launch of Prada’s Christmas campaign this week, featuring hand-drawn animation by Disney veteran John Pomeroy. These two contrasting moves reflect a broader distinction emerging in luxury: AI for product discovery, and human craftsmanship for consumer-facing brand storytelling.

The news: Anthropic’s IPO filing reveals the huge costs and risks of the AI boom.

Why it matters: Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO filing offers a rare look inside the economics — and extraordinary risks — of the AI industry. As the Claude AI maker prepares for a potential $2 trillion valuation, the Financial Times reports that its revenues exceeded $33 billion in the first nine months of 2026, while its computing costs have fallen dramatically relative to sales, all suggesting a path to profitability. Yet Anthropic has also committed more than $800 billion to computing infrastructure through 2045, much of it supplied by technology giants including Amazon and Google, who are also major investors.

Crucially, the prospectus devotes 92 pages to risks, warning that future AI models could resist shutdown, manipulate information or cause harm too large for insurers to cover. For businesses embedding AI into everything from creative production to customer service, the filing exposes a central contradiction: the technology is becoming commercially indispensable even as its developers acknowledge profound uncertainty over its long-term risks.

The news: Anthropic plans European AI consultancy.

Why it matters: Anthropic is reportedly partnering with private equity firm Hg to launch a European consultancy that’ll place AI engineers and advisers in external businesses to help them integrate Anthropic’s technology, according to the Financial Times. Expected to launch by the end of 2026, hubs are currently planned in London and Berlin, with the Claude developer likely using the venture to accelerate corporate AI adoption — and even capture some of the work traditionally handled by consultancies such as Accenture and the Big Four.

Fashion and luxury businesses, many of which are still grappling with how to deploy AI, could be fertile ground for these services. But the model raises an obvious tension: while companies may welcome direct access to AI expertise, how independent can the advice be when the consultancy is backed by a company with a commercial interest in driving adoption of its own technology?

The news: Anthropic launches Claude Duet AI agent to rival OpenAI and Meta.

Why it matters: Anthropic has released Claude Duet, an AI agent rivaling Meta’s consumer-focused Muse and OpenAI’s more enterprise-oriented Dots; the Duet has both brand and consumer use cases for fashion. It can purchase products on consumers’ behalf using Shopify’s Shop Pay and Stripe Link, while merchants can instruct the agent to set up, design and manage their Shopify stores, including inventory and orders, Anthropic announced in a blog post. Meanwhile, a “richer visual editor” — which allows brands to design and preview their storefronts within the agent’s interface before anything goes live — is “coming soon”.

It was only a matter of time until Anthropic followed Meta and OpenAI in launching a personal AI assistant. Now, the battle is on between these tech companies to capture both consumer and brands’ trust, so that the integration these agents depend on across stores and payment providers is realized. The growing competition here signals a shift towards AI-mediated purchases, potentially reducing direct customer interactions for brands and making product visibility and seamless checkout across AI platforms increasingly important.

The news: Major banks and retailers block AI shopping agents like Meta Muse.

Why it matters: A growing list of US banks and retailers are blocking AI agents like Meta Muse and Instinct from acting on their websites. Amazon and Ebay have both prohibited these models from browsing or purchasing items on their respective marketplaces, while Citigroup, Bank of America, JPMorgan and Charles Schwab have each moved to prevent outside agents from logging into customer accounts and transacting on their behalf.
