#6457. How One Live-Wire Stylist Puts His Meta Glasses to Work on Set

When Meta announced the latest generation of its genre-defining smart glasses, the response from the fashion industry was, well, kind of tepid. Wearable technology has a shaky track record, after all, and we’ve been down a similar road before. (Google Glass, we hardly knew thee.) To win over folks more fluent in Ai Weiwei than AI, Meta would have to fulfill a much trickier mandate than simply developing a groundbreaking product: it’d have to develop a product that looks good while doing the ground breaking.

So when I got the chance to put Meta Glasses to the test during a typically frenetic day on set shooting for GQ, I didn’t hold back. It helps, obviously, that they actually look cool—especially the limited-edition pair I requested, a collaboration with the chart-topping Blackpink member LISA. Now, though, I’m convinced of their genuine, potentially game-changing utility, too. Here’s how I put the Meta Glasses by LISA through the paces of my chaotic 9-to-5, and emerged all the less stressed for it.

On shoot days, I make a point of arriving on set an hour before our model so I can lock in our looks with minimal distraction. The clothes on the racks, though, tend to play second fiddle to the clothes on me, at least when it comes to my AM fit check. (Like a true sicko, I wore a fluorescent Prada jacket to match the pink tint on my special-edition, LISA-designed Meta Glasses.)

Without fail, every shoot I’ve been on comes together very dynamically—read: absolutely last minute. So even though we boarded each look weeks ago, and styled them all out yesterday afternoon, no fewer than 15-ish items arrived that morning. To sort through them, I tell Meta to put on the new Sophia Stel album so I can lock in and land on the right roster of looks.

The looks have been landed on—it’s time to present them to the team. GQ commerce director Michael Nolledo—the magnanimous Miranda Priestly of the entire operation, if you will—is off-site for the day, so I tell Meta to video call him for approval. He can now see what I see, and I stay totally hands-free.

During the run through, I describe each look down to its socks, clarifying the logic behind my styling decisions with near-comical specificity. (Yes, that minuscule sliver of waffle thermal peeking out from beneath that fleece is, in fact, transformative and entirely nonnegotiable!) I tend to love this part of the day because the looks always end up in a sometimes-different-always-better place once the braintrust has weighed in—and tempered some of my, uh, kookier impulses.

It doesn’t matter how nice the clothes look hanging limply on the rack: they don’t really come to life (or die in front of your very eyes) until you get them on the guy. Luckily, our guy for the day is Gabriel, whose easy, unaffected chill makes everything we put him in look effortlessly incredible.

As we noodle on a few minor alternations (bringing in a suit jacket just-so; adding hefty cuffs to a pair of appropriately hefty trousers), I have Meta snap a photo of each look in its final form. On my command, Meta then sends those photos to Michael and GQ senior editor Avidan Grossman—my closest collaborator on set and our in-house tailoring geek—who has final say on all things pleated pants, dimpled ties, and more. Once Meta beams out the fitting photos, it’s speak now or forever hold your peace.

The next six hours are a frenetic blur, set to a fittingly chaotic blend of ‘80s pop hits and Tate McRae (it’s all about balance, really). Beth, our prodigiously talented photographer for the day, becomes my partner, as we both try to ensure Gabriel ignores the camera as much as possible. The best photos happen when the guy forgets he’s being photographed—like we’re capturing a genuine moment of relaxed solitude.

Problem is, when I’m laser-focused on all that, I hate pulling out my phone to capture content of my own. So the option to have Meta snap a fast photo or record a snippet of video is kind of a godsend.

We made it, folks. Three green teas, four minor hand injuries, and 18 or so looks later, it’s time for the fun part: reviewing the photos, and duking it out over which of them will make the final cut. There really is no greater satisfaction than seeing a slapdash deck of product flats transform into an all-killer, no-filler album of actual outfits.

Because I have no patience (and am beaming with so much pride it's nearly blinding), I have Meta snap a few shots of my favorite moments and then post them to my IG story. The official GQ story won’t run for a few weeks, so I like to think of my story as an unofficial teaser of sorts. We pack up and roll our racks out of the studio and back into the fashion closet, where I promptly ask Meta for directions to the closest bar.

#6454. Gravy-Braised Turkey

Cooking a whole turkey is a commitment. Between the schlepping, trussing, and constant babysitting, it’s a serious investment—and one that doesn’t always pay dividends. For a more laid-back affair, and one that practically guarantees success, might we suggest turkey legs cooked directly in gravy? Yes, in the gravy.

This recipe will defy everything you have probably done to cook a turkey until now. The first important step is searing the whole turkey legs for optimal browning. Now you are ready to create a base for the gravy with all those drippings and toasty bits left in the pot. No need to make a full-on roux either: Just sprinkle in the flour over the melted fat, whisk to combine, and slowly pour in the broth. Once the gravy is done, in goes the turkey and aromatics for braising. The rest is you worrying about something else, because that turkey will cook itself.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Season 4 whole turkey legs (thigh and drumstick; about 6½ lb. total), patted dry, all over with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper. Heat 3 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large braiser or Dutch oven over medium-high. Working in 2 batches if needed to avoid overcrowding, arrange turkey legs, skin side down, in pot and cook, undisturbed, rotating pan on burner a few times to ensure even browning, until browned underneath and they easily release from pot, 8–12 minutes. Transfer turkey legs to a rimmed baking sheet, arranging skin side up. (No need to brown other side; turkey will still be raw at this point.)

Add more oil if pot looks dry; arrange 2 large oranges and/or lemons, halved, and 2 heads of garlic, tops trimmed to expose cloves, cut side down in pot and add 3 large shallots, peeled. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 2–3 minutes. Transfer each to baking sheet with turkey as they are done (it’s okay if some fall apart slightly).

Add 6 Tbsp. (¾ stick) unsalted butter to pot and cook until melted. Sprinkle in ⅓ cup (42 g) all-purpose flour and cook, stirring constantly, until no pockets of dry flour remain, about 1 minute. Gradually pour in 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth, stirring constantly to combine. Bring to a simmer and cook until gravy is just starting to thicken, about 2 minutes. Stir in 3 Tbsp. Worcestershire sauce and season with salt and pepper.

Nestle turkey legs into gravy, skin side up, then tuck oranges, garlic, and shallots around, arranging oranges and garlic cut side up. Add 1 small bunch thyme (about 10 sprigs), tied with kitchen twine, and cover pot tightly with a lid or foil. Braise 2 hours. (If your pot is too small to comfortably fit everything, transfer gravy to a 13x9" baking dish before adding turkey legs and aromatics.) Uncover pot and continue to bake until turkey legs are deeply browned, meat shreds easily off the bone, and gravy has thickened a little, 45–55 minutes.

Let turkey and gravy cool slightly before serving. Transfer to a platter if desired. (If gravy has excess fat on top, skim off with a spoon and discard before serving or spooning over legs on platter.)

#6452. Sticky Miso Chicken and More Recipes We Made This Week

It’s no secret that Bon Appétit editors cook a lot for work. So it should come as no surprise that we cook a lot during our off hours too. Here are the recipes we’re whipping up this month to get dinner on the table, entertain our friends, satisfy a sweet tooth, use up leftovers, and everything in between. For even more staff favorites, click here.

My husband and I recently took our 3-year-old daughter apple picking. As expected at the tail end of the season, the only apples left were Granny Smith. A perfect apple for baking, I decided to peruse our new app to see what fit the bill and found Zaynab Issa’s Caramel Apple Snacking Cake. After scanning the instructions, it seemed like a fairly straightforward one-bowl situation—the perfect pace for my lazy Sunday. I grated the apples right into a large bowl, and mixed it with the dry and wet ingredients before baking. The cake is elevated with a quick caramel that gets drizzled on top, which makes it feel fancy. —June Kim, executive editor

Armed with a fresh trio of cumin, coriander, and turmeric from Diaspora Spice Co., I decided to make Alison Roman’s Chicken Tikka Masala. It’s a bit of a project, but the payoff is worth it. The spice-rich sauce takes 30 to 40 minutes, but let it go closer to 40 for something thick, concentrated, and luxurious. Broiling is a genius move: Set on a wire rack, the yogurt-marinated chicken gets air on all sides, so it blackens instead of steaming before being added to the sauce. To accompany the main, we made a side of Priya Krishna’s Aloo Gobi in the air fryer. It came out crispy and caramelized, at least until I coated it in the creamy sauce. —Olivia Tarantino, senior shopping editor

With a name like Just-Keeps-Getting-Better Lentil Salad, how could you go wrong? My former colleague Sarah Jampel’s rightfully beloved recipe is one of those staples I’ve made so many times, I don’t even need to look at it to double-check quantities or instructions anymore. It’s become second nature. And when I’m feeling inspired, or my pantry has seen better days, it’s pretty adaptable too. This week I whipped up a huge bowl with walnuts and cashews in place of the almonds, a blood orange standing in for the lemon, and added some lovely chicories to mingle with the kale. As always, it was crunchy and fresh, tender and filling, even three days after I whipped it up. —Kelsey Jane Youngman, senior cooking editor

I love cookbook author Samantha Seneviratne’s recipes and her recent one for a tahini cake crusted with sesame seeds called to me. Just the thing for a fall weekend. I scaled down the recipe for my 8x8" pan using Kendra Vaculin’s handy conversion guide. And I did a mix of white and black sesame seeds on top for fun. It was plush and not too sweet—great for dessert and even better for breakfast the next day. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director

I’ve been holding on to this recipe for years, and it’s finally time I release it into the world. Be free Sticky Miso Chicken! It’s made with a three-ingredient marinade with stuff you probably already have in your cupboard. Equal parts miso and honey, plus a healthy splash of soy sauce mixed together creates a million-dollar burnished glaze. I slather the marinade onto chicken thighs, but you could also do chicken breast, salmon, shrimp, tofu. Go wild. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking

Every fall I stuff my pantry with cans of pumpkin purée. And fortunately our annual Pumpkin Week tells me exactly what to do with the haul. I’m always in search of more savory uses for the ingredient, and my coworker Jesse Szewczyk’s Pumpkin Black Bean Enchiladas were right up my alley. I did a mix of black and kidney beans (what was around) and I toned down the spice for my toddler who—the universe laughs—refused to eat them anyway, instead opting to smear the sauce all over his clothes. C’est la vie! —Emma Laperruque, cooking director

There is a new vendor at my greenmarket who makes incredible buffalo milk yogurt. My favorite is flavored with tangy, floral passion fruit. It’s not too sweet and works beautifully with fruit and granola. To showcase its power as a sauce, I made David Tamarkin’s apple olive oil cake (baked in an 8" round instead of a loaf) and served the yogurt underneath. For the cake, you shred a couple of apples then squeeze out their juices, which you can then drink for a baker’s treat. —Joe Sevier, senior editor, SEO & cooking

One of my favorite things is to use a banana bread recipe to make muffins and call it meal prep. I pack this gluten-free batter into tins, sprinkle on some flaxseed and pecans, and reduce the bake time. They can easily pass for breakfast, an afternoon snack, or dessert, and the recipe yields enough muffins to be enjoyed throughout the week with a scoop of yogurt or swipe of nut butter. —Kate Kassin, editorial operations manager

With a recipe entitled Bob’s Chicken and Cabbage Salad, I’m sure you’re wondering: Who the heck is Bob? Author Melissa Broder’s late father, who happened to be fervently devoted to purple cabbage. Well, Bob, me too—especially after trying this one. Per the instructions, I chopped up half a head of cabbage, baby bok choy, scallions, bean sprouts, and water chestnuts, then tossed the roughage with pulled chicken. This time around, I did cheat with a store-bought rotisserie bird to jump-start cooking (it was 8 p.m. when I started, okay?). That also meant halving the heavenly soy-ginger dressing, since I no longer needed some of it for the marinade. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking

My Test Kitchen buddy Rebecca Firkser has a wild little pasta up her sleeve that I can’t get enough of: Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates. When she first made it for the team, I was blown away. I would have never thought to throw dates into a pasta, but alas, it’s delicious. Each bite has something sweet, something creamy, a bit of crunch, and endless fun. —Jesse Szewczyk, senior Test Kitchen editor

Since my son started daycare in September, our household has been sick more than it has been healthy. So it makes sense that I have been on a chicken soup kick. I have it for lunch and dinner and drink mugfuls of stock between meals. My latest batch was my colleague Rebecca Firkser’s Toasted Orzo Chicken Soup, which has a beautifully spiced broth and lots of nourishing spinach. It may not be a cure-all, but close enough. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director

Delicata squash should be as popular as butternut. It’s far easier to cut (no hacks or hacking necessary), the thin skin is not only edible but tasty, and it’s got a sweet potato-like flesh that’s creamy and, well, sweet. I usually treat it simply (oil, salt and pepper, hot oven, done), but I treated myself to my former colleague Rachel Gurjar’s gussied-up Roasted Delicata Squash With Crispy Onions and I’m so glad I did. The squash itself takes no extra effort, but gathering up some toppings, like store-bought fried onions tossed with extra spices, juicy pomegranate seeds, and seasoned yogurt, transformed it into a dish I was proud to serve to guests. —Kelsey Jane Youngman, senior cooking editor

We have a new Friday tradition at our house: Pasta Alla Vodka and Caesar salad. Not rocket science, I know, but after a rough-and-tumble week of work and school, we are all reaching for some semblance of comfort. It is also easy enough to whip up that I can often beat the timing of our former Friday tradition, take-out pizza. The Caesar dressing is usually made in advance (I keep a batch in the fridge because my family lurves it) and the pasta of choice is usually rigatoni. It cooks in about the same amount of time as the sauce—I just love when that happens. —Hana Asbrink, deputy food editor

There’s nothing more perfect than a tuna melt. Buttery slices of sourdough or rye that leave a shine of grease on your fingers. Tuna salad mashed into tender flakes, speckled with crisp celery, onion, and herbs. A blanket of American cheese, so stretchy it’ll rival a mozzarella stick. And a mandatory pickle, to offer added tangy solace after each bite. I ate mine with salt-and-vinegar kettle chips stuffed inside because that’s how my favorite diner does it. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking

#6451. HexClad Bakeware Review: This Set Is So Sturdy and Nonstick, I’m Ditching Parchment Paper

As an avid baker, I've been waiting for such a sturdy set.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

Serious bakers will appreciate the hefty, high-quality materials in this 6-piece set. It's also gloriously nonstick.

When I got married a few years ago, I put a cohesive bakeware set on my registry to replace years of mismatched Goodwill finds. While it worked well for a few months, within a year it began to show serious signs of wear and tear. Baked-on grease stains, rust spots and even warping had me in the market for a new bakeware set much sooner than I expected.

So, when I heard that my favorite cookware brand was releasing a bakeware set promising a sturdy, nonstick experience, I jumped at the chance to test it. Here’s everything you need to know about the new HexClad bakeware line, including my honest thoughts after two months of testing.

HexClad’s new hybrid bakeware set features six core pieces:

It merges the benefits of stainless steel and nonstick into one easy-to-clean package. HexClad’s “hybrid technology” combines hexagonal steel peaks with nonstick valleys to improve heat circulation and release after baking. In other words, this bakeware browns your food evenly without it sticking to the pan.

Other features include ergonomic handles and a 2.5mm tri-ply construction to prevent warping. It’s also oven-safe up to 900 degrees Fahrenheit and dishwasher-safe. You can even use your favorite metal spatula or tongs without scratching the surface. And, like all HexClad cookware, it comes with a lifetime warranty against manufacturer’s defects.

I’ll admit: I’m already a big fan of HexClad. I reach for the brand’s skillets and knives daily, and I’ve hoped for years that they would release a bakeware line.

So, when the offer to test the new set landed in my inbox, I couldn’t say no. But would it live up to the hype I’d built up in my head? I put all six pieces through the paces for two months to find out.

Like all HexClad products I’ve tried, the bakeware packaging experience is impeccable. The set arrived securely in one big box, separated with foam. Each piece was also wrapped in a protective dust bag, which is a nice touch.

Immediately, I was awed by the construction of these pans. Just by touch, I could tell they were high quality. I grabbed my food scale to compare the weight of the HexClad pans to my go-to carbon steel pans. The HexClad options weighed more than twice as much as my existing bakeware. Talk about heft!

Now, some folks might not appreciate that extra weight—especially since the pans get even heavier when full of food. But as someone who often replaces her bakeware every few years due to warping or rusting, I’m excited for a sturdier option. I hope this is the last set of bakeware I ever need to order.

As a final step, I washed each piece and got ready to bake!

One of my favorite things to make with sourdough discard is a big loaf of focaccia bread, so that was a natural first test in the 13×9 HexClad pan. Focaccia dough is sticky, but a generous coating of olive oil helps prevent it from gluing to the pan. Still, after proofing and baking my bread as usual, I was impressed that the final product pulled slightly away from the pan’s edges, making it slide out with complete ease. The bottom and edges got nice and toasty brown, too.

A few nights later, I used the same focaccia dough to make a focaccia pizza. Same sticky dough, made even stickier with tomato sauce, cheese and toppings. Plus, since it’s such a rich dish, I cut back on the amount of olive oil I used. Despite all the add-ons, this focaccia baked and released from the pan just as beautifully as the first loaf.

Next, I made a chocolate layer cake with the 9-inch round cake pans. Now, I’m typically a ride-or-die parchment paper user. I find cutting out perfectly sized parchment circles a tedious task, but it’s worthwhile insurance against my cakes sticking. But to truly put the HexClad pans’ nonstick properties to the test, I skipped adding parchment and simply greased my pans with a little butter and flour.

After baking and 10 minutes of cooling came the moment of truth: Would it stick? Luckily, no! Both cakes released with minimal effort. I simply ran a butter knife around the rim of the cake before using the cooling rack to flip ’em out. It’s a good thing, too, because this was my dad’s birthday cake!

My nonstick tests continued with the 8×8 square pan when I whipped up a batch of candy bar blondies. These blondies used an assortment of leftover Halloween candy, so I thought for sure the caramel ooze from a Baby Ruth bar would cause some issues. But nope! Even without parchment paper, treats slipped right out of the pan.

But how does HexClad bakeware perform with healthier treats? For one final test, I baked a completely made-up “brownie” recipe with pumpkin seed butter, applesauce, molasses and cocoa. It was a gooey, chocolaty mess by the time I put it in the pan, yet it baked and released beautifully.

Finally, I put the baking sheet to the test.

Now, I already own the HexClad pizza steel, which I use almost daily. It’s my go-to for everything from frozen pizza to galettes to roasted broccoli, and I find that it works even better than an air fryer to yield crisp, golden brown bakes. I’ve said on many occasions that it’s my all-time favorite piece of bakeware, especially for savory foods.

Both the pizza steel and baking sheet utilize HexClad’s tri-ply construction with an aluminum core and TerraBond nonstick coating. The former is a jet black colorway, while the baking sheet is gray.

Across the board, I found the baking sheet could handle every task I threw its way—including roasting a spaghetti squash. Oftentimes, I find myself scrubbing for what feels like days after roasting squash and scouring off that sticky, burnt-on residue. The HexClad pan cleaned with a simple swipe from a damp paper towel.

During testing, I found the bottoms and handles of the HexClad bakeware smudged a bit. After all, it is made of stainless steel. This didn’t bother me, and it was easy to clean by handwashing and drying it immediately. Over time, I may need to use a more abrasive regimen to clean stainless steel.

While the HexClad pans are very sturdy, you should still let them fully cool before washing. Don’t throw a hot pan directly in the sink. The pans are also dishwasher-safe, though handwashing is recommended. (And honestly, so easy thanks to the nonstick coating.)

Across the board, I’m impressed with the new HexClad bakeware line. I hope we see even more pieces in the future, like a muffin tin and loaf pan. Only time will tell exactly how it holds up, but from what I’ve experienced so far, this set really is designed to last a lifetime. (And I’ll be continuing to long-term test the set, and update this review accordingly.)

Ready to take your bakes to the next level? This all-in-one set is great for beginners and pros alike.

You can shop the full 6-piece bakeware set on the HexClad website for $399. Select styles, like 2-pack sets of small and medium baking sheets, are also available.

#6450. Buttered Nut Squash

We rate butternut the most affable winter squash—relatively easy to prepare, consistently delicious, and available at most grocery stores. The buttered nut dressing is more than just cheeky wordplay. Bold from brown butter and balsamic vinegar and bright from lemon, the crunchy topping is an excellent foil to the sweetness of roasted squash. Cook the squash a couple hours ahead of time and all you’ll have left to do before dinner is make the dressing.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 425°. Lightly crush 2 tsp. fennel seeds with a mortar and pestle or place on a cutting board and gently crush with a heavy pan. Peel 1 medium butternut squash (about 3 lb.) and halve lengthwise. Scoop out seeds; discard. Cut squash into 2" irregular pieces, aiming for sharp, jagged shapes. Transfer to a large rimmed baking sheet; drizzle with 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil and sprinkle with fennel seeds, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. crushed red pepper flakes. Toss squash to coat, arrange in a single layer, and roast until browned and tender, 30–35 minutes.

Do Ahead: Squash can be roasted 2 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

While the squash is roasting, cook 6 oz. thick-cut bacon, cut into 1" pieces, in a medium skillet over medium heat, stirring often, until browned and mostly crisp, 8–12 minutes. Transfer to a small plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to low; combine 1 cup raw pecans and 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter in same pan. Cook, stirring often, until butter browns and nuts have slightly darkened, 6–8 minutes. Remove from heat. Stir in 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped (this will give it a head start to take off the raw edge), then add bacon, zest and juice of 1 large lemon, 3 sprigs sage, and 2 Tbsp. balsamic vinegar and stir to combine. Taste dressing and season with kosher salt if needed.

Arrange squash on a platter and spoon dressing over.

#6449. Two Menswear Darlings Just Made the Most Covetable Boots of 2026

Say you wanted to create the perfect pair of vintage-style military boots. First, you’d need a designer with impeccable taste and encyclopedic knowledge of vintage workwear; then you'd need a bootmaker with the requisite skills to produce it at the highest level. If everything went right, the result would be something like the Modèle 1917, a new collaboration between famed Parisian creative director Gauthier Borsarello and renowned Canadian bootmaker Viberg.

In basic terms, the Modèle 1917 is a pair of boots based on the French Army’s 1917 “brodequin,” a design used by soldiers in the trenches of WWI, available in soft brown suede (Mud) and glossy textured black leather (Pavement). But there’s nothing basic about them. The design comes courtesy of Borsarello, a top-tier collector of vintage workwear and the creative mind behind Gersaint Paris and L’Etiquette magazine. Viberg, a third-generation, family-owned boot specialist, got its start making footwear for forestry crews in British Columbia, and it still builds every pair in its Vancouver Island workshop. While it doesn’t make boots for smokejumpers and loggers anymore, old-school shoemaking techniques like a channeled insole Goodyear welt and stitchdown construction ensure their footwear retains its heirloom-level durability.

The backstory of the “brodequin” begins with the Mdl. 1893, a hobnail-soled marching boot created for French infantrymen in the late 1800s that remained in use until the 1950s. In the First World War, the brodequin’s iron-studded soles and sturdy uppers proved ideally suited to the muddy conditions of the trenches, and American troops soon adopted them in place of their inferior M1904 Marching Shoes. “To me, it’s the blueprint for many combat boots across different countries after WWI,” says Borsarello. “I love the idea that France inspired others after fighting side by side in the trenches. They’re very simple, yet instantly recognizable at the same time.”

For all of its strengths in the field, the original brodequin—whose nickname pays tongue-in-cheek homage to a medieval torture device—wasn’t what you’d call a comfortable boot, especially by modern standards. “They were so stiff that they were almost impossible to walk in,” Borsarello admits. This created something of a design challenge.

To stay as true as possible to the original, Borsarello and Viberg designed the boots on a period-correct “pied haricot” (bean-shaped) last, with a cotton twill lining, solid brass hardware, and reinforced panels that support the midfoot so the forefoot can move freely. To make the Modèle M1917 something you’d actually want to wear, they replaced the hobnailed soles with rubber ones and swapped the original roughout leather for supple American-tanned Horween. The result is a pair of boots that are as comfortable as they are durable, not to mention surprisingly versatile. In other words, exactly what you’d expect from a meeting of these formidable talents.

#6448. For Malin Åkerman, ‘The Hunting Wives’ Is (Still) a Dream Come True

“Girl, that one’s always a good one,” Malin Åkerman says. I’ve just told her how many times I’ve rewatched her 2008 rom-com 27 Dresses, in which she played the charming, wedding dress-and-crush-stealing Tess, younger sister to Katherine Heigl’s responsible Jane. Tess is, in my view, one of the great 2000s-era villains—though Åkerman doesn’t see her as such.

“She was just a young, stupid girl who fell in love, and it was really wrong. That’s your sister’s crush. Don’t do that, girl. Not cool.” She laughs. “But there was a life lesson in it, and she learned and she grew from it. It’s less villain, more just human.”

Some of that sympathy also exists in the way Åkerman plays the audacious, gun-toting, bisexual Texas queen Margo Banks in Netflix’s The Hunting Wives, based on May Cobb’s novel, which returns for season two this week. Margo has done some bad things, but she’s certainly looked good doing ’em—and former Democratic campaign strategist Sophie (Brittany Snow) can’t help but be drawn into her orbit. Their Bonnie-and-Clyde love story continues in the new season, and the stakes have never been higher.

Here, Åkerman talks to Vogue about the Margos in her own life, performing with Snow at the Las Culturistas Culture Awards, and why it’s the perfect time to watch a show about lesbians in Texas.

Vogue: It’s a great time to be releasing a show about Texas.

Malin Åkerman: It’s unbelievable. There was a great little picture, Dermot [Mulroney] sent it to us gals, and it was like, “The Hunting Wives Turns Texas Votes,” or something like that. All the lesbians came out [to vote]. I’m going to misquote it, but it’s out there.

Do you think there’s a future where Jed loses the governor race to–

…I was going to say, to Margo Banks? Maybe she takes over, the Lady Macbeth in the back just pulling all the strings.

That could be really fun if he has someone that he’s up against, a powerful female that maybe Margo has an affair with. Let’s see.

Season two shows us a different side of Margo—she’s in a more vulnerable state. I’m curious what you thought of her season two arc. Where do you think her mindset is at the beginning of the show?

It’s really nice to see the power dynamic shift. Sophie came into her power and Margo’s softening and actually letting someone in, which is huge for a person like Margo, who has been a survivor and keeps everyone at an arm’s length. You see these cracks in her veneer that she’s created for her whole life, really. We start off in a pretty bad place for Margo in season two. She’s in the doghouse, so to speak. She does not like being there.

I loved playing with her vulnerability and really just softening, enveloped in Sophie’s love and protection. That was really nice because I just don’t think that Margo has ever really had that other than [from] her brother, in a weird way, who was the only person that she trusted. I feel like we finally get to see her trusting someone else. Because she doesn’t really trust Jed, that’s just a means to an end. She knows how to play him, she knows how to do her thing to get what she needs.

The Margo–Jed relationship is interesting this season. He acts like a man with power but he is also very vulnerable to her charms. What kind of discussions were you and Dermot having?

All men in power are vulnerable to women if they know how to play their cards right. You know what I mean? There are those women out there who know exactly how to get the guys, they know exactly the buttons to push. Dermot and I, we have a lot of fun conversations. We never like it when we have to play angry at each other because we really love each other. All of us, by the way, on this show, we hate when we have to hate each other. But Dermot and I definitely have much more fun when we get to be in love, so to speak. I don’t think Margo actually loves Jed, but it was fun to have those moments.

I just love playing Margo and all her agendas behind everything and trying to play it as real as possible, especially with Jed, because she’s really a player. She’s got Sophie on the side [while she’s] telling Jed that he’s everything. Yeah, Dermot and I have a lot of fun. Mostly we just goof around on set, to be really honest with you.

Well, you guys do have a rom-com that’s coming out in a few weeks.

Listen, Dermot asked me when we were on set—it was the last couple weeks of shooting [season one], it was his last day of shooting. He’s like, “I’m about to go do this rom-com on a cruise.” And I was like, “Nope, not doing it, never. I don’t ever want to go on a cruise, it’s not my thing. Too claustrophobic. Don’t want to be on for three weeks. Are you nuts?” And he goes, “Well, the first week it would just be us and you can bring your family and it’ll become this free vacation.” I was like, “Oh, okay. When do we start?” And he goes, “Four days after you wrap this show.” It’s like, Oh my God. But it was my son’s summer break, so I ended up convincing a girlfriend of mine, one of my best girlfriends who’s also a makeup artist, to come along with her kids on the trip. I don’t know how it’s going to turn out, but we had a blast making it.

We had a little too much fun. We were like, “Is there even a movie in this? I don’t know, but we’re having a great time.”

I’m a big Dale Dickey fan, and she plays a fun role in this season. What was it like filming with her?

She’s phenomenal on every level. She’s a phenomenal human being—the nicest, loveliest human you’ll ever meet and a phenomenal actress. I remember seeing her in Winter’s Bone and just going, “Wow, this woman is just great.” And what a face—the realism in the expressions. And she’s just beautiful to watch when she works and she really is invested. She believes in her craft and she’s so collaborative and lovely. All the greatest things you can say about a person, I would say about Dale Dickey.

Dale Dickey as Zelda and Cam Gigandet as Gentle John in Episode 204 of The Hunting Wives.

Thinking about Margo and Sophie this season, they’re both killers, so they can be on a more even playing field. But Sophie does have this secret at the beginning of the season…

The audience question is, do they really love each other? And listen, that’s an open-ended question. There’s no real answer to that. I think there is love there, for sure. I think on Sophie’s part towards Margo, it’s almost an extension of her addictive personality. Margo’s an addiction. Margo fluctuates between necessity and love because Margo’s just not honest with herself. She’s not open, honest, and vulnerable, so you can’t be that with someone else.

I felt like there were parts of this season where Sophie was scarier than Margo.

Totally. You let the beast out and you’re like, Holy shit, she needs something. She’s going to get it. That’s also what attracts these two to each other, is that drive. You get to see why they’re kind of meant for each other in this season. It’s not just Margo. Margo’s not just the crazy one and the wild one. Sophie’s got it in her, she just needs to be unleashed.

Have you had a Margo type in your life, or have you been that type? Someone who draws you into their orbit or brings out something in you that you’re like, Oh, I love being around this person?

Yeah, sure. I mean, I think it’s gone both ways. I think I’ve been in the shoes of a Margo and I’ve been attracted to it. I had a little bit of a fun time in between marriages, so to speak, and there were definitely people who were absolutely wrong for me, but I was very drawn in. Also knowing they were wrong for me, but just couldn’t get enough…it’s such a wild experience. And then I also played the part of drawing people in and just using them for what I needed. I knew it wasn’t going to become a relationship, and just having fun with it almost felt…I don’t know, it was a great time. I understand why Margo is having a great time, but [I haven’t experienced] anywhere near the extent of the deception and the games that she plays. But the draw, I can understand that, where there’s just this sexual energy that pulls you in.

Brittany Snow and Akerman in Episode 205 of The Hunting Wives.

After season one, there was some time where you weren’t totally sure if Hunting Wives was getting picked up again. Now you have a season three renewal already locked in. How does it feel to have that kind of stability?

It’s a fucking dream come true, it really is. I feel so, so lucky. I love this character, it’s a character of a lifetime. I love the people I get to work with. I couldn’t have wished for it…and it’s a steady job. If this goes for 10 years, I’ll be elated. Although maybe we can make Margo just chill a little bit on the working out and looking top-notch all the time, and tanned and everything. Maybe she just lets herself go a little. Let me just enjoy my pizza and my pasta on a daily basis, okay guys? Let’s not judge.

Do you know when you’ll go back for season three?

I’m flying out to Atlanta on November 29. We get started December 2. We’re premiering [season two] and then off we go, Season 3. I’m excited. I miss my Hunting Wives family.

I loved your and Brittany’s performance at the Las Culturistas Culture Awards. How did that come about?

Well, Bowen Yang was sat in front of us at the Emmys, where we ended up surprisingly presenting. We weren’t supposed to present, and so he was with us on that journey. It was so much fun. We were like, “Bowen, we have to present.” He’s like, “What? Right now?” He’s such a lovely person. From that, maybe that seed was planted in his head. We met Matt Rogers as well, and they’re such a great duo. They were the ones who came to us and said, “We have an idea. Hunting Wives and Heated Rivalry have been such a huge hit in the LGBTQ community that it would be really fun to do this, to have you guys open the whole ceremony.” We were super game for that. Like, “Okay, we’ll wear the hockey jerseys, but we need to bring in the Hunting Wives into it all.”

Do you think there is any kind of connective tissue that links The Hunting Wives and Heated Rivalry’s success beyond the queer relationships? Do you think there’s anything that both shows have in common?

I think it’s the forbiddenness of it all. That’s always something that we’re all drawn to because I think we all have our own secret thoughts that we don’t share with everybody. We all have our own fantasies, we all have our own things that we lust [over]. These shows kind of open them up. Heated Rivalry has a more important message in a way, because this is really something that the author was talking about. Being in such a macho world as hockey is, that’s a really brave thing, to come out publicly and to have a relationship publicly within that. I loved it, I thought it was really beautiful.

It’s different from Hunting Wives because Hunting Wives is…we’re a little more on the camp side. We’re true just raw entertainment and craziness, but we have that element of exploring sexuality in a town, in a world, where it’s frowned upon.

I’m sure that Margo and Sophie will be some people’s queer awakening in the years to come.

I sure hope so. Bring it on. Come on out, everybody. It’s a great place to be.

When you think back to when you were in maybe your early or mid-20s, were you dreaming of projects like this? What kind of arc did you want your career to have when you were very young?

Oh, gosh. Early 20s, I didn’t know what I wanted more than five minutes ahead of me. I was not one of those people who was planning ahead and goal-oriented. I was along for the ride. I really was letting life take me. I got swept away in this romantic-comedy film era with 27 Dresses and Heartbreak Kid and Couples Retreat. I was just enjoying every moment of it, not thinking about, Oh, this can come to an end.

After a few of those romantic comedies, I really started craving something that I could sink my teeth into a little more and to try my hand at drama. I started seeking out little independent films, which is something that I love watching: the little indies or foreign films. That’s when I remember The Ticket came along with Dan Stevens, and Billions came along—I feel like that’s a precursor to Margo Banks, Lara Axelrod.

Hunting Wives came at the perfect time because I had had that moment during COVID and after, where there were a lot of projects that were, I call them “yes projects.” I was saying yes because I needed to work, but I wasn’t feeling passionate about them anymore and it was really making me sad. I felt like projects that I really wanted to do, I couldn’t get in the room, and I started to have a lot of, I call them “head gremlins” talking to me, dark voices in my head. The voices telling me, Yeah, this is it. You’re expired. I mean, you had a good run. Say thank you, feel grateful. I just went, No.

For the past five years I’ve been working on my true passion project. Won’t say anything yet, but hopefully it’ll come to fruition. It’s something that I’ve built from the ground up and it’s written, I’ve got a director attached. We just need to get out there and get it made. But other than that, when Hunting Wives came along, it just felt like, oh, this was the hit that I really needed as far as getting passionate again about the work that I’m doing, because I just love this character and this job. It was incredible to not only be passionate about a character, but to feel relevant in my business again.

Do you think your definition of success has changed over the years?

I do think so. Becoming a parent changed all of that. Success for me, really, the most important success is the success of my family. And in business, I feel like I look back and I go, I’ve had a great career and how lucky am I if it continues? This is wonderful. So I’m happy for this show to have its success because all the people who are in it are so deserving. But success is a really…for me, it’s not linked to my work anymore. It really is linked to, am I successful as a person? Am I succeeding in my day-to-day life? Am I handling life well? In your 20s we talk a lot about being successful and a lot of it is linked to work. And then as we grow older and we realize what’s really important, then it shifts.

I’ve been asking myself those questions a lot lately, like, how do you define yourself outside of work?

Exactly. And that success is, how do people see you and how are you presenting to the world? Have you succeeded in becoming the person that you want to be, the best version of you? And where’s the work still need to be done? I have a 13-year-old boy who still wants to cuddle me at night and tells me he loves me [when I] drop him off at school. He is like, “Bye, Mom. Love you. See you later.” Thirteen. I’m like, “I have succeeded. This is a huge success.”

This conversation has been edited and condensed.

#6447. Is Pink Turkey Safe to Eat?

Pink turkey doesn't necessarily mean your Thanksgiving feast is ruined. Here's how to know if your bird is safe to eat so you can stay calm and turkey on.

I’ll never forget the Thanksgiving when I was convinced I’d ruined the holiday for everyone. I wasn’t an experienced cook at the time, and it was one of my first attempts at making a Thanksgiving turkey. I used a helpful guide for how long to cook a turkey and even invested in a meat thermometer to be sure it reached at least 165°F. It looked great, and I was so proud!

Imagine my surprise and horror when I carved that gorgeously browned roast turkey and discovered it was pink inside. I was so nervous my guests would assume the turkey was undercooked. I didn’t know then that pink turkey can be perfectly safe to eat—as long as it’s cooked to that vital internal temperature.

Cooked turkey can look pink for a few reasons that have nothing to do with doneness, including the age of the bird, how it’s prepared and natural pigmentation.

“Poultry naturally can have a pink hue,” says Heidi Diestel of turkey farm Diestel Family Ranch in Sonora, California. “The legs and thighs have more of the natural pigments that give meat its darker color. Those pigments, along with changes that happen during cooking, can leave some pink even when the turkey is fully cooked.”

The pigments Heidi refers to are proteins called myoglobin and cytochrome c. The more of these proteins the meat has, the darker it will be. Older animals tend to have more proteins, and therefore darker pigmentation, as do any regularly exercised muscles. That explains why leg meat is darker than breast meat, as turkeys spend the bulk of their days walking and running.

Cooking can also cause a chemical reaction with these proteins that contributes to a pink color. Smoked turkey often stays pink from the reaction of the meat to the smoke inside the grill or smoker, but even oven-roasted turkey can have a pinkish hue. Myoglobin usually turns white during the cooking process, but cytochrome c is more resistant to heat and can maintain a pink blush.

Using a meat thermometer is the best way to know if your turkey is safe to eat.

Poultry is considered safe to eat when it meets a cooking temperature of at least 165°. However, the Taste of Home Test Kitchen recommends cooking the leg and thigh meat to 170° for the best texture. For stuffed turkeys, don’t forget to take the temperature of the stuffing as well, which should reach at least 165° when the thermometer is inserted in the center of the stuffing.

If your turkey comes embedded with a round plastic doneness indicator that pops when the turkey is ready, don’t use that as an absolute; they are notoriously inaccurate.

To check if the turkey is done, insert the thermometer in a thick, meaty area, making sure the tip doesn’t touch any bones (bone will show a higher temperature).

If you’re using a probe thermometer that you insert before cooking, double-check its position once the turkey has been cooking for a while. Meat contracts as it cooks, so it may no longer be in the best spot.

If any part of your turkey is below 165°, you should continue cooking the turkey until all parts reach a safe temperature. It’s common for the thermometer to register different temperatures in different areas, since white meat cooks at a faster rate than dark meat. Don’t be tempted to cut off the parts that aren’t ready and return only them to the oven. It’ll increase the risk that undercooked juices will run onto your cutting board and contaminate the properly cooked turkey.

If the legs and thighs aren’t done but the breast is, I like to baste the white meat and loosely tent it with foil to try and lock in as much moisture as possible. If the dark meat is ready but the breast needs more time, there’s no need to sweat it. Dark meat has enough natural fat and moisture that it won’t become dry with a little extra time in the oven.

You should never knowingly eat undercooked turkey. According to the CDC, undercooked turkey can contain harmful bacteria, like Salmonella, Clostridium perfringens or Campylobacter, that can cause foodborne illnesses.

There’s also a risk of bacteria if the turkey isn’t thawed or prepared correctly. Give yourself plenty of time to thaw a frozen turkey, either in the refrigerator or in a cold water bath. Also, make sure to keep the counter or cutting board where you’re prepping the turkey clean and sanitized before and after handling the raw bird.

#6446. Collard Greens Vinaigrette

For those who might shudder at the thought of eating raw hardy greens like collards or kale, this vibrant side inspired by the French bistro classic leeks vinaigrette is the answer. Simmered past squeaky-raw yet well short of meltingly braised, they offer substantial bite, like al dente pasta. The mustard dressing couldn’t be simpler to make—use it as a base for any salad you might serve this season. It’s punchy enough to stand up to winter vegetables or any sturdy bitter green.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Toast ½ cup raw walnuts on a rimmed baking sheet, tossing halfway through, until golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Meanwhile, cook 2 bunches collard greens, ribs and stems removed, leaves cut into 2" pieces, in a large pot of generously salted boiling water until just tender, 9–11 minutes. Using tongs, immediately transfer to a large bowl of ice water and let cool.

Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ¼ cup white wine vinegar, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, preferably country-style, ⅓ cup extra-virgin olive oil, ¼ cup (packed) coarsely chopped tarragon, 2 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl to combine. Set dressing aside.

Transfer toasted walnuts to a small bowl and drizzle with remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Sprinkle with a generous pinch each of sugar and salt and toss to coat. Taste and add more sugar if needed (nuts should be more sweet than salty). Set seasoned walnuts aside.

Drain collard greens and squeeze gently to remove excess water. Transfer to bowl with reserved dressing and toss to coat evenly. Cover and chill at least 15 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Arrange greens in a shallow bowl or on a platter and spoon any dressing remaining in bowl over. Top with seasoned walnuts and tarragon leaves.

Do Ahead: Walnuts can be toasted and dressing can be made 1 day ahead. Store walnuts airtight at room temperature. Cover dressing and chill.

#6445. Sheet-Pan Cider Vinegar Chicken

Slashing bone-in chicken thighs (carefully, around the bone, of course) allows a punchy maple-Dijon-ACV marinade to permeate the meat deeply in a short amount of time. And that waiting time is well spent: Scatter torn sourdough bread on a baking sheet and bake until crisp, then toss croutons aside to make way for the thighs. Once the chicken is cooked through, toss the croutons in the rendered fat and cook until everything is bronzed and glistening. A few handfuls of arugula make an elegant finish—who needs a side salad?

Whisk 5 garlic cloves, finely grated, ½ cup plus 3 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar, 5 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, 3 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, 1 Tbsp. plus 2 tsp. pure maple syrup, 2½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) in a measuring glass or small bowl to combine. Transfer 2 Tbsp. vinegar mixture to a small bowl; set aside.

Arrange 3 lb. skin-on, bone-in chicken thighs (6–8), skin side up, on a cutting board. Season lightly with salt. Turn over and season lightly on other side with salt, then carefully use a sharp paring knife to make 3 long slashes, going most of the way through meat (avoid the bone). Transfer to a large bowl and pour vinegar mixture in measuring glass over. Toss chicken to coat, making sure to get liquid into slashes. Let chicken sit at least 30 minutes and up to 1 hour.

Meanwhile, place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 425°. Place 8 oz. country-style or sourdough bread (about ⅓ loaf), torn into 1" pieces, on a rimmed baking sheet. Drizzle remaining 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil over and sprinkle with a pinch of salt and a pinch of freshly ground black pepper; toss to coat. Arrange bread in a single layer and bake until golden, 12–15 minutes. Transfer croutons to a plate; reserve baking sheet.

Arrange reserved chicken on reserved baking sheet and nestle 3 large shallots, quartered lengthwise through root ends, around; pour any excess vinegar mixture in bowl over. Bake chicken until golden, cooked through, and an instant-read thermometer inserted into thickest part, avoiding bone, registers at least 165° (it should be well over), 25–30 minutes.

Scatter croutons over empty areas of baking sheet and toss to soak up juices. Roast until chicken and croutons are deeply browned, 10–12 minutes. Let cool 5 minutes, then top with 2 oz. arugula and drizzle with reserved vinegar mixture in small bowl.

#6443. The Garment Pre-Fall 2027

Interiors, and interiority, are recurring subjects of Charlotte Eskildsen’s collections for The Garment. For pre-fall, the designer imagined a woman living in a townhouse in central Copenhagen near the Marble Church, a very chic area, who wears clothes in “her own really private way... Nothing in this collection is too tied up,” the designer said. “Even if it’s suiting, it will stretch, and it’s comfortable to wear.”

Some of the garments have a feeling of intimacy that comes from their origin in the boudoir. Lingerie dressing is a trend that Eskildsen isn’t ready to give up as she sees it as an expression of femininity that counters the outward strength often expected of women. So next to a lace-trimmed skirt with an asymmetrically inserted godet and a collarless jacket, the many slip dresses in the collection looked somewhat saccharine and less street-ready than the more structured looks. She’s “dressed, but she doesn’t know if she wants to go out or not,” the designer said of her muse. (This cozy, hazy should-I-or-shouldn’t-I feeling assumes win-win options.)

In betweenness is at the heart of all pre-fall collections which need to adapt to snow and sun. For cooler temps there is a smart cropped black leather jacket shown with tailored white pants. An injection of romance comes in the form of a flowy Daisy Buchanan-ish dress the color of a snowflake with bias cut lines which combines silk chiffon, jacquard, and silk wool. There are “a lot of cut lines to be able to mix all the fabrics so it’s like a blanket of different fabrics,” as Eskildsen put it. Hygge, in other words, but make it haute.

#6442. Which Thanksgiving Foods Belong in the Same Bite?

Some Thanksgiving food combinations are obvious. Others might earn you some questioning looks at the dinner table.

For years, my kids refused to let any two foods touch on their plates. I found this particularly maddening at Thanksgiving. There’s an entire table of food to fit onto a single plate and only so much room to negotiate separate territories for the mashed potatoes and green bean casserole! Thankfully, they’re a little more accommodating these days and, like me, have come to appreciate the occasional overlap between dishes.

Of course, plenty of adults also have strong opinions about which Thanksgiving foods should mingle. There are those who insist on keeping every dish separate, those who permit a little gravy to stray onto the stuffing but draw the line at cranberry sauce, and those who deliberately assemble the perfect combination on every forkful. Then there’s always the unhinged relative who stirs the entire contents of their plate into a single, gravy-saturated mass and eats it with the serene confidence of someone who has never once questioned their choices.

Personally, I’m firmly in favor of combining foods, although I do believe a little discretion is in order. Thanksgiving dinner offers a wonderful assortment of rich, savory and tart flavors, and knowing which ones to bring together is part of what makes the meal so satisfying. There’s a culinary reason that cranberry sauce belongs alongside turkey, and that stuffing and mashed potatoes are particularly good together. And once you understand why those combinations work, you can start building some excellent bites of your own.

Absolutely. In fact, some of the most familiar food pairings are built around the idea that one ingredient can supply something another lacks. Think of a rich cut of meat served with a sharp, acidic sauce, or a creamy dish finished with something crisp. Neither component is necessarily lacking on its own, but the contrast makes the combination much more interesting.

The same principle applies to Thanksgiving foods. Acidity helps balance richness, sweetness can temper salty or intensely savory flavors, and a change in texture can make a forkful more interesting. It’s not particularly complicated, but there’s a difference between understanding why two foods complement each other and simply hoping for the best.

Some combinations are simply better than others, though saying so at Thanksgiving dinner may invite more opinions than you bargained for.

Turkey and cranberry sauce: There’s a reason this pairing has endured for generations. Turkey, particularly the breast meat, is relatively mild, and the tartness of cranberry sauce gives it a welcome lift. It’s also an excellent remedy for turkey that’s spent a little too long in the oven, a situation that has befallen even the most conscientious Thanksgiving cooks.

Mashed potatoes, stuffing and gravy: I consider this one of Thanksgiving’s greatest achievements. The smooth, buttery potatoes and herbaceous stuffing are excellent together, and a generous spoonful of gravy makes the whole arrangement even better. There’s nothing particularly subtle about it, but Thanksgiving dinner isn’t generally celebrated for its subtlety.

Sweet potatoes and turkey: The natural sweetness of roasted sweet potatoes makes a lovely contrast to savory turkey, particularly the richer dark meat. A traditional sweet potato casserole can work, too, although I draw the line somewhere around the marshmallow topping. I have nothing against marshmallows, but I prefer to encounter them after dinner.

Green bean casserole and mashed potatoes: These are two of my Thanksgiving essentials, and I see no reason they shouldn’t share a fork. The creamy green beans and buttery potatoes are lovely together, but it’s the crispy fried onions that really make the combination work. That salty crunch is a welcome addition to the softer textures.

Turkey, stuffing and cranberry sauce: This is probably my favorite combo of the bunch. The savory turkey and seasoned stuffing are practically made for one another, while a little cranberry sauce cuts through the richness. It’s essentially a Thanksgiving leftover sandwich without the bread, although I wouldn’t object to adding a dinner roll to the equation.

Macaroni and cheese and cranberry sauce: I realize this combination may call my culinary credentials into question, but hear me out. Rich, creamy mac and cheese practically begs for something sharp and acidic to cut through it, and cranberry sauce does exactly that. It’s not so different from serving a sharp cheddar with fruit preserves on a charcuterie board, although I concede that putting cranberry sauce on macaroni and cheese is a considerably harder sell. But that’s half the fun of Thanksgiving dinner: discovering which combinations you’re willing to defend.

#6441. The Gap Black Friday Sale Is a Holiday Miracle

The Gap Black Friday Sale kills two birds with one stone. The stone? Up to 60% off sitewide. The birds? Gifts for loved ones and gifts for you. Since its founding during the Summer of Love in the epicenter of the hippie revolution, the American fashion label has outfitted generations with stylish clothes both timely and timeless. And while it’s come a long way since its early days slinging Levi’s jeans and vinyl records, Gap’s designs are as relevant now as they were during Haight & Ashbury’s heyday. The prices, too, have remained accessible for the average American, even with inflation going insane.

#6440. Butter Mochi Cake With Maple-Miso Pecans

For Shuai Wang, chef of King BBQ in North Charleston, South Carolina, mochi brings back memories of holidays with family. His other dessert love? Classic Southern pecan pie. This Hawaiian-style butter mochi cake draws on both, pairing a rich, chewy cake with a generous layer of maple-miso pecans.

The batter gets its signature bounce from mochiko, a distinct style of rice flour that gives butter mochi its chewy texture—not the fluffy crumb of a conventional cake. Coconut milk and melted butter add richness, while the pecans provide crunch. Let the cake cool completely before slicing so the texture has time to set.

The secret to the pecan topping is a little white or yellow miso, which brings savory depth to the maple syrup, much like the salt in salted caramel. The nuts need only a brief head start in the oven; they’ll continue to toast as the cake bakes.

Can I use regular rice flour instead of mochiko?

No. Mochiko, also called sweet or glutinous rice flour, has a different starch composition from regular rice flour. It’s responsible for butter mochi’s characteristic springy, slightly sticky chew. Regular rice flour or all-purpose flour won’t produce the same texture.

White and yellow miso are both good choices for this cake. White miso tends to be milder and slightly sweeter, while yellow miso has a somewhat more pronounced savory flavor. Either adds complexity to the maple-coated pecans without overwhelming their buttery, nutty flavor. Learn more about the different types of miso and how to use them.

Mochiko is naturally gluten-free, despite the sometimes confusing name glutinous rice flour. This recipe can be gluten-free, but check your miso: Some varieties contain barley or wheat. If you’re baking for someone who needs to avoid gluten, choose a miso labeled gluten-free and check your other packaged ingredients.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Lightly oil a rimmed baking sheet with vegetable oil. Whisk 2 Tbsp. pure maple syrup and 2 tsp. white or yellow miso (gluten-free if needed) in a medium bowl until smooth. Add 8 oz. raw pecans, coarsely chopped (about 2 cups) and 1 Tbsp. sugar and toss until evenly coated. Spread out on prepared baking sheet; bake until fragrant and matte looking, 6–8 minutes (nuts won’t be fully toasted). Let cool.

Lightly grease a 9"-diameter cake pan with unsalted butter and line bottom with a parchment paper round. Vigorously whisk 2 large eggs, 1¼ cups (250 g) sugar, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl until smooth. Add one 13.5-oz. can unsweetened coconut milk, well shaken, heated slightly if fat is solid, 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, and 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter, melted, slightly cooled, and whisk well. Add 1⅔ cups (254 g) mochiko and 1 tsp. baking powder; whisk vigorously until combined and batter is smooth and thick. Scrape batter into prepared pan.

Toss pecans to break up any clumps and scatter evenly over batter, going all the way to the edges (it may seem like a lot). Bake cake until sides start to pull away from pan, top is golden brown, and a tester inserted into the center comes out clean (some pecans will sink), 50–55 minutes. If pecans begin to brown too quickly, loosely tent pan with foil. Transfer to a wire rack and let cake cool in pan 15 minutes. Turn cake out onto rack; peel away parchment and discard. Carefully turn cake right side up and let cool completely (at least 1 hour).

To serve, slice cake and top with scoops of vanilla ice cream.

Do Ahead: Cake can be made 1 day ahead. Store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

#6438. The New Rules of Complexion Makeup

A decade ago, many of us wouldn’t leave the house without a full-coverage beat. As Instagram selfies and YouTube tutorials took over pop culture, meticulously sculpted, perfected complexions reigned supreme—until the pendulum swung in the opposite direction, ushering in an era of barely-there coverage and skin-care-infused formulas. And while the early 2020s were defined by ultra-dewy, almost damp-looking skin, today’s complexion ideal strikes a more nuanced balance: coverage without the weight, radiance without the shine.

“Modern complexion formulations have come such a long way, and the new-Gen complexion products give medium to buildable coverage that glides and melts into skin, while giving a soft-focus matte finish that reads radiant rather than shiny,” says celebrity makeup artist and Vogue Beauty Board member Fara Homidi. “We can now get more coverage, while the final look is breathable and has flex to it, never heavy and cakey.” Nowadays, lightweight texture, skin-friendly ingredients, and flexible coverage are non-negotiable. The ideal product perfects your complexion without looking or feeling like makeup.

“I want the complexion product to be able to be great, without the help of a concealer or bronzer,” says content creator and fellow Board member Toni Bravo. “It also needs the right undertones that bring out dimension naturally,” she says, to create a second-skin effect.

Mastering your complexion, however, is both the science of formulation and the art of application. While formulas are more advanced than ever, technique and placement have simultaneously evolved. Homidi points out that it’s not about wearing less makeup, but about how it’s placed on the skin. Her best advice is to put the product only where you need it like under the eyes or around the nose, with lighter coverage around the the rest of the face. She prefers pinpointing blemishes and discolorations with fuller coverage, while letting the rest of the skin breathe.

Looking ahead, beauty lovers and experts alike can expect complexion makeup to keep evolving. “Hopefully, complexion products continue to evolve shade-wise,” says Bravo. “We’ve seen brands truly expand the meaning of inclusivity in the last few years, in ways 14-year-old me wouldn’t believe. Folks understanding undertones, and how to apply them to our complexion products, will make for a more conscious consumer and intentional brand.” Meanwhile, Homidi expects further advancements in texture and innovative application methods (roller ball foundation applicator, anyone?). In short, the future looks more inclusive, with advanced formulations and better shade matches for everyone.

Below, a look at some of the latest foundation and skin tint launches that we believe are pushing the category forward; with some helpful insights from the Vogue Beauty Board members who have tested them.

It pulls fairly neutral, so if you have a warmer undertone, I’d pay close attention to the swatches before applying, especially since it includes SPF.

#6435. Thanksgiving Cornbread

Traditionally, cornbread stuffing requires making cornbread, cubing it and letting it dry out, mixing it with stock, eggs, meat, and aromatics, then transforming it into a stuffing (or dressing). This process produces some truly memorable casseroles, but I have an alternative that streamlines the process without compromising flavor: stuffing cornbread. It still smells enticingly like the classic Thanksgiving side as you set the baking dish on the table. I’ve still packed in a medley of woodsy herbs, sweet onions, vegetal peppers, and savory sausage. And it still slices into lofty servings to perch on your plate next to the sweet potatoes and green beans. It just takes half as long to make.

The intentional two-to-one ratio of cornmeal to flour in this cornbread results in a moist, tender crumb that still has enough structure to hold up against the sturdy mix-ins. The sugar might seem like a lot, but it balances out the savory sausage and aromatics perfectly.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Line a 13x9" baking pan with parchment paper, leaving generous overhang on long sides. Coat pan and parchment with unsalted butter. Melt ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium-low heat, then pour into a small bowl.

Cook 1 green bell pepper, halved, ribs and seeds removed, finely chopped, 1 medium white onion, finely chopped, and 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, in same skillet, stirring occasionally with a wooden spoon, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 1 lb. spicy and/or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and cook, breaking up and stirring occasionally, until browned (it may still be a little raw in the center at this point), about 5 minutes. Remove from heat.

Stir together 4 cups (624 g) fine-ground yellow cornmeal, 2 cups (250 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup (200 g) sugar, 1 Tbsp. plus 1½ tsp. baking powder, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 tsp. baking soda, and ¼ cup finely chopped sage, thyme, and/or rosemary in a large bowl. Gradually pour in 3½ cups buttermilk, then melted butter, stirring constantly until combined. Add 4 large eggs one at a time, mixing to incorporate after each addition. Fold in sausage mixture, then scrape batter into prepared pan.

Bake cornbread, rotating pan front to back halfway through, until golden brown and top springs back when gently pressed, 38–45 minutes. Let cool in pan 15 minutes. Using parchment paper overhang, lift cornbread out of pan and transfer to a cutting board. Cut into 12–18 slices; arrange on a platter.

Do Ahead: Cornbread can be baked 4 hours ahead. Store at room temperature; cut just before serving.

#6434. The Maldon Salt Scandal, Explained

Welcome to Open Tab, a weekly column covering the news, gossip, and stories that have stayed open in my tabs all week. Last time we covered the ever-escalating advent calendar wars.

The long-awaited sixth installment of the Grand Theft Auto franchise was released this week. Why in God’s name am I talking about it for a food magazine? Because the game was so highly anticipated that food delivery apps saw noticeable spikes in demand as players stayed home, many skipping work to play the game for hours at a time without breaks for cooking. A Miami cafe even released a specialty roast of coffee beans, and one Florida restaurant chain partnered with Rockstar, the game’s developer, to bring an in-game food spot to life. (The game is set in a fictional state modeled after Florida.)

This is the kind of widespread, obsessively orchestrated marketing plan you’d expect around a Beyoncé album. We have arguably not been this close to a true monocultural moment since The Dress debate in February of 2015.

In other news, Alison Roman’s podcast, Having People Over, which I teased in last week’s Open Tab officially debuted this week. Episode one features Bowen Yang, and the next couple will be with Lauren Graham and Jenny Slate—and then that’s it until 2027, as Roman told me.

Also in today’s Open Tab: the salty, salacious scandal around Maldon’s sourcing, a new study on GLP-1s for children, the case for cocktail brutalism, and a Tuscon restaurant alchemizing desert ingredients.

At Bon Appétit, we love flaky Maldon salt. Like, we really love it. So when a report from The Observer detailed how Maldon’s famed UK sea salt was in fact also made with German rock salt, gasps rippled around the Bon Appétit office. I mean, not gasps exactly, but everyone was like “whaaaat? That’s crazy.”

The gritty details: Maldon’s been harvested in Essex’s Blackwater estuary for more than a century, and the label on each box lists its only ingredient as 100% sea salt. The Observer’s report reveals that the company imports mined rock salt from Germany as part of the “salt-on-salt” process in which the sea salt is enriched with minerals. The company is allowed to call their product 100% sea salt because the salt that comes from mines was at one point in a sea—in prehistoric times.

Origin and processing matters because these factors can affect the final flavor, color, and how salty it tastes. Maldon is a finishing salt, and it's largely prized for the crunch of its big flakes. But consumers don’t love feeling like they’ve been lied to, and judging from the comments under Maldon’s apology post on Instagram, that is precisely how many feel.

I would wager that Maldon will survive this controversy. It’s a legacy brand that’s a staple in professional and home kitchens alike. And while it’s not a great look, I think the majority of consumers would say that salt is salt, and as long as Maldon stays crunchy and salty, they’ll be on board.

Semaglutide, the GLP-1 compound in brand name drugs Wegovy and Ozempic, is already approved for use in children older than 12. But a new study published in the New England Journal of Medicine shows that the drug is effective for treating obesity in kids as young as six. According to the New York Times, drug manufacturer Novo Nordisk, plans to ask the FDA to authorize the drug’s use for kids in that age group.

It's hard to know what the long term effects on developed adult brains and bodies would be, let alone the quickly growing, changing brains and bodies of young kids. We’re beginning to see that GLP-1s can have a profound effect on mental health in adults, but though it seems the drugs can indeed contribute to weight loss in children, there are many other facets of its use that we simply don’t understand and haven’t studied yet.

When I helped build our Best Bars list last year the question of what exactly makes a great bar was one we pondered over for many hours. Order a drink from a Bar of Note (i.e. one of the many bars sitting on a Best-of list somewhere on the internet), and you’ll quickly get a sense of how they answer that same question. Namely: spectacle.

Cocktails across the country and abroad have ramped up in complexity and presentation in recent years fueled mostly by the reason you might expect: spectacle and theatricality performs well on social media, according to a report in the Times.

As a reporter who has often been forced to order the most attention-grabbing, loudest, most obnoxious drink on the menu in the name of journalism—and as a cocktail-enjoyer in my free time—I would like to propose a paradigm shift. Cocktail brutalism. Cocktail minimalism. Cocktail absurdism—actually anything besides the overwhelming maximalist cocktail moment that we’re stepping into. The ideal drink special? A beer, a shot, and a genuine compliment.

At Tuscon’s Ursa, ingredients from the surrounding desert are transformed. Chef Aaron Lopez and June Chee who lead the restaurant see cacti and brittlebrush as deeply flavorful staples of their menu. Read on to see how these ingredients come to life.

#6433. 8 Best Gua Sha Tools to Expertly Sculpt, Lift, and Tone

Over the last few years, lymphatic drainage has gone from an IYKYK technique to an all-out wellness obsession. Oft described as the “Cinderella of medicine,” the lymphatic system is responsible for collecting excess fluid from tissues, transporting immune cells, and carrying certain waste products away from cells. This system, however, doesn’t work on its own to get the lymph flowing. Lymphatic drainage is a more manual practice; you can try your hand at deep breathing or dry brushing, but few things offer offer as excellent lifting benefits as the best gua sha tools.

“The literal gua sha Mandarin translation is ‘to scrape sand,’” explains Lin Chen, cofounder of Pink Moon. “Gua sha tools have been used as a unique approach for holistic healing in China for 4,000 years. It has been traditionally used over the body to help aid in the movement of qi (which is energy flow), increase circulation, and release tension.” That said, Chen continues saying that research shows that the practice was first used in the Paleolithic Ages, dating back to the Ming dynasty in China.

“Gua sha is an effective technique for enhancing the face’s natural contours and reducing puffiness through lymphatic drainage,” explains Charlotte Yau, traditional Chinese medicine expert and founder of Muihood. The upward-scraping technique is meant to stimulate blood circulation, encourage collagen production, and reduce the appearance of fine lines and wrinkles, adds Yau. “While it doesn’t permanently change facial structure, it can create a more sculpted look over time by reducing fluid retention and enhancing skin elasticity.”

Of course, when you’re shopping for your first one, the options can feel endless. “When choosing a gua sha, I think the material, shape and weight all matter,” says Ava Lee, K-beauty expert and founder of byAVA. Ceramic and stone feel smooth and give you a gentler massage, while stainless steel stays cold, which helps with puffiness. “Ultimately, it’s about finding something that feels good to use and that you’ll reach for every day,” Lee says. Ahead, the best gua sha tools to add to your routine from Lanshin, Wildling, and more.

What are the benefits of incorporating a gua sha tool?

“While its popularity in the US and Europe is largely tied to its ability to ‘sculpt’ the face, its healing capabilities extend far deeper!” Chen instructs, explaining that the gua sha is used for lymphatic drainage, addressing stagnant energy, promoting blood flow, soothing headaches, reducing inflammation, shortening acute illnesses like colds and flus, as well as releasing tension from head to toe. Daily gua sha practice has the ability to enhance not only your appearance (think reduced puffiness, contoured facial muscles, and improved skin elasticity), but your mental and emotional well-being. Just think of how calming it is to glide a roller or stone across your skin. What’s more, Chen says you can expect results instantly, though you should continue to use daily.

“Both steel and stone gua sha tools have their benefits, and the choice depends on personal preference and skin needs,” explains Chinese Medicine expert and founder of Muihood, Charlotte Yau.

Curious how to use a gua sha? So you’re ready to try the restorative practice at home. Aside from the tool you choose, a proper technique is key to reap the anticipated benefits. Always start with clean skin, then prep with an emollient face oil or balm. “You also want to apply an oil that’s silky and doesn’t absorb right away or you might tug your skin,” Chen advises. With skin ready, keep the stone as flat and close to the skin as possible, gliding at a 15 degree angle to avoid any unnecessary friction. According to Chen, you’ll want to avoid passing over active breakouts, even if you just target the chest and neck to increase circulation and decrease inflammation. Perform slow strokes, in upward and outward motions, for about three to five passes, and you’re all set.

Yau recommends starting from the neck and moving upward to the jawline, cheeks, and forehead to promote proper lymphatic drainage. “For best results, use your gua sha three to five times per week. Daily use can enhance benefits, but overuse may cause sensitivity,” she says. After each use, Yau says it’s important to cleanse tools with warm water and soap to prevent bacteria build-up and unnecessary breakouts.

We’ve all experienced growing pains when adding a new tool to our beauty arsenal. Yau breaks down the most common mistakes she sees when people first attempt to incorporate a gua sha into their regular routine—and shares her top tips on how to avoid them.
