#6421. Gifting, Resale and the Power of Experiences: The Watch Industry Is in Its Customer Service Era

A mixture of high-level customer service, personal experiences, and frictionless shopping has helped watchmakers improve their image and perceived value among consumers this year.

Watch brands’ awareness among consumers is on the rise, and this moves in lockstep with overall positive associations. In this scenario, established brands have strengthened their position, while smaller brands have found fertile ground to grow.

Despite pressure from higher gold prices and a strong Swiss franc that has forced watchmakers to raise prices across the board in recent years, respondents still consider watches a good investment, increasingly purchase them as gifts, and remain loyal to their brands of choice even when confronted with price rises.

The recent excitement around resale schemes, limited editions, in-person services, immediate stock availability and exhibitions spotlights an appetite for proximity, access and the human touch, offering opportunities for brands that can support customers across multiple touchpoints and build communities.

At the top of the innovation table, the best performers — Rolex, Cartier, Omega, Patek Philippe, and Tag Heuer — each maintained their position in the 2026 Vogue Business Watch Index, even improving their score. Rolex keeps its crown for overall consumer sentiment, achieving 99% aided awareness, and Tag Heuer boosts its aided awareness score by 2 percentage points. Despite Breitling, in sixth position, improving its overall brand awareness ranking from 72% to 73%, driven by improvements in aided awareness, the gap with Tag Heuer for overall awareness widened to 8 percentage points.

The most striking result of the Index is that 75% of the brands surveyed have seen their awareness score improve, bringing the overall average awareness score up by 1.6 percentage points, which means the public is more aware of the watch category as a whole and readily recognizes brands.

Chopard takes the crown as the top performer by improving its awareness score by 6 percentage points from 62% last year to 68% this year. It is followed by Longines, A. Lange & Söhne, and Vacheron Constantin, which improved by 4 percentage points, and Piaget, Audemars Piguet, IWC, and Movado, which improved their score by 3 percentage points.

Interestingly, this year the top five brands improved their overall awareness (combined aided and unaided awareness) score by 1 percentage point to an average of 90%, while the other 15 surveyed brands registered a higher increase of 1.8 percentage points. This means the challengers are putting more pressure on the top five, but with an average aggregated awareness of 58.4%, the gap is still wide.

The awareness ranking is particularly relevant because it shows a strong correlation with brand equity, consumer sentiment, and purchase intent, particularly for the top five performers.

But awareness alone does not translate into purchase intent across the board, as purchase intent far lags awareness. Rolex, the top performer, ranked first across all criteria, has only 38% purchase intent, but in a ranking methodology, becomes the “100%” player to which all other brands are indexed. Across the board, purchase intent is relatively flat vs. last year, with actual purchase intent sitting at 16% on average across all brands. This means that brands with relatively modest purchase intent, such as A. Lange & Söhne at 14%, perform above average when ranked (coming in at 58% in the ranking), given the economic pressures on purchase intent. Yet this methodology does expose just how competitive the landscape is. When we rank purchase intent, A. Lange & Söhne is comparable to IWC, despite the latter enjoying significantly higher brand awareness, with aided awareness sitting 25 percentage points higher. In contrast, brands such as Breitling, Hublot and Tudor display high awareness ranking scores (Breitling 73%, Hublot 66%, and Tudor 49%) but actual purchase intent of just 12% and 13%.

Interestingly, brand loyalty has increased to 64.3% vs 63% last year, as consumers resist the temptation to switch to a more affordable brand even if prices increase, with the 45-64 age group having the strongest resolve. Nevertheless, that same demographic demonstrates a higher propensity to explore discounts and resale options, still showing some price sensitivity.

In 2025, Vogue Business asked luxury watch consumers about their watch-buying habits for gifting occasions in the Middle East. This year, we extended that question to all markets. The results reveal interesting motives for buying luxury timepieces, as well as how this varies by local culture.

Overall, key occasions include birthdays (34.1%), Valentine’s Day (29.7%) and Christmas (27.6%), as well as weddings and engagements, particularly for Gen Z (30%) and Gen X (31%). Interestingly, the 40% of luxury consumers who spend more on luxury watches (over $5,000 in the last five years) show a higher propensity to buy luxury watches as gifts for others across every occasion.

Self-gifting has also become a prevalent trend. China is the leading market for personal birthday buys, at 55%, compared with 32% when buying for others. In the Middle East, self-purchasing for birthdays sits at just 32%. Instead, Eid is the leading self-gifting occasion, at 38% — far outpacing buying for others at 24%. This indicates many shoppers are taking advantage of seasonal deals for their own interests. The self-gifting trend also reveals interesting behavior for romantic occasions: a fifth (20%) of luxury consumers in the UK say they have bought themselves luxury watches as an anniversary present in the last two years — double the percentage of French consumers who’ve done the same (10%). Curiously, the opposite is true for weddings and engagements, where only 10% of UK luxury watch consumers shop for this occasion, but 17% of French consumers do. This shows how nuanced gifting occasions are by market, and how the hierarchy of milestones and relationships differs across cultures.

For many years, watch brands have pursued partnerships with the automotive industry, but lately this association seems to be influencing the watchmaking business model, which is increasingly leaning toward the car-making industry’s emphasis on service, a greater focus on experiences and integrated resale options.

When it comes to executing the latter, interestingly, it is the youngest, independent brands such as Richard Mille, MB&F, F.P.Journe and Urwerk that have grasped the importance of owning their secondary market, which leads not only to better control over prices and the products’ retained value but also promotes proximity to clients who, in turn, tend to be more loyal to the brand, act as natural ambassadors, and form communities.

The launch of certified pre-owned schemes has been one of the most significant milestones in the watch industry. While Cartier pioneered the concept in the 1990s, other watch specialists such as Vacheron Constantin and Rolex joined only in the last five years. At the end of October, Audemars Piguet introduced its “Watch Keepers”, its own certified pre-owned program, which will operate as a digital platform enabling sales at a fixed price as well as auctions. It is launching in Europe and Switzerland first before expanding into the United States.

Brand-owned retail platforms allow brands to retain customers who are loyal to the brand but seek more cost-effective options when prices rise. It’s a concern that affects nearly half of all luxury watch consumers, at 47%, with this rising by age as older shoppers say they will shop more for sales and discounts.

Last year’s Vogue Business Watch Index highlighted how brands with low awareness scores were associated with strong purchase intent. This insight is driving brands to purposefully cultivate their niche and strengthen their bond with clients through ad hoc partnerships, without venturing into high-cost, high-visibility collaborations.

The most interesting success story is that of A. Lange & Söhne because, unlike all other brands surveyed, it is not Swiss but German — and its history, which began in 1845 in Glashütte, stalled between 1945 and 1990, when the brand was relaunched.

From the start, A. Lange & Söhne has cultivated its difference, expanded organically, and gradually grown its base of collectors and buyers with a laser focus on products and selected partnerships. The brand forged strong links early on with prestigious cultural institutions in Dresden, the capital of Saxony, where Glashütte is located. These include the brand’s support for the Dresden State Art Collections (Staatliche Kunstsammlungen Dresden) and the Semperoper opera house, which have run for over 20 years. As part of these tie-ups, the brand supported the exhibition “Paula Modersohn-Becker and Edvard Munch. The Big Questions of Life” this year. Such partnerships show collectors who visit the brand’s manufacture how the brand is deeply interwoven into the cultural fabric of the area it comes from.

More recently, A. Lange & Söhne has built on that art legacy by partnering with car events such as the Concours d’Elegance in Hampton Court (UK), Como (Italy) and Newport, Rhode Island (US), known as Audrain Newport Concours & Motor Week. At the end of 2025, the brand opened two new stores, one in London and one in Singapore, while in June this year, it opened its first store in Lisbon.

Other brands following this approach are Jaeger-LeCoultre, with 58% aided awareness, Piaget at 70% awareness, and IWC at 59%. For these brands, criteria such as “its products are a good investment”, “interesting story brand”, and “heritage” seemed to move the needle strongly in consumers’ perceptions.

These brands have all followed the same restrained and laser-focused blueprint. Boasting an uninterrupted history since its founding in 1833 in Le Sentier, Switzerland, Jaeger-LeCoultre has privileged experiences and exhibitions. At the end of last year, the brand inaugurated its installation “The Dream Shaper” in Shanghai, which showcased over 70 archival pieces and celebrated the brand’s heritage in crafting ladies’ watches. The event was attended by the brand’s ambassadors, including South Korean actor Kim Woo-bin. This year, Jaeger-LeCoultre celebrated its signature Reverso design with a series of dedicated in-store experiences, “Reverso Stories”, as well as some limited-edition pieces presented during Homo Faber in Venice in September.

Piaget has strengthened its commitment to the arts by renewing its partnership with The Andy Warhol Foundation, which led to new limited-edition pieces this year. The brand also sponsors the Prix Solo Art Genève, a prize awarded to the best solo show during Art Genève. Meanwhile, IWC has cultivated its difference by continuing its association with Formula 1 and highlighting the uniqueness of its heritage with the launch of IWC. Curated — since the end of 2025, some IWC watches from the Maison’s museum have been selected for reproduction and sold in limited quantities.

Cartier staged the second part of its brand exhibition in Melbourne, Australia; Panerai unveiled a showcase in its hometown of Florence, while Patek Philippe brought its retrospective exhibition to Milan. The exhibition, which ran from October 2-18, showcased over 500 pieces and attracted 68,000 visitors. Analysts agree that such exhibitions not only boost the brand equity of the company organizing them, but also increase the general public’s interest in watchmaking.

This year’s most significant trend was the relaunch of milestone designs that ticked most of the boxes that get consumers excited, namely vintage, heritage and limited editions.

One of the most recent examples is Hublot’s Classic Fusion Tributo, which the brand developed with its founder, Carlo Crocco, who also served as the unofficial ambassador for the occasion, marking the first time he has collaborated with Hublot since selling it to LVMH in 2008.

The new watch, launched in October in Milan this year, is an almost identical reproduction of the model that made Hublot famous in 1980. It features a gold case with screws that also serve as hour indices, mounted on a black rubber strap that, thanks to technological advances, is odorless and does not need to be infused with vanilla like the original 1980s version. The launch allowed clients to meet the brand’s founder and hear directly from him how the watch ended up on the wrist of King Constantine II of Greece, who also gifted one to his brother-in-law, King Juan Carlos of Spain, among other illustrious personalities such as Princess Caroline of Monaco, Elton John and Giorgio Armani.

Hublot’s executive team told the press at the launch that Gen Z’s interest in vintage pieces with a small dial prompted them to launch the project three years early, ahead of the model’s 50th anniversary.

Chopard’s relaunch of the original Happy Diamonds watch also marks the celebration of its 50th anniversary. At a party during New York Fashion Week hosted by brand ambassador Bella Hadid, Chopard introduced the new Happy Sport Heritage, reproducing the original cushion-shaped, golden case framing an onyx dial over which diamonds float freely, and mounted on a black leather strap. Chopard also seized the opportunity to relaunch the original Happy Sport designed in 1993 by the creative director and co-president Caroline Scheufele. Happy Sport was conceived as an evolution of the original Happy Diamonds watch and marked the first time diamonds were paired with steel.

In your latest annual report, client experience is mentioned as a growth pillar. What does it mean?

Watches of Switzerland excels in two very different categories: one-time buyers and serial collectors who own hundreds of timepieces. This means we have to offer a variety of services to satisfy the very different demands of these two groups.

For example, those who only buy one or two watches in their lives may welcome our financing options, as well as the education our salespeople provide to help them buy with confidence something they can treasure and pass on. For dedicated collectors, we focus on providing access to exceptional timepieces and bringing them closer to the brands and the world of watchmaking.

We regularly treat our best clients to manufacturer visits, take them to watch fairs such as Watches and Wonders, and secure exceptional watches. For example, this week, we are inviting them to discover all the timepieces recognized with prestigious GPHG watchmaking awards (Grand Prix d'Horlogerie de Genève), including the independent Rexhep Rexhepi and the gem-set Piaget Sautoir watch.

Watches of Switzerland’s Knightsbridge store. About half of the retailer’s business comes from supply-limited brands such as Rolex and Patek Philippe, and it uses AI to decide what else goes in its windows.

Stock availability is a top priority for clients. What do you do to ensure your stores have the right products?

About half of our business relies on brands such as Rolex and Patek Philippe, which have limited supply and are sold to customers who have waited patiently. But we use artificial intelligence tools to identify trends. For example, when customers browse our watches online, our tool ignores the brand and detects specific watch attributes, such as case size, price point, and strap material; these criteria help us adjust our stock accordingly.

How do you turn digital activity into a commercial opportunity?

Unlike other apparel items, watches can be appreciated even more online, as we can show minute details that are not visible to the naked eye, and we can even show the movement, the beating heart of a timepiece, which is often hidden. We, of course, offer online chats with experts, and one of our points of difference is that we own Hodinkee, the most trusted online watch magazine, with shopping links to our website.

Women are becoming more important for the watch industry; how are you supporting this growth?

Our new store in Glasgow is a good example: the team there is led by a woman, and the salesforce is evenly split 50-50 between men and women. We also have three watchmakers in residence to service timepieces: one man and two women.

The Vogue Business consumer sentiment ranking assesses brands based on consumers’ opinions and willingness to buy. The criteria analyzed range from basic brand awareness to brand loyalty and purchase intent. Brands are also evaluated on perceived quality, with survey participants answering questions about customer service, in-store experience, design, and sustainability, among others. Respondents have also appraised a brand’s storytelling, role in society, perceived timelessness, digital content, trust, and sense of style.

#6420. The Secret to the Creamiest Mac and Cheese Comes in a Can

Making a truly excellent bowl of mac and cheese shouldn't take an entire afternoon. Here's the one ingredient I rely on to get the creamiest cheese sauce every time.

I’ve made enough macaroni and cheese over the years to have developed some fairly strong opinions about it. Having two kids has given me plenty of opportunities to experiment, from throwing together the familiar blue box to baking versions that require several kinds of cheese and a considerable amount of attention. I appreciate a proper cheese sauce as much as anyone, but there are evenings when dirtying another saucepan to make a roux and standing over the stove with a whisk feels like an unreasonable amount of ceremony for a bowl of macaroni.

Which is why I’m particularly fond of a method that requires just three ingredients: pasta, grated cheese and evaporated milk. It produces an exceptionally creamy mac and cheese without butter, flour or any of the usual fuss, and it’s so simple that even boxed mac begins to look complicated.

Evaporated milk is regular milk that’s been heated until about 60% of its water is gone. The result is thicker and more concentrated than ordinary milk, with a richness that makes it especially useful for cheese sauces.

More importantly, those concentrated milk proteins help the cheese melt into a smooth, cohesive sauce. Ordinarily, adding cheese directly to hot liquid can be a temperamental business. The fat may separate, the proteins can tighten up, and the sauce can become grainy instead of silky. Evaporated milk helps keep everything together, doing much of the work that a traditional flour-and-butter roux would otherwise accomplish.

One of the things I like most about this method is how little precision it demands. If you’re cooking a pound of macaroni, start with a 12-ounce can of evaporated milk and roughly 12 to 16 ounces of grated cheese. Sharp cheddar provides plenty of flavor, while Monterey Jack or fontina will give you a smooth melt. I generally prefer a combination, but there’s no reason to make a special trip to the store if you already have a perfectly good block of cheese in the refrigerator.

I do recommend grating the cheese yourself, since the anti-caking ingredients in bagged shredded cheese can keep it from melting smoothly. Beyond that, there’s plenty of room for flexibility. There’s no need to measure everything down to the last ounce, which is part of what makes this method so wonderful.

Boil the pasta in generously salted water as you normally would, then strain it and return it to the pot, reserving about a cup of pasta water. Add the cheese and evaporated milk, warming them gently over low heat. Keep stirring until everything melts into a smooth sauce, adding splashes of pasta water as you go until it reaches your desired consistency.

The same trick works beautifully in more elaborate recipes, whether you’re making a baked southern mac and cheese, a big pan of potluck mac and cheese or a comforting crockpot mac and cheese. All have their merits, but for an ordinary weeknight, I rather like knowing that one pot, three ingredients, and about as much time as it takes to boil pasta are all I need.

#6419. I Tested Peloton's New, More Affordable Folding Treadmill

In my mind and, I think the minds of many others, Peloton has always been a stationary bike brand. The Bike, after all, was its first product, turning the Peloton name into a catch-all term for at-home cycling that we now hear everywhere, from broadcasts of the Tour de France and Giro d'Italia to television sitcoms. (A running gag online is that Peloton's upscale, soothing video workout content is worlds away from The Office's Dwight Schrute leading a group of stationary riders off an imaginary cliff.)

Nevertheless, Peloton actually has been making treadmills since 2018. The first Tread delivered the same proposition as the Bike: premium hardware that looks good enough to bring out of the basement, as well as access to interactive, instructor-led runs and HIIT classes on a big, immersive screen. Over the years, Peloton has brought improvements to that first Tread: larger screens, voice controls, AI-informed movement tracking for form analysis and coaching.

The new Tread Flex, however, heads in a slightly different direction. It has a simpler belt, simpler speakers, a smaller screen. It's $1,300 cheaper than the next step up, and $4,500 cheaper (!) than Peloton's slat belt-equipped Tread+ Vision. Its affordability isn't even its main selling point, however, because the Tread Flex has a nifty final trick: it folds up to save space.

Could these space and money-saving tactics make the Tread as popular as the Bike? Well, I run nearly every day, and ever since a tester Tread Flex showed up at my door, I've been doing it indoors much more frequently. In my experience, here's what makes Peloton's latest worth considering.

Treadmills tend to have a problem that stationary bikes don't: the nicer they get, the bigger they get. Premium models have larger motors and roomier running platforms. In short, they're heavy. (The Tread+ Vision is a hefty 460 pounds.) The Tread Flex is 170 pounds less, and that's crucial to its ability to fold up, because that feature wouldn't be much of a selling point if it felt like adding a power clean to the end of every run.

In reality, stowing the Tread Flex is quite easy. You just lift up the running deck from the end and push it forward until a hydraulic cylinder locks into place. There's a pin clip to lock it. To drop it down, you push forward on the deck and then on the hydraulic support, then walk it back. At about 45 degrees, the hydraulics take over completely; you can go put on your running shoes while a gentle thump lets you know the deck is back on the ground.

Folding up the Tread Flex drops its area from about 16.5 square feet to half that. (The Tread+ Vision is around 19.25.) Just as importantly, I've discovered, is that lifting the deck brings the machine up onto a set of locking wheels. I've kept mine in a designated corner, but it's so easy to move that it wouldn't be much hassle to wheel it out and lower it for every workout, if your space required it. Get your cardio out of the way, then get your cardio out of the way.

Okay, so folding and moving a treadmill might be a pain if you're using it every day. But I suspect if you're running that often, you're doing some of it outside. I live less than an hour away from the Canadian border, and run on roads and trails five or six times a week all year round. Good layers get you pretty far, and there's a reason why run clubs continue to boom while SoulCycle-adjacent Mile High Run Club closed all its studios this year.

Treadmills are for something else. They're for a warm-up prior to lifting, or for bootcamp-style HIIT workouts that combine sprinting intervals with weight intervals. The prioritization value of time spent doing these doesn't seem to align with the space investment a treadmill requires if you don't have a pool house or big garage. (I have a sun porch-slash-mudroom where I keep firewood and ski boots in the winter and a napping couch in the summer.)

This is how, I think, the Tread Flex makes the ultimate proposition as the ideal home treadmill. A treadmill doesn't replace a usual running routine; it adds to it. On Monday I do my usual seven miles down the road and back on the river trails; on Tuesday I let Andy Speer kick my ass with sprints and kickstand deadlifts. (And, sure, when it's -10° and blowing in late January, I might run inside, now that I have the option.)

None of the above would matter as much if it came at the cost of quality. I've run on hotel treadmills that sound like your grandma's washing machine and feel similar to how they look, i.e., stomping around on hollow plastic. The Tread Flex may not have the cushioned slat belt the Tread+ Vision has, but it's definitely not that.

What it does have is a spec that's right in line with top-notch treadmills. Its max speed is 12.5 miles per hour (a 4:48 mile, in runner's units), a 12.5% max incline grade (but no decline), and a 20-inch by 59-inch running surface that, though not cushioned, feels good to run on. The swiveling screen is nice and big at 21.5 inches, with HD resolution and a touchscreen interface. I particularly like how adjusting speed and incline is done with rolling knobs, which feel much better—and more natural—to engage with than buttons when you're gasping at threshold pace.

On top of that is Peloton's interactive experience: You can take live classes where you can pit yourself against others and get kudos from the instructor. The pre-recorded catalogue includes thousands of classes for yoga, Pilates, and meditation, in addition to strength and the running, cycling, and rowing the company makes machines for.

The Tread Flex also provides personalized training plans, smart pacing guidance based on where you're at, automatically adjusting incline for classes, and of course leaderboards and an entire ecosystem of badges and achievements to earn, if you're into all that. For $50 per year, that is.

Oh, and did I mention it's a good-looking machine? It's sleek; an attractive, soft-edged Z with a minimal screen instead of a board of colorful buttons. Nobody's throwing around the word "console" to describe this thing. That's good; home gym setups deserve different consideration than gym rigs. If images of Crunch Fitness flash through your head every time you glance into the corner, something has missed the mark.

Where Peloton's Tread Vision treadmills are clearly high-end, the Tread Flex toes the line against mainstream consumer models. Its features match up with some of the most popular machines, and its price, while at the higher end of the spectrum, does too. But the Tread Flex gets there with more style, and with Peloton's huge ecosystem of live and archived class content.

So, if we're looking at other treadmills out there, my quick answer is yes. The Tread Flex is the utilitarian Peloton Treadmill, but it's still a Peloton treadmill.

How you answer this question really requires asking yourself a series of other questions first. What do you want a treadmill for? How much do you want to invest? Do you want access to fitness classes—especially ones other than running—and are you okay with the $50/month subscription fee?

Form factor and access to classes and content are non-negotiables. The Tread Flex might be Peloton's new entry-level treadmill, but it's far from a simple running machine. Flex refers to that nifty fold-up feature, but also to this treadmill's ability to integrate into an exercise program that also includes strength training, HIIT workouts, yoga, and on and on.

As a runner who prefers to log miles outside whenever possible, I was encouraged by how much I enjoyed running on the Tread Flex. The classes are fun, and Peloton's instructors are real pros, but even in Just Run mode, the Tread Flex proved responsive and comfy. It's getting dark around 4:30 PM these days, and my daylight windows for running on the well-used roads around me have narrowed like a Death Star trash compactor. It's nice to know I can snag seven miles after sundown if need be.

Well, if you aren't limited by space or cash, the Tread Vision and Tread+ Vision get you bigger screens, AI-enabled running form feedback and coaching, and a more cushioned, broader running area. If you just prefer running or walking on a treadmill to doing it outside, investing more heavily in a treadmill is worth considering (though the Tread Flex will still be great).

The Tread Flex's real competition is the NordicTrack Commercial 1750, which you'll find recommended on just about every treadmill buying guide on the internet. The machines are similar in function and specs, but there are some differences. The NordicTrack's running surface is two inches wider and one inch longer; it has a slightly more powerful motor; it can decline to -3% grade; its belt is slightly cushioned; it has a built-in fan; and NordicTrack's class and entertainment platform, iFit, is cheaper at $39 a month.

In comparison, the Tread Flex takes up slightly less space, has a higher max speed (12.5 mph over 12 mph), a steeper incline (12.5% over 12%), and a larger screen (21.5 inches over 16 inches). The rolling knobs to adjust speed and incline are nicer to use. My partner, who designs commercial and residential interior spaces, agrees with me that the Tread Flex is a better-looking machine.

List price for the Tread Flex is $300 cheaper, but the NordicTrack seems to be perpetually on sale. So it might come down to looks, that 3% decline, or what class platform you'd like to buy into.

#6418. This Egg Wash Secret Makes the Prettiest Pie Crusts Every Time

The secret to a beautifully golden Thanksgiving pie might be the simplest ingredient in your kitchen.

Thanksgiving pies have a way of bringing out the perfectionist in even the most relaxed bakers. Yet you might spend half an hour creating the perfect pie dough design, carefully crimping the edges or cutting little leaves from scraps of pastry, only to pull the finished pie from the oven and discover that your beautiful handiwork has browned unevenly. It’s a small disappointment in the grand scheme of things, but after all that effort, a little indignation is understandable.

An egg wash is supposed to give pastry a lovely golden color and delicate sheen, but getting it to cooperate isn’t always as simple as beating an egg and picking up a pastry brush. Fortunately, there’s an easy trick that makes a noticeable difference, and it comes courtesy of a familiar face in the baking world: Great British Baking Show judge Paul Hollywood.

Paul’s secret is simply to add a pinch of salt to the beaten egg. He lets it sit for about five minutes before brushing it onto pastry dough. In a BBC Food demonstration, Paul uses the technique to glaze scones, but it works just as well for giving pie crusts a beautiful, even finish.

Beat an egg with a small pinch of salt until they’re well combined, then set the mixture aside for a few minutes. Give it another quick stir before brushing a thin, even layer over the pastry. The amount of salt won’t affect the flavor, and there’s no reason to make any other adjustments to your favorite pie recipe.

The difference is subtle but useful. Instead of clinging stubbornly to your pastry brush or collecting in the little crevices of a crimped edge, the egg wash spreads more easily.

If you’ve ever tried brushing a plain beaten egg onto pastry, you’ve probably noticed that it can be surprisingly thick and stringy. That’s because the proteins in the egg give it structure—a nuisance if you need to spread it evenly. Adding salt loosens those proteins, making the egg wash thinner and more fluid after a few minutes. It glides over the pastry more smoothly, leaving a light, even coating rather than stringy puddles.

The egg itself is what gives pastry its golden color and glossy sheen. Salt doesn’t make the crust magically browner; it simply helps the egg wash do its job better. The result is a more consistent finish, particularly around the edges and decorative details where egg wash tends to collect.

A pinch of salt won’t turn a lopsided pie into a masterpiece, but it can help a well-made crust look its best. And after we’ve spent an unreasonable amount of time weaving strips of pastry into a lattice for a Thanksgiving pie, I think we’re entitled to a little help with the finishing touches.

#6417. Who Topped the 2026 Vogue Business Watch Index?

Following a challenging 2025, 2026 has offered some green shoots for the luxury watch industry.

Overall Swiss export value has grown by 2.7%, driven by unexpected pockets of growth in emerging markets (India +28.5%, Thailand +8.6% and Mexico +6.2%), which offset drops in traditionally strong markets like China (-5.9%) and Saudi Arabia (-10.3%). The latest consumer research from Vogue Business highlights nuanced market trends, underscoring the need for watch brands to pay particular attention to local cultural needs. In China, for example, despite a broader market slowdown, 55% of luxury watch consumers surveyed have bought themselves a timepiece to celebrate their birthday. Recognizing these behaviors can help brands make their messaging more impactful — a strategy that will become increasingly important as shoppers rely more on emerging channels to discover products and brands.

The digital audit highlights how brands are appointing high-profile cultural influencers in newer markets, from K-pop stars to Thai actors, as brand ambassadors. As the geography of growth shifts, so too must campaign strategies.

And while mainstream sports like motoring and equestrianism have historically provided key partnerships for luxury watches, more niche sports are helping brands reach new audiences. Yet our digital analysis also exposes some tensions the industry is grappling with; the channels relied on for sourcing trusted information are not always the channels consumers use to discover new brands and products and, as use of generative AI becomes more widespread, brands will need to adapt their digital strategies to boost visibility in this emerging space. Opportunities also remain to strengthen the omnichannel experience, with our survey highlighting shopper frustration over limited online service options.

In a market steeped in tradition, established leaders have defended their positions in the ranking, while collaborations with the worlds of film and art are helping legacy brands stay fresh. Consumers also continue to favor buying directly from brands, with 47.8% on average having bought their most recent watches this way or from multibrand specialists (22.5% on average). Yet while brand awareness has risen year on year, purchase intent remains relatively flat, even as enthusiasm for resale grows. As much as the availability of digital product passports (DPPs) and authentication services may encourage shoppers to engage with resale platforms, economic pressures expose a bigger driver: price sensitivity. Older consumers are particularly likely to wait for sales and discounts before making a purchase. This suggests that the demand for innovation in the pre-loved watch environment is as much a reflection of price sensitivity as it is the result of improved services in this space. It also means that, over the coming year, luxury watch brands will need to work harder to defend those “brand new” watch sales in the primary market.

Cartier retains its leadership position for the third year. This summer, Cartier added actor PP Krit Amnuaydechkorn to its portfolio of Thai ambassadors, which already includes singer and actor Jeff Satur, actress Kimberley Anne Woltemas and actor Tor Thanapob Leeratanakachorn. This has helped it to maintain momentum on platforms like Instagram and gain ground on TikTok. Yet while awareness has risen, consumer opinion is more mixed, with small declines in perception of innovation, value for money and experience, showing even leaders cannot rest on their laurels.

Improved consumer perception, the highest recognition and highest purchase intent have helped Rolex to secure the second spot in this year’s ranking. The availability of certified pre-owned Rolexes at official stockists means the brand is well-positioned to take advantage of the rising demand for pre-loved luxury timepieces. Small but steady gains on all Western social media platforms have also helped the brand to stay front of mind for consumers in a cluttered digital landscape.

Omega narrowly misses out on second place this year. The brand benefits from high awareness and improved perception across several metrics. Its strong digital performance is helped by high-profile collaborations, for example, its James Bond/Spectre partnerships, but the provision of omnichannel features and innovation performance leave room for growth.

After breaking into the top five last year, Tag Heuer has managed to hold on to fourth position. The brand benefits from significant gains in consumer awareness, perception of quality, and positive association with more emotional drivers, as well as increased purchase intent in a market where this is relatively flat. Against a backdrop of rising price sensitivity, its positioning may help it to weather a volatile economic period.

After two years spent in sixth position, IWC moves into the top five for the first time this year. The brand ranks second for both Digital and Innovation, with a focused strategy on social media helping it reach new audiences. Its ongoing partnership with F1 is also helping to recruit more female followers, while its IWC.Inspired series celebrates women from all walks of life. Meanwhile, its partnership with Watchfinder enables consumers to part-exchange pre-loved IWC timepieces when making their next purchase, providing a seamless way to engage with the increasingly relevant resale market.

Twenty brands are assessed for the Vogue Business Watch Index, with brand performance evaluated against over 100 data points spanning consumer sentiment, digital marketing and innovation.

The weightings of each assessment category and their metrics are determined by industry relevance and importance to the consumer, allowing for an objective assessment of a brand’s performance. The final weighting for each category is agreed upon following a review process with our data analysts and expert editors. This year, we removed Chinese platforms from our digital audit due to lack of data availability, with weightings being reassigned proportionally to retained digital platforms (Facebook, Instagram, YouTube, TikTok and Google Search).

Consumer research remains fundamental to the Vogue Business Watch Index, with readers across several Condé Nast titles — including Vogue, GQ, Vanity Fair and Condé Nast Traveler — participating in an annual consumer sentiment survey that ensures granularity is achieved when it comes to understanding awareness, customer challenges and brand perception. This year, we surveyed 1,020 qualified luxury watch consumers in seven markets (the US, UK, France, Germany, Italy, the Middle East and China). Among them, 60% of luxury watch consumers spent between €1,500 and €4,999 on luxury watches in the last five years, while 40% spent over €5,000.

Future iterations of the Vogue Business Watch Index will continue to maximize the brands, metrics, and digital platforms assessed, with additions prioritized in line with industry needs and developments.

#6414. This Is What Was on the Menu at the First Thanksgiving in 1621

Somehow, turkey has spent the last four centuries getting all the glory.

For a meal that has been discussed, depicted and reenacted for more than four centuries, the first Thanksgiving has left us surprisingly few details about what anyone actually ate. We know there were roughly 140 people, three days of feasting and exactly five deer. Beyond that, the historical record is rather unhelpful. Apparently, nobody thought to write down the menu.

The gathering took place in Plymouth in the fall of 1621, when about 50 English colonists celebrated their first successful harvest alongside 90 Wampanoag, including their leader, Ousamequin, better known to history as Massasoit. It was a meeting between two communities whose relationship was far more complicated than the cheerful scene that would eventually find its way into American classrooms. Although they had formed an alliance earlier that year, cultural differences and tensions of an English settlement on Wampanoag land were hardly going to disappear over dinner.

And while the English had much to celebrate in bringing in their first harvest, they owed a great deal of that success to Indigenous knowledge. The Wampanoag understood the region’s growing seasons, its waterways and the foods that could be grown and gathered in the surrounding landscape. Their traditions had helped sustain communities there long before the colonists arrived.

The two surviving English accounts of the gathering offer only a few details about the feast itself, but taken together with what historians know about the food traditions of both communities, they give us a rather interesting picture of what may have been on the table.

Edward Winslow, one of the English colonists who attended the gathering, recorded that the Wampanoag went hunting and returned with five deer, which they presented to the colony’s leaders. It’s one of the few specific foods mentioned in his account and an especially substantial contribution to a celebration that lasted three days.

Deer were an important source of food for the Wampanoag, who also made use of their hides, bones and other materials. In England, however, deer hunting was largely reserved for the wealthy, making venison something most ordinary people rarely got to enjoy. The meat may have been roasted over a fire or simmered in a hearty venison stew, although Winslow neglected to tell us how it was prepared. We know exactly how many deer arrived, but what became of them in the kitchen remains a mystery.

Roast turkey has become so thoroughly associated with Thanksgiving that it’s difficult to imagine the holiday without one occupying the center of the table. The trouble is, we don’t actually know whether turkey was served at the original celebration.

Winslow wrote that four Englishmen went hunting for wildfowl and returned with enough to feed the colonists for nearly a week. What he didn’t do was tell us which birds they shot. Wild turkeys were present in the region, but so were ducks, geese and other game birds, all perfectly suitable for roasting over a fire. There’s every possibility that turkey was on the menu, but nothing to suggest it enjoyed the distinction we’ve since bestowed upon it. For all we know, the centerpiece was a duck, and we’ve spent the last few centuries giving credit to the wrong bird.

Corn was one of the most important foods available to both communities, although the English were relatively new to growing it. The Wampanoag had cultivated maize for generations, developing agricultural practices suited to the region’s soil and growing seasons. Their knowledge was enormously valuable to the colonists, whose first attempts at establishing a food supply had been anything but fruitful.

One traditional Wampanoag preparation was nasaump, a thick porridge made from ground corn, sometimes cooked with other ingredients. Corn could also be ground into meal for simple breads, early relatives of the cornbread we bake today, or used to thicken stews and make other hearty dishes.

The waters around Plymouth were full of food, provided you knew where to look and how to catch it. The Wampanoag had long fished the region’s rivers and coastline, gathering shellfish and catching everything from bass and cod to eels. Clams, mussels and lobsters were plentiful too.

The English were beginning to take advantage of these resources by 1621. William Bradford, the Plymouth colony’s governor, wrote of the colonists catching substantial quantities of cod and bass during the summer. A freshly caught fish could be roasted or boiled, while clams and mussels might be cooked over a fire. Lobster was another plentiful local catch that was enjoyed regularly. The variety of ocean fare available might have made for a Thanksgiving spread that looked rather more like a seafood boil than the feast we know today.

Squash and pumpkin were important crops in Wampanoag agriculture, and their ability to keep well after harvest made them especially useful as the colder weather set in. Both could be roasted, boiled or added to stews, much like we still prepare winter squash today, though without the benefit of a balsamic glaze.

The English called pumpkins pompions, a name I think we abandoned prematurely. They were familiar with the vegetable, although the varieties growing in New England differed from those they might have seen at home. A pumpkin dish would have been entirely plausible at the harvest celebration, but anyone hoping for a slice of pumpkin pie would have to wait almost two centuries. The colonists had limited supplies of wheat flour, butter and sugar, and the familiar custard-filled pie wouldn’t appear in American cookbooks until 1796.

The Wampanoag grew beans alongside corn and squash, three crops that complemented each other remarkably well. Cornstalks supported climbing beans, while squash vines spread across the ground and helped shade the soil. The combination was as useful in the garden as it was on the plate.

A traditional Wampanoag stew called sobaheg combines ingredients like corn, beans, squash and meat or fish, depending on what’s available or in season. The combination of corn and beans also appears in succotash, another dish with Indigenous New England roots that remains an American favorite.

The forests and wetlands of New England offered plenty beyond cultivated crops. Chestnuts, walnuts, hazelnuts, acorns, wild grapes and cranberries were among the foods the Wampanoag knew how to gather and prepare, each with its own season and uses.

Nuts could be eaten plain, stored or ground into meal, while fruits could be enjoyed fresh or preserved for later. Acorns required particular attention, since their natural bitterness had to be leached out with water before they could be used in cooking. It’s one of the few ingredients we’ve more or less surrendered entirely to the squirrels.

Of all the wild fruits available, cranberries have perhaps the most recognizable place on a modern Thanksgiving table. Their natural tartness eventually found a friend in sugar, giving rise to the cranberry sauce that’s become nearly as much a part of the holiday as the turkey itself.

#6413. 30 Classic Photos of John F. Kennedy Jr., in Honor of His 66th Birthday

If you weren’t familiar with John F. Kennedy Jr. in the ’90s, chances are that you are now, thanks to the overwhelming popularity of Love Story, this year’s hit FX series about the marriage of President John F. Kennedy’s son to fashion publicist and style icon Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy, and the couple’s tragic death in 1999.

Love Story may have piqued Gen Z’s interest in “John-John,” as John F. Kennedy Jr. was known in the press, but the real man would have turned 66 today. In his honor, we’re taking a look back at some of the images that helped define the presidential scion’s public persona.

President John F. Kennedy and his wife, Jackie, during the christening of their son, John Jr., in the chapel at Georgetown University Hospital. John Jr.—dressed in the same gown his father had worn in 1917—was just 13 days old at the time.

As the New York Times reported: “The child, christened John Fitzgerald Kennedy Jr., gave one subdued cry during the eleven-minute ritual and opened his eyes when a news photographer took his picture. Otherwise the baby appeared relaxed and drowsy.”

A young JFK Jr. playing with his mother’s ropes of pearls at the White House.

President John F. Kennedy walking with his toddler son along the White House’s West Wing colonnade.

John F. Kennedy Jr. was just three days shy of his third birthday when his father was killed in Dallas in November 1963. Here, he’s pictured with his mother and his older sister, Caroline, during President Kennedy’s funeral ceremony.

Awaiting his results at St. Bernard’s 17th Annual Horse Show in New Jersey, where his sister also competed.

Feathery-haired and 10-ish, hitting a forehand return in Central Park.

Posing with Willie Mays at New York’s Shea Stadium.

With a head full of curls—and his first cousin Anthony Radziwill—at the kickoff party for that year’s Robert F. Kennedy Memorial Tennis Tournament in New York.

Celebrating his graduation from Phillips Academy, Andover.

Cutting a lithe figure—and carrying a boombox!—in Hyannis Port.

Kennedy as Bonario in a production of Ben Jonson’s Volpone during his freshman year at Brown.

Wearing cowboy boots with his graduation robes on Commencement Day at Brown. (His bachelor’s degree was in American Studies.)

In a jaunty little red bow tie at a fundraising event.

With his cousin Maria Shriver at Caroline Kennedy’s wedding to Edwn Schlossberg on Cape Cod. (Caroline’s dress was by Carolina Herrera.)

Looking matinee-idol handsome during a portrait session in New York.

Speaking to the press about passing the New York bar examination on his third attempt. (He also passed the bar in Connecticut.)

Enjoying a courtside snack at the US Open.

At the HBO premiere of The Attack of the 50 Foot Woman—starring his then-girlfriend Darryl Hannah—in Los Angeles.

Outside of his mother’s building with his sister, his brother-in-law, and Mrs. Onassis’s diamond dealer—and “private companion”—Maurice Tempelsman following her death. The funeral Mass took place a few blocks away, at the Church of St. Ignatius Loyola on Park Avenue and East 84th Street, before her body was flown to Washington, DC, to be buried beside her first husband.

During a press conference announcing the launch of his political magazine, George.

With his then-fiancée, Carolyn Bessette, at an event. Bessette’s engagement ring—said to be modeled after one worn by Kennedy’s mother—was made of round-cut sapphires and diamonds on a platinum band.

The couple at a fundraising gala for the Whitney Museum.

Turning his camera—a Leica Minilux point-and-shoot—back on the paparazzi outside his Tribeca apartment.

Exiting their building on North Moore Street.

Bessette-Kennedy and Kennedy back home in New York after their wedding on Cumberland Island, Georgia.

Meeting with President Bill Clinton in the Oval Office.

Looking plenty sportif, walking Friday in New YorK.

Attending the Municipal Art Society’s presentation of the Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis Medal—formerly the President’s Medal—to Stephen Swid.

#6412. I Tested 6 Popular Store-Bought Pumpkin Pies to Find the Best One for Thanksgiving Dinner

Sometimes, all there's time for on Thanksgiving is buying a store-bought pumpkin pie. I tested six to find out which one tasted the most homemade.

Planning, shopping and preparing a full Thanksgiving dinner is a Herculean task for even the most experienced home cook. There are many moving parts, and it can certainly be overwhelming when there is a houseful of hungry guests ready to dive into the biggest family meal of the year. That’s why I think there is no shame in turning to store-bought options for some elements of the meal. If baking isn’t your forte, but you still want to offer a traditional pumpkin pie for dessert, stores across the country are ready to help.

I recently drove around town and picked up pies from six major grocery store chains so I could conduct an official taste test before the big day. The contenders are:

I sampled and ranked each one based on overall appearance, the flavor and texture of the crust, and, finally, the consistency of the filling and spices used. I was certainly surprised by my top choice.

Coming in at the bottom of my ranked list is the Bakeshop pumpkin pie from Aldi. This 8-inch pie is 1-1/2 pounds and costs $5.29. Before cutting a slice, I noticed that the crust on this pie was quite pale. So much so, I even checked the label to make sure I wasn’t expected to bake it before serving. When I took a bite, the taste was what I would expect from an undercooked crust. It was gummy and almost tasted raw. The filling was quite sweet, with the sugar, brown sugar and molasses flavors being the most prevalent and the pumpkin pie spices taking a backseat.

Bottom Line: The pumpkin pie from Aldi is a bargain at only $5.29, but the undercooked, super-sweet filling didn’t impress.

Selling for a bargain at $4.94, the pumpkin pie from Walmart was the least expensive pie I sampled. This 8-inch pie is 1 pound, 6 ounces. You might notice from the photograph that with this pie, the crust separated from the filling after cutting a slice. Sometimes this occurs when the custard is overcooked. Once again, I wasn’t impressed with the color of the crust and hoped for more browning and flavor. The filling also had a similar overly sweet taste that I noticed in the Aldi pie. I wish the spices in this pie were kicked up a notch or two as well.

Bottom Line: The price of a Walmart pumpkin pie can’t be beat, but the dessert isn’t the most flavorful of those I tested. Next time I might jazz it up with some spiced pecans just before serving.

The pumpkin pie from Trader Joe’s was quite different from all the other pies in this sample group. Right out of the box, I noticed both the crust and the filling were a deep brown color. Quite a departure from some of the other anemic-looking pies. Selling for $6.99, this 9-inch pie is larger and heavier at 1 pound, 9.4 ounces. Reading the ingredient list, this pie included cinnamon, nutmeg, ginger, cloves and allspice. As someone who loves these flavors, I couldn’t wait to dive in.

This pie definitely didn’t hold back. The flavors are very bold, and the crust is well-browned. However, these spices are so bold that you almost lose the pumpkin’s flavor. This pie might have benefited from pulling back slightly on the spices to further highlight the star of the show, aka the pumpkin.

Bottom Line: If you like very bold pumpkin pie spices, this dessert from Trader Joe’s will fit the bill. However, the strong flavor might be divisive around the dinner table.

Marie Callender’s is a brand known for pies, and you can pick up an unbaked pie in the freezer section of many grocery stores for a budget-friendly $5.97. It weighs 2 pounds, 4 ounces, and measures 8-1/2 inches across. There are both benefits and drawbacks to purchasing an unbaked pie. Since it’s kept frozen, there’s no need for a bunch of preservatives and fillers used in some of the shelf-stable pies I picked up at other stores. However, when you have to bake the pie yourself, there is room for user error and a risk of an overbaked or underbaked dessert.

In terms of flavor and texture, this pie was middle-of-the-road across the board. The crust was good, it just wasn’t a showstopper that I’d be excited to bring to the table. I appreciated the creamy filling, but once again, I just wanted a more pumpkin-forward flavor.

Bottom Line: The flavor and texture of the Marie Callender’s crust was delightful, but it was not as visually appealing as some other store-bought options.

At almost 2-1/2 pounds and 10 inches in diameter, the $7.99 pumpkin pie from Kroger (Mariano’s in my neck of the woods) was the largest of the pumpkin pies in this taste test. In addition, the perfectly fluted crust on this pie was lovely. It looked homemade and baked to perfection. The most prevalent flavor in the filling is cinnamon, with nutmeg, allspice and ginger lingering in the background. The pie cut well and sat nicely on the serving plate, but had a slightly gelatinous texture rather than a rich, creamy custard consistency. I would certainly buy this pie again, but next time I think I would kick it up a notch by serving with a bourbon whipped cream to really wow my guests.

Bottom Line: This was the most visually impressive pumpkin pie on the list and one that I’d be proud to present at the dessert table.

The pumpkin pie at my local Albertson’s (we call it Jewel in the Chicago area) is just shy of 8 inches wide and weighs 1 pound, 4 ounces for $7.99. Ultimately, in this taste test, this pie came closer to tasting homemade than any other option. This was the only pie I found that struck the ideal balance between warm fall spices and signature pumpkin flavor. I loved the prevalent cinnamon notes and the velvety texture of the filling. The crust was attractively presented and perfectly baked. It was actually the smallest of the pies I sampled and on the higher end in terms of price, but every bite was worth it.

Bottom Line: If I’m not making a homemade pumpkin pie this year, I’ll be relying on Albertson’s to do the work for me!

Which store-bought pie is your fave? Let us know in the comments below!

#6411. In Alison Roman's World, Curation is King

With only weeks before opening, Alison Roman’s Brooklyn brick-and-mortar is still unfinished. “Today they’re doing up the walls and putting in the floors,” Roman says. In short, it does not yet look like a dreamy European-inspired grocer. There are still a mountain of calls to be made, meetings to be had, speed bumps to overcome.

The chaos doesn’t seem to be getting to the cookbook author, chef, and aspiring empire-builder. “It’s been so fun,” Roman, a Bon Appétit alum, says of the process. Perhaps that shouldn’t be a surprise; this breezy effortlessness is at the bedrock of the Alison Roman universe. You know the kind of nonchalant magic I’m talking about: chilling wine bottles in a bathtub of ice, buckets of take-out fried chicken at dinner parties—I mean, this woman was one of the foremost proponents of brothy beans.

What Roman has built has grown beyond recipes and bean propaganda. The ever-creeping edges of her lifestyle brand now encompass a jarred tomato sauce brand, once cheekily titled A Very Good Sauce, now renamed Roman’s. There’s also the new podcast, Having People Over, where she hosts guests for a meal and a yap, plus the speaking tour she’s calling “Food, Life and Other Strong Opinions.” There are the shoes (sleek mules and chunky clogs) she made in collaboration with New York–based footwear brand Margaux. And now First Bloom, the grocery store–slash–wine bar–slash–café that—as of mid-November—is on track to open in December.

The Brooklyn shop is an extension of the original Catskill’s location of the same name. Roman says this new outpost is “a totally different proposition of what we are offering people.” There’s more budget to work with, there’s more staff, there’s more space, and there’s more food.

Whereas the upstate location’s function is closer to utility—meat and produce from local farms are a major feature—in Brooklyn (where specialty grocers abound) Roman is focusing on something more akin to world-building. But do not call First Bloom a shoppy shop, those whimsically designed boutiques that seem to pop up everywhere selling the same $45 squiggly candlesticks and squeeze-bottle olive oils everyone seems to have. “I think ‘shoppy shop’ is derogatory,” Roman says. “In a world where you can buy anything from anywhere, sometimes it’s nice to be told what to do.”

At Brooklyn’s First Bloom, the shelves will be stocked with products that Roman herself deems “hyper-defensible.” There’s a reason they’re stocked, and a reason for how they’re priced. They’re best in class or a personal favorite of Roman’s. “Perspective and curation is a really special thing to be able to convey,” she says.

The vision for First Bloom is set, but with the opening just a month out, Roman doesn’t have all the details nailed down. “We are going to have a rotisserie chicken,” she says. “I don’t know how much it’s going to cost yet,” she follows up quickly, before I can ask. There will also be a couple salads and a couple sandwiches on offer—plus another secret off-menu sandwich for the neighborhood regulars and the real Roman-heads who know to ask for it. “I’m very if-you-know-you know,’” she says. But Brooklyn’s First Bloom isn’t just for popping into—you’ll be able to lounge with a glass of wine or relax with a snack and a coffee.

Alison Roman’s world is organic, craft-centered, and easy but considered. To step into it is an enticing foil to the AI-fueled tasteslop tilt-a-whirl on which we find ourselves. It’s a vision of a slow, steady, wabi-sabi life that many of us only aspire to. A life where one can even somehow enjoy, say, a monthslong commercial renovation project in one of America’s most competitive real estate markets. That’s the draw of First Bloom. The hard-to-find tinned fish, yes, but also the ease of living in Alison’s world if only for an hour.

And if not, well, it seems like there’ll be a pretty good rotisserie chicken, at least.

#6410. Spinach Artichoke Baked Potatoes

This baked potato stuffed with spinach-artichoke dip is the ultimate solo comfort meal. Classic twice-baked potatoes require two trips to the oven to deliver a pillowy, gussied-up filling and crispy skins all in one bite. Here, I’ve streamlined the workflow with a microwave. By zapping your spuds to start, you can reduce the overall baking time without sacrificing texture. Pick a large russet (or Idaho) for the best results; their relatively high starch and low moisture content helps them bake up airy and light, not gummy.

The rich, velvety filling that melts over top comes together in moments while your spud cooks. Cream cheese and mozzarella pack in enough dairy richness for a satisfying cheese pull and mellow out the subtle bitterness of baby spinach and nutty tang of artichoke hearts. (It’s important that your cream cheese is room temperature before you mash it in with the veggies. If it’s still got a chill from the fridge, it won’t fully incorporate.) The Worcestershire sauce is optional, but just a few shakes from the bottle bring instant savory depth to the filling.

Most recipes serve multiple people. In Me, Myself, and Dinner, each dish serves one and only one. That's you! Because whether you live solo (almost 30% of Americans do) or are enjoying a night to yourself, sitting down to a meal should be something to look forward to.

Preheat oven to 425°. Poke 1 large russet potato (about 12 oz.) all over with a fork; rub with avocado or vegetable oil to coat and sprinkle with kosher salt. Microwave potato on a microwave-proof plate on high 5 minutes. Turn potato over and microwave on high until fork-tender, about 5 minutes more. Let potato sit until just cool enough to handle.

While potato is cooling, microwave 5 oz. baby spinach with 2 Tbsp. water in a medium microwave-proof glass bowl until wilted, about 2 minutes. Carefully press leaves to release as much liquid as possible, then drain off liquid. Coarsely chop spinach.

Mix 2 Tbsp. cream cheese, room temperature, in a medium bowl until smooth. Add spinach, 4 quartered artichoke hearts (from a 14-oz. can), coarsely chopped, 2 Tbsp. finely grated Parmesan, 2 Tbsp. coarsely grated mozzarella, ½ tsp. garlic powder, and ¼ tsp. Worcestershire sauce (if using) and fold to combine; season with salt and freshly ground pepper.

Slice potato in half lengthwise and lightly fluff flesh in each half. Set on a small foil-lined rimmed baking sheet. Divide spinach mixture between potato halves, piling high (don’t pack too tightly). Sprinkle more Parmesan over. Bake potato halves until very tender when squeezed and skin is wrinkled and crisp, 20–25 minutes. Let cool slightly before eating.

#6409. Where’d You Go, Crêpes Suzette?

There’s something simultaneously comforting and dazzling about setting a dessert on fire: Candles atop a birthday cake; the meringue encrusting a baked Alaska; the caramelized fruit in a classic bananas Foster. But chief among them is one whose very name promises something different, something with French sophistication and an air of mystery that demands a moniker all its own: crêpes Suzette.

Crêpes Suzette is a surprisingly simple dish considering its decadent, theatrical reputation. The drama comes from the flames—thin, traditional French crêpes are drenched in a sauce made of orange liqueur, which is then set ablaze (typically tableside in many restaurants), causing the spirits to simmer and the sugars to caramelize. French chef Andrea Calstier, of Michelin-starred La Bastide in North Salem, New York, grew up eating them with his family, and in the brasseries of his home country.

For such a famous dish, though, its appearance on restaurant menus is increasingly rare. And for such an iconic French dessert, well, it may not technically be French at all. So where did these flaming pancakes come from? Where did they go? And isn’t it about time we bring them back?

While there are conflicting reports about the original creator of crêpes Suzette, the top candidate is Henri Charpentier, chef at the Café de Paris in Monte Carlo, Monaco, in the late 1800s. But while multiple roads lead back to Charpentier, the path gets murky, contradicted by both general plausibility and Charpentier himself.

Originally, Charpentier claimed credit for the iconic dish in his autobiography, Life à la Henri: Being the Memoirs of Henri Charpentier. In this 1934 volume, he suggested that the dish was a happy accident, tinged with drama. He alleged that as a young man working at the Café de Paris, he had been carrying a platter of crêpes to the Prince of Wales (the future King Edward VII) and stepped too near a chafing dish, setting the crêpes on fire, to the shock and delight of the prince, who proposed naming the newly created dish after his dining companion, a young woman named Suzette. (Frustratingly little information is available on who this Suzette may have been, if she was a real person at all.)

The story has the right theatrical touches for the dish, but it is almost certainly apocryphal, not least because Charpentier himself, in an interview with American writer Elsie Lee for the 1950s “Compleat Imbiber” series, said that he had developed the dish by taking a beloved childhood fruit crêpe and adding the then-fashionable touches of a liquor-based sauce and, presumably, a flame.

Wherever it came from, though, and whatever Charpentier had to say about it, Suzette’s unwitting legacy has endured for more than a century—her crêpes have remained a household name, even if they have fallen somewhat out of style. While chef Calstier notes that they’re still “served in many restaurants” in his native Marseille and that “French customers…are accustomed to seeing crêpes Suzette in any brasserie,” he admitted that “here in the U.S., they are more difficult to find.”

Part of the reason may be that, as with many dishes that predate the Edwardian era, it simply went out of fashion. But according to Lucile Plaza, executive chef at Benoit New York, it’s a result of the dish’s inherent service requirements: “True tableside service requires high staffing levels and precise choreography that a busy modern kitchen can’t always support daily,” she says. In London’s West End, fine-dining heavyweights Savoy Grill and The Ritz take this showmanship to the extreme, with portable burners and bottles of Grand Marnier on wooden trolleys.

But while there are complications to adding an edible spectacle to a restaurant menu, there are benefits, too. Chef Plaza notes that for the kitchen, “Suzette is brilliant because it is the ultimate way to use leftover crêpes. The intense bathing in the hot, rich citrus sauce revives the starch perfectly.” But not every restaurant that serves crêpes Suzette does so with a tableside flourish: In London’s St. John’s Wood, Oslo Court Restaurant, which is famous for its retro menu of classics like steak Diane and sole Veronique (two more of Edward VII's girlfriends, perhaps?), crêpes Suzette are brûléed with a torch in the kitchen rather than set aflame at the table. Adding crêpes Suzette to a menu may only be as hard as a restaurant wants it to be.

A burst of blue-tinged flame may not be necessary for the dish to achieve its signature caramelization, but it is key to the show—and a major point in favor of the dish’s present-day revival. As the old saying goes, “we eat with our eyes first,” and it’s truer than ever today. In fact, for many diners in the age of social media, it’s the phone that eats first, and that’s where crêpes Suzette has real potential for a modern renaissance. Nearly 400,000 viewers have watched a YouTube video of the tableside crêpes Suzette service at the London Ritz, and more than a million have viewed a TikTok of crêpes Suzette being prepared tableside at Switzerland’s five-star Suvretta House in Saint Moritz.

Spectacle is cool again, and whether dining out or cooking at home, we want to feel astonished and excited by the foods we eat. While a tableside flambé may prove logistically complicated at a restaurant scale, the feat is significantly easier to pull off at home—all it takes is a lighter or a match and a little confidence. Chef Calstier, for one, says that crêpes Suzette are a favorite of his wife, Elena, adding, “You can prepare everything in advance and do the flambé in front of your guests to wow them.” Plus, he says, “they don’t require many ingredients, beyond that bottle of Grand Marnier that we all have stashed away somewhere. They’re quite simple to make.”

Moreover, as delectable as classic crêpes Suzette are, they lend themselves well to new takes and customizations. Chef Plaza’s version at Benoit has a cherry twist: “Replacing Grand Marnier with kirsch is a natural match,” she says. “The dry cherry distillate brings an incredible aroma to the tableside without adding cloying sugar.” Meanwhile, at La Bastide, chef Calstier dishes up a twist that uses French toast instead of crêpes while sticking to the classic flavors and flambé. We asked one of our favorite pastry chefs, Caroline Schiff, author of Daily Desserts: Treats on Repeat, to develop a savory version for us, which she describes as “a cheeky little twist” on the classic. In her take, inspired by French onion soup, crêpes layered with caramelized onions and nutty gruyère are set ablaze with a splash of sherry. “They are at once a novelty and a nod to the classic,” she says.

Charpentier, one imagines, would approve.

#6408. This Is Why Your Mashed Potatoes Are Gluey (and How to Fix It)

Consider this your mashed potato primer, complete with tips on how to fix gluey mashed potatoes and how to prevent them from the start.

My mom’s potato masher is one of my favorite kitchen tools, from its retro design to the thick, grid-patterned bottom that hasn’t bent or warped over the years, despite heavy use. I attributed her consistently perfect fluffy mashed potatoes to this simple tool, even when she was experimenting with new mashed potato ideas. And it turns out there is some truth to it because it created smooth mashed potatoes quickly yet thoroughly, preventing her from pummeling the spuds into a sticky, gummy mess.

You see, overworked potatoes are the biggest reason for gluey mashed potatoes, so using the right tool is the best way to prevent them in the first place. And if you came here because your potatoes are already gummy, we have some helpful tips for how to fix gluey mashed potatoes after the fact.

The biggest culprit for gluey mashed potatoes is overworked potatoes. Potatoes are naturally starchy, and a little bit of starch is a good thing. Just as aquafaba (starchy cooked chickpea liquid) can be whipped into a rich vegan mayonnaise, potato starch thickens mashed potatoes and contributes to a creamy texture. But there is a limit.

As you mash chunks of potatoes into a mostly smooth mixture, the spud’s cell walls collapse, freeing the starch within those cells. The more you mash, the more cells are broken down, and the thicker, starchier and gummier the potatoes become. This can happen when you mash potatoes too long by hand, but it happens more quickly when using electric tools.

Food processors and immersion blenders have incredibly fast, sharp blades. As they whip around, they cut through the potatoes’ cells so rapidly that the once silken mash becomes gluey in a flash. I can’t urge you strongly enough to pass on these tools when mashing potatoes.

There are three components to avoiding gluey mashed potatoes: Choosing the right potato, using the right tool and considering temperature.

For starters, choose a starchy or all-purpose potato, like a russet or Yukon Gold. These potatoes are relatively low in moisture, helping the potato break down into a creamy mixture. They’ll give you more wiggle room as you mash than waxy potatoes, so the potatoes will turn out delicious even if you lose yourself in exuberant mashing.

Next, use the right kitchen tool for the job and reach for a potato masher, food mill or ricer. These handheld tools give you more control over speed and power as you mash. I prefer a potato masher with a crisscross grid pattern over those with a wavy design because there’s less open space, making each mash more productive.

Finally, warm your butter and milk before adding them to the potatoes. This step may sound finicky, but it prevents the warm potato starches from seizing against cold ingredients and becoming dense. Switch to a spatula and stir them in to keep a gentle touch and retain a fluffy texture.

You’ll never be able to totally remove the excess starch and get rid of the gluey texture without starting over, but you may be able to improve it. Adding more fat or liquid can improve the mouthfeel, and stirring in other ingredients can alter the overall texture.

If your potatoes are truly a gluey mess, don’t fret; you can repurpose the potatoes by turning them into leftover mashed potato recipes. Here are some of my favorite ways to use gluey mashed potatoes:

Knowing what types of potatoes are best for which recipes can save you a lot of grief—and this knowledge will go a long way to preventing gluey potatoes. For the creamiest, smoothest, lightest-as-air mashed potatoes, go with a starchy russet potato. Some people like using all-purpose Yukon Gold potatoes for their naturally buttery flavor, but I prefer to use all russets (or a blend of russets and Yukon Golds for flavor).

It’s best to avoid waxy potatoes, like red or fingerling potatoes, for mashed potato recipes. They keep their shape when they’re cooked, which is why they’re better for potato salads and soups than creamy mashes. They do make an excellent smashed potato, though, if you’re looking to do something a little bit different with your side dish.

As with all cooking rules, this one is made to be broken. If you only have red potatoes in the pantry, you can still use them to make mashed red potatoes. Just keep the potatoes a little bit chunkier so they don’t get gummy. And make sure you refer to them as a “rustic” mash when you bring them to the table to properly temper expectations.

An unusual pair of seated figurines was discovered in a Stone Age grave in Romania in the 1950s.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Two Stone Age figurines ‪—‬ the Thinker and the Seated Woman ‪—‬ were discovered in a prehistoric cemetery in Romania.

In 1956, archaeologists unearthed two unique figurines from one grave while excavating a Stone Age cemetery in southeast Romania. The unusual figurines — known as the Thinkers of Cernavodă or the Thinker and the Seated Woman — were made by people from the Hamangia culture and may be linked to ancient astronomical beliefs.

The Thinkers of Cernavodă are in the collection of the National Museum of Romanian History and are a key part of the country's cultural heritage. They were crafted from fired clay and measure about 4.5 inches (11.5 centimeters) tall. The two figurines may represent a man (the Thinker) and a woman (the Seated Woman), according to the museum.

The Thinker sits on a low, four-legged stool. He bends forward slightly, rounding his back and neck, and his arms are bent. He rests his elbows on his knees and his head in his hands. This pose gives him a meditative quality, according to the museum, which is why he has been named after Auguste Rodin's famous 1904 bronze sculpture. The Seated Woman also has a long, bent neck and a small face. She has prominent hips, thighs and breasts. Her right leg is bent, and her hands rest on her knee.

The figurines are about 7,000 years old and were made by the Hamangia people, a Late Neolithic culture that stretched from the Danube River to the Black Sea. According to archaeologist Dumitru Berciu, who excavated the Cernavodă cemetery, the Hamangia culture lasted from about 5200 to 4500 B.C. The people focused primarily on sheep and goat herding, and they built defensive hilltop settlements. They also crafted spiral-decorated pottery and human-shaped figurines. But while Berciu found dozens of male and female figurines in the Cernavodă cemetery, he noted that both Thinkers were unusual for being depicted seated rather than standing.

The specific meaning of the Thinkers is unclear. Berciu suggested that the figurines were somewhat stylized, rather than realistic, because they served a magical or religious purpose. Since solar worship was common among later Bronze Age groups in Europe — as evidenced by artifacts like the Nebra sky disc from Germany and an ornate sun chariot from Denmark — Berciu interpreted the figurines as possibly connected to sun worship.

But the National Museum of Romanian History has suggested that the two figurines may have been made specifically as a pair, representing the complementary principles of masculine and feminine natures or a Neolithic family unit. Another interpretation is that the sculptures depict a pair of mourners who were buried with the deceased.

While the original meaning of the 7,000-year-old sculptures remains a mystery, people continue to be drawn to the contemplative pair, and the male Thinker figures prominently today in the logo of the National Museum of Romanian History.
