#6365. NASA’s Voyager 1 Just Made History One Light-Day From Earth

NASA’s Voyager 1 has made history after 49 years in space, reaching an astonishing 16.1 billion miles from Earth, where even light takes 24 hours to bring its signals home.

NASA’s Voyager 1 has reached a remarkable new milestone, becoming the first spacecraft to travel one light-day from Earth. After more than 49 years in space, humanity’s most distant spacecraft is now so far away that even light takes a full 24 hours to reach it.

A light-day is the distance light travels in one day, approximately 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers). Voyager 1 officially reached that distance at 2:16 a.m. PST (5:16 a.m. EST) on November 18.

The extraordinary distance means that communicating with the spacecraft now requires immense patience. Scientists at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Southern California, which is managed by Caltech, received a radio signal from Voyager 1 early Thursday, exactly 24 hours after the spacecraft reached the milestone. Although the signal traveled at the speed of light, it still needed an entire day to cross the enormous distance separating the probe from Earth.

“Traveling a light-day is a singular feat for a spacecraft, but Voyager is so much more than a distant traveler. The Voyager mission would be remarkable just for what it contributed to planetary science with the Grand Tour of the outer planets,” said Joe Westlake, director, Heliophysics Division at NASA Headquarters in Washington. “But it went on to become central to NASA’s fleet of heliophysics missions offering insights into the star that we all revolve around, the Sun.”

Because distances in space are so enormous, astronomers often measure them using the time it takes light to travel between locations. In a vacuum, light moves at approximately 186,000 miles (299,000 kilometers) per second, making it the fastest known way for information to travel.

Consider a beam of sunlight passing Earth. It would reach the Moon in approximately 1.3 seconds and take about four hours to arrive at Neptune. From Neptune, that same beam would need another 20 hours to reach Voyager 1.

For an even larger comparison, a light-year, the distance light travels over an entire year, measures approximately 5.88 trillion miles (9.46 trillion kilometers).

Despite the historic achievement, Voyager 1 is currently experiencing a technical problem. NASA engineers have not received science or engineering data from the spacecraft since November 14. However, the probe continues to transmit a carrier signal, the radio signal normally used to send that information back to Earth. By detecting this signal and combining it with calculations of Voyager 1’s trajectory, engineers were able to verify that the spacecraft had reached the one light-day mark. They are continuing to investigate why the expected data are not arriving.

Voyager 1 and its companion, Voyager 2, began their extraordinary journeys in 1977. NASA launched the twin spacecraft during a rare alignment of the outer planets that made it possible to explore multiple worlds on a single mission.

Operated by JPL, the Voyagers became the third and fourth spacecraft to visit Jupiter and Saturn. They also delivered the first high-resolution images of these planets, revealing extraordinary new details about the giant worlds and their moons.

Voyager 2 continued farther along its unique route, becoming the first spacecraft to closely examine Uranus and Neptune, the two distant planets known as ice giants. Today, both probes are traveling through interstellar space, making them the only human spacecraft to have ventured beyond the Sun’s protective bubble. Their instruments continue monitoring magnetic fields and other conditions influenced by the Sun at extraordinary distances.

“Voyager 1 crossing the light-day threshold is yet another historic feat on an extraordinary voyage of discovery,” said Dave Gallagher, JPL director. “Above all, this milestone stands as a testament to the exceptional teams who built, programmed, and fly these spacecraft today, and who have overcome countless challenges to keep them connected to Earth across the vastness of space. As NASA pushes toward new frontiers in human and robotic exploration, Voyager and the people behind its success continue to inspire us to reach farther and dream bigger.”

The spacecraft are carrying more than instruments designed to explore the cosmos. Each Voyager also holds a Golden Record, a gold-plated copper phonograph record containing images and sounds representing life on Earth. The records were created as messages for any advanced civilization that might encounter the probes in the distant future.

“Nearly half a century after leaving Earth, the Voyager mission continues to push the boundaries of human exploration. Its epic journey reflects the vision of Ed Stone, the Caltech physicist and JPL director who guided the mission for decades, and the curiosity and tenacity of generations of scientists and engineers who have carried that vision forward,” said Ray Jayawardhana, president, Caltech. “Beyond its immense contributions to science, Voyager also captures something profound about the human spirit. We may never know where its journey will ultimately lead, but it will venture on, an enduring affirmation that humanity was here and we yearned to explore.”

Voyager 1 is currently traveling at roughly 38,000 mph (61,155 kph). In 2012, it became the first spacecraft to cross the boundary of the heliosphere, the enormous region surrounding the Sun that is filled with particles and magnetic fields generated by our star.

This protective region helps shield the solar system from cosmic radiation arriving from elsewhere in the galaxy. Beyond its outer boundary lies interstellar space, an environment that scientists had never directly explored with a spacecraft before Voyager 1 arrived. Voyager 2 crossed the same boundary in 2018, following a different path.

Although both spacecraft are now beyond the heliosphere, the Sun’s effects extend much farther than scientists once understood. By measuring conditions in this distant environment, the Voyagers are helping researchers investigate how far the Sun’s influence extends into the space between stars.

“The Voyagers are revolutionizing our understanding of interstellar space, a previously unexplored region outside the heliosphere,” said Linda Spilker, Voyager project scientist at JPL. “One big surprise is the extent to which our Sun continues to affect interstellar space, all the way out to Voyager 1. Where does the Sun’s influence end and pristine interstellar space begin? Perhaps Voyager may endure long enough to answer that question.”

Maintaining spacecraft that have operated for nearly half a century presents enormous engineering challenges. Over the years, the Voyager team has developed inventive solutions to problems involving aging components, including clogged thrusters and a malfunctioning computer.

One of the greatest challenges is the spacecraft’s steadily shrinking supply of electrical power.

Earlier in 2026, engineers took a calculated risk by shutting down three devices aboard Voyager 1 and replacing their functions with three alternatives that require less energy. This approach is helping the spacecraft conserve its remaining power and extend the useful life of its nearly 50-year-old radioisotope thermal generator.

The generator works much like a nuclear battery. Rather than relying on sunlight, which is extremely weak at Voyager’s distance, it produces electricity using heat released as plutonium undergoes radioactive decay.

As that process continues, the amount of available electrical power gradually decreases. Both Voyager spacecraft lose approximately 4 watts of power each year, forcing engineers to make increasingly careful decisions about which systems can remain active.

NASA expects the latest power conservation measures to allow both probes to operate their current collections of scientific instruments until at least the summer of 2027, when they will celebrate the 50th anniversaries of their launches.

Even after nearly five decades, NASA maintains regular contact with Voyager 1. Communication is handled by the agency’s Deep Space Network, a worldwide system of powerful radio antennas at three facilities that supports missions exploring the Moon and more distant regions of space.

The immense separation between Earth and Voyager 1 now makes even a simple exchange of messages a lengthy process. A command sent from Earth requires approximately 24 hours to reach the spacecraft. If Voyager 1 immediately sends a response, that signal takes another 24 hours to return.

In other words, a complete exchange of signals now requires about 48 hours, even though those signals travel at the speed of light.

“We listen to Voyager 1 every day and send commands to the spacecraft weekly. It just takes a little longer to communicate than it used to,” said Suzanne Dodd, Voyager project manager at JPL. “Even traveling at the speed of light, signals now take 24 hours to reach the spacecraft and 24 hours to reach us. One day in the future, when it can no longer communicate with Earth, Voyager 1 will become humanity’s silent ambassador to the stars.”

#6364. Complex Life on Earth May Not Have Appeared Without Tall Mountains

The more scientists learn about Earth, the more habitability appears to involve an almost kaleidoscopic array of variables and interactions. Though our current search for potentially habitable worlds is mostly restricted to finding rocky planets with liquid water and atmospheres, it will have to advance well beyond that to bear fruit. Things like exoplanet plate tectonics to keep climates moderate, and stars with long, stable lifetimes that let life fluorish and evolve are factors in habitability.

New research suggests that another factor may come into play: mountains. The research is titled "Raising mountains for a habitable Earth," and it's published in Science Advances. The lead author is Dr. Matthijs Smit of the University of British Columbiaâs Department of Earth, Ocean and Atmospheric Sciences.

Their main claim is that mountains are critical because they increase the surface area exposed to weathering, and that makes important chemicals and nutrients available, as well as changing the chemistry of the oceans and the atmosphere. That, in turn, led to the eventual appearance of complex life.

"The formation of mountain belts (orogens) elevates rocks above sea level, making them available for chemical weathering and altering the composition of the atmosphere and oceans, which in turn control habitability," the authors write.

K2 is the second tallest mountain in the world. The crust underneath it is some of the thickest in the world. Research shows that in Earth's past, the crust thickened in some places, leading to the growth of very tall mountains. Increased weathering from those mountains preceded the planet's episodes of oxygenation, and researchers hypothesize that episodic spurts of mountain growth enabled Earth's habitability, and the eventual appearance of complex life. Image Credit: By Zacharie Grossen - Own work, CC BY-SA 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/42469860

"Continental silicate weathering controls the oceanward flux of carbon and bioactive nutrients that limit marine primary productivity, thus exerting control on atmospheric chemistry, climate, and marine biomass and biodiversity," they explain. "The majority of the global terrigenous runoff derives from mountainous regions."

The researchers focused on the last three billion years of Earth's history. They examined metamorphic rocks that were pushed deep underground by overlying tectonic plates. When mountains formed where plates collided, the mountains were able to reach much greater heights. That raised nutrient levels in the oceans, which helped photosynthesizing lifeforms oxygenate Earth's atmosphere.

âChanges that occurred deep in the Earth ultimately gave rise to much taller mountains over time, which may have made our planet habitable by providing the nutrients needed for life to form and flourish,â lead author Smit said. âNutrients such as phosphorous are essential ingredients for life on our planet, but prior to three billion years ago, these elements were locked in the Earthâs crust and the oceans were quite nutrient-starved. All this changed when tall mountains started to develop.â

The research shows that two periods of peak metamorphic pressure inside the planet, between 2.7 to 2.2 and 0.8 to 0.7 billion years ago, led to thicker crusts in mountain-forming regions, and that let taller mountains form. The growth of Earth's mountains spiked, and those orogenic growth spurts were synchronous with other important changes on the planet.

âThe first growth spurt may have led to the emergence of land on a large scale for the first time, while the second growth spurt thrust mountain ranges to enormous heights,â said co-author Dr. Douwe van Hinsbergen of Utrecht University, The Netherlands. âGiven such profound effects, mountains may well have played a far greater role in the creation of a habitable planet than previously assumed.â

Earth's atmospheric oxygen rose in distinct periods, and the most well-known and consequential one was the Great Oxygenation Event (GOE) from about 2.4 to 2.0 billion years ago. The researchers say that by the time the GOE occurred, Earth's mountains had grown substantially. They rose from near sea-level to about half the height of the modern-day Himalayas. Another distinct period of rising atmospheric oxygen was the Neoproterozoic Oxygen Event (NOE) from around 700 million to 500 million years ago. Mountain growth spiked at that time, too, according to the researchers. Various other atmospheric factors and oceanic factors related to habitability and complex life increased, too.

This figure shows time on the x-axis and more other information throughout. Blue shows how atmospheric O2 pressure rose compared to modern levels, especially during the GOE and the NOE. Purple shows the rise of sulfur isotope diversity, a measure of biological sulfur metabolism over time, and grey shows the percentage of oceanic strontium that comes from continental mountain erosion. Green shows the rise of organisms capable of oxygenic photosynthesis. The snowflake symbols show Earth's main icehouse stages. Image Credit: Smit et al. Science Advances 13 Nov 2026 Vol 12, Issue 46

The timing of these spurts of mountain growth coincided with the growth of crustal thickness in mountain belts. In these belts, the thickness of the upper accreted crust grows as plates collide. The first episode increased thickness from 30km to 60 km, and the second episode saw an increase to almost 90 km. âWe suspect that these increases are ultimately linked to the cooling of our planet,â Dr. Smit said. âAs a result, the process that makes mountains changed, allowing mountains to grow taller.â

"Causes for environmental upheaval culminating in the GOE and NOE have been sought in various external forcing mechanisms, such as increased runoff resulting from supercontinent breakup, enhanced weathering of basaltic rocks at low latitude, and a dwindling CO2 (carbon dioxide) flux from arc volcanism," the authors write. While the researchers agree that these are valid hypotheses, they also point out that they're transient. That doesn't match the "irreversible nature of global oxygenation," and other changes. They're also not restricted to periods preceding the GOE and NOE.

The two episodes of crustal thickening and resulting spikes in mountain elevation and erosion are a better fit. "In contrast to all of these processes, the orogenic growth associated with tectonic revolutions R1 and R2 broadly coincide with the major periods of environmental upheaval in terms of their approximate timing, paucity, and irreversibility," the authors write.

The researchers couldn't measure the height of long-gone mountains, but they were able to determine the density and thickness of ancient crust. Since crustal thickness and density correlate with mountain height, they could calculate the height of ancient mountains.

Earth's tallest mountains today, Mount Everest, K2 and Kangchenjunga, are almost certainly some of the tallest ever produced. They approach nine km above sea level, and the crust under them is about 80 km thick. That's twice as thick as other continents. They illustrate how crustal thickness generates tall mountains, and emphasize the hypothesis that mountain growth helped enable Earth's habitability.

âItâs likely not a coincidence that life on Earth developed and diversified approximately during the same period that the two growth spurts occurred,â said co-author Dr. Ellen Kooijman of the Swedish Museum of Natural History, Stockholm. âItâs exciting to think that mountain belts were once non-existent and that their development over the past three billion years may have driven the environmental and biological change that shaped our planet.â

#6363. Space Entrepreneurs Should Look To 16th Century Spice Trade For Inspiration

Despite all the hype about a new space economy, humanity has yet to reap much benefit offered by the prospect of offworld mining, manufacturing, or space tourism.

But historical precedent dictates that ventures into the unknown need to be driven by commerce to achieve profitability. Such was the case five centuries ago, when most of Western Europe was agog over the importation of precious spices from East Asia.

The idea was to circumvent the Silk Road from and drive the spice trade from overland camel caravans to large cargo-holding ships.

For centuries, camels had enabled trickles of spices such as cloves, nutmeg, and ginger to make their way into the kitchens of the high and mighty, be they landed gentry or royalty.

Cloves originally grew in the volcanic soils of only a handful of small islands in the northern Moluccas archipelago, author Lewis Dartnell notes in his 2019 book âOrigins: How the Earth Shaped Human History.â And the nutmeg tree appeared on only nine pinprick-sized islands --- the Bandas-further south, Dartnell writes.

But as early as the late 15th century and the Age of Columbus, middlemen had run up the cost of these rare spices to such a degree that Portugal and Spain, in particular, were in competition for a sea route to the Moluccas. That is, the Moluccan archipelago in what is now Indonesia.

The idea was to travel point to point by sea and weed out a multitude of middlemen along the long Silk Road --- mostly stretching overland from the Black Sea and Mediterranean through northern India to China.

Thus, Portuguese explorer Ferdinand Magellan had a novel idea.

Magellan, born into a family of minor nobility and modest possessions, had somehow convinced Spainâs King Charles V that it was possible to reach the eastern riches by traveling west, author Romeu Gaspar writes in his 2026 book âThe Revolution of Magellan: How 500-Year-Old Rocket Science Changed the World.â

And even though Magellan tragically lost his life en route at least a remainder of his crew did circumnavigate the globe. In the process, they forever changed the course of history, commerce, and human exploration.

Dried spices were a lightweight, high-value, reasonably imperishable product with which to stuff a ship's hold on long voyages, John Keay writes in his 2005 book âThe Spice Route: A History.â The profits were huge; in 1515, the return on such cargo docked at Lisbon was 700 per cent, Keay notes.

By 1520, the income from Portugalâs spice trade provided 40 percent of the Crownâs total revenue, Dartnell writes in his book. Spices eventually became so prized that in 1677, the Dutch swapped the island of Manhattan for the nutmeg-rich island of Run Palau, he notes.

A 21st century analogy to such commercial exploration might be if by the end of this century, space entrepreneurs were able to extract and then process rare minerals from the Moon or Mars or even accessible Main Belt asteroids. And then in a cost-efficient manner, reap the profits by bringing them back to Earth. Or at least low-Earth orbit.

To that end, NASA Apollo 17 astronaut and geologist Harrison Jack Schmitt has long argued for Helium-3 mining on the Moon. But until someone fulfills the economics of making cislunar Space profitable human exploration of our solar system is likely to lag. That's because throughout history, scientific innovation usually goes hand in hand with someone's quest for a large profit margin.

A durable commercial reason for people to work in space could give human space science the transportation and infrastructure it needs, Ret. U.S. Brigadier Gen. Pete Worden, an astrophysicist, chairman of the Breakthrough Prize Foundation, and Laureate Professor at the University of Arizona in Tucson, told me via email.

Within the next fifty years at least, the future of scientific space exploration is arguably best served by robotic means rather than astronauts.

Iâd rely heavily on robots for science and give commercial companies a larger role in developing and operating human spaceflight systems, Worden, who directed NASA Ames Research Center from 2006 to 2015, told me via email. NASA should return to its roots in the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics (NACA) by emphasizing research and technology development that industry and scientists can build on, he says.

Routine human sorties beyond low-earth orbit are key.

If commercial space transportation becomes routine, agencies such as the National Science Foundation (NSF) could support research that uses it, Worden argues.

Meanwhile, we are left with space programs that for decades have been hampered by both politics and economics and as a result, have limped along in fits and starts.

Over the past 30 years, NASAâs plans for the Moon and Mars have had to survive changes in administrations, budgets, and priorities, says Worden. When a program needs agreement from too many people, it becomes harder to take sensible risks, he says.

If humanity can ever succeed in making forays beyond low Earth orbit that are commercially viable in the same way the 16th Century spice trade was profitable, then this new ocean of space-time could be ours for the taking.

#6362. Scientists Shine New Light on One of the Greatest Mysteries in Modern Physics

The search for more efficient power grids could benefit from understanding a hidden rivalry inside copper-based superconductors, where a mysterious quantum state appears to compete with superconductivity.

When researchers used a pulse of light to temporarily suppress superconductivity in a copper-based material, a mysterious quantum state emerged. As superconductivity returned, that state faded. The experiment offers new evidence in a decades-old debate about how certain materials can carry electricity without losing energy.

These materials, known as cuprates, were discovered in 1986, a breakthrough that earned Bednorz and Müller the Nobel Prize in Physics the following year. Their ability to become superconducting at relatively high temperatures has made them especially promising for future technologies, including more efficient power grids, medical equipment, and quantum computers. Yet nearly 40 years later, scientists still do not fully understand what makes their remarkable properties possible.

One of the biggest uncertainties involves the pseudogap, a poorly understood quantum state that appears in cuprates. Scientists have long debated whether it helps superconductivity emerge or competes with it.

“The pseudogap is one of the greatest mysteries in condensed-matter physics. Understanding how it interacts with superconductivity is essential if we want to explain why these materials can carry electricity without energy loss at unusually high temperatures,” says Fabio Boschini, a professor at INRS and specialist in ultrafast spectroscopy of quantum condensed matter.

Boschini, who led the research, holds the Canada Research Chair in Quantum Materials’ Dynamics and is a recipient of an Alfred P. Sloan Research Fellowship.

To investigate the relationship between the two states, his team used a pulse of light to briefly suppress superconductivity and then tracked how the material’s electrons behaved as it recovered. The researchers used time- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (TR-ARPES), a technique that allows scientists to observe rapid changes in the electronic properties of materials.

The experiments took place at the INRS Énergie Matériaux Télécommunications Research Centre, using the TR-ARPES endstation at the Advanced Laser Light Source (ALLS).

The measurements revealed electronic states that had remained hidden from conventional techniques. For the first time, researchers directly observed a temporary pseudogap induced by light. When superconductivity was suppressed, the pseudogap emerged in its place. As the material regained its superconducting properties, the pseudogap gradually faded.

“Thanks to the unique capabilities of the TR-ARPES system at the ALLS laboratory at INRS, we were able to directly observe what happens when superconductivity temporarily disappears and then re-emerges. It is a bit like uncovering missing frames from a film that scientists have been trying to piece together for decades,” says Dario Armanno, a PhD student at INRS and first author of the study.

Published in Nature Physics, the findings support the idea that the pseudogap and superconductivity compete rather than cooperate. This challenges the long-standing hypothesis that the pseudogap acts as a precursor, or an earlier state that helps superconductivity develop.

The project also involved international collaborators, including the Center for Computational Quantum Physics at the Flatiron Institute in New York.

“The pseudogap and superconducting states in cuprates are among the most complex phenomena to reproduce theoretically. Our study reveals that they compete with one another and provides new insight into their behavior when both are excited simultaneously,” said Olivier Gingras, Associate Research Scientist at the Flatiron Institute’s Center for Computational Quantum Physics.

Although the work is fundamental research rather than a demonstration of a new technology, a clearer understanding of these competing quantum states could help guide the development of next-generation superconductors and more energy-efficient technologies.

“This research is essential to advancing the quantum technologies of the future. It contributes to the training of highly qualified personnel in a field that is critical to Canada’s technological sovereignty and to the implementation of its National Quantum Strategy,” says François Légaré, Director of the INRS Énergie Matériaux Télécommunications Research Centre.

Reference: “Light-induced asymmetric pseudogap below the critical temperature in cuprates” by D. Armanno, O. Gingras, F. Goto, J.-M. Parent, A. Longa, A. Jabed, B. Frimpong, R. D. Zhong, J. Schneeloch, G. D. Gu, G. Jargot, H. Ibrahim, F. Légaré, B. J. Siwick, N. Gauthier, A. Georges, A. J. Millis and F. Boschini, 20 October 2026, Nature Physics. DOI: 10.1038/s41567-026-03446-6

#6361. Excellent Boiled Potatoes

Never in your life have you had such an exemplary vegetable as these boiled potatoes, inspired by the version featured in the 2005 film adaptation of Pride and Prejudice. While the moment is not part of Jane Austen’s classic novel, the simple dish has developed a bit of a cult following. Our interpretation has a little garlic and lemon zest in addition to plenty of butter and parsley; we think Mr. Collins would approve—dare we say, he may even declare them excellent. Don your finest Regency-style garb and place a pot of water on the hearth: We have potatoes to boil.

Even more excellent potato recipes this way.

Combine ¼ cup Diamond Crystal or 2 Tbsp. plus 2 tsp. Morton kosher salt and 10 cups water in a large pot.

Peel 1½ lb. Yukon Gold potatoes (about 3 large or 4 medium). Quarter if potatoes are large, halve if medium, adding to pot as you go. Potatoes should be covered by at least 2" water when finished; add more if needed.

Place pot over high heat and bring water to a boil. Reduce heat to medium-low and simmer until potatoes are cooked through (a fork should slide easily into flesh), 15–20 minutes. Drain in a colander.

Set pot over medium-low heat to cook off any excess water, then add 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter and cook until melted. Stir in 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, and ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper. Remove from heat; mix in ¼ cup finely chopped parsley and 1 tsp. finely grated lemon zest. Add drained potatoes and toss to coat. Taste and season with more salt if needed. Transfer potatoes to a large shallow bowl to serve.

Pregnancy and the postpartum period profoundly transform the brain — yet science is only beginning to understand how that transformation can affect a mother's mental health.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Look closely at the medical illustrations used in textbooks to depict the physiological changes of pregnancy, and you'll notice something strange: The bodies often have no heads. Generations of physicians learned to picture the pregnant patient as a torso — a uterus, a placenta, a growing belly — with everything above the neck left blank.

That blank space is not an oversight by the illustrator. It is a faithful map of what medicine chose to study. We need to move on and create a complete picture of what happens during and after pregnancy so we can develop measures to prevent maternal deaths.

For hundreds of years, we have devoted enormous effort to characterizing how pregnancy remodels nearly every organ and system in the body: the cardiovascular changes, the recalibration of the immune system, the metabolic adjustments — most of them orchestrated by hormones the placenta pours into the bloodstream. That knowledge of what is normal is exactly what lets us recognize and treat what is not, from gestational diabetes to preeclampsia. But the brain, one of the most important organs in the human body, was left out altogether.

It wasn't until 2016 that my colleagues and I published the first study showing that pregnancy profoundly and measurably changes the structure of the human brain. That finding, which we described in the journal Nature Neuroscience, became the seed of my lab. In the years since, a remarkable picture has emerged. The brain changes associated with pregnancy and the postpartum phase are more pronounced, or at least occur more rapidly, than those of adolescence — the transformation we usually treat as the epitome of a remodeling brain.

Today, neuroscientists consider the months of pregnancy and the postpartum period to be one of the most plastic periods for the adult brain. These changes are dynamic; some regions shrink in volume during gestation and grow after birth, while others follow the opposite pattern. They are driven by hormones, tracking with the enormous swings in estrogens and other hormones across pregnancy. And they are long-lasting — some of these structural changes persist for years, and preliminary evidence suggests they may last decades. Or, as folk wisdom has long put it, once a mother, always a mother.

For centuries, we drew the pregnant body without a head. We now have the tools to fill in what we left blank.

These findings raise a question I'm asked constantly: Are these brain changes behind the phenomenon of "mommy brain," sometimes called "momnesia"? It is an effect many women report, and it deserves a careful accounting of its possible causes — among them sleep deprivation and the enormous mental and metabolic load of gestating and raising a human being. We are still investigating, but the data so far point in a reassuring direction: These brain changes are not associated with worse cognitive functioning. If anything, it's the opposite: We have evidence that the women whose brains changed the most were the ones who reported greater well-being and, in turn, an easier time bonding with their newborns.

But not every change is benign. The same plasticity that helps a mother adapt can also carry risk. In one of our most recent studies, published in the journal Science Advances in 2025, we found that certain brain changes were associated with a greater rise in depressive symptoms during the postpartum period. And here is the other side of the coin: A highly plastic brain is also a vulnerable one.

During pregnancy and the postpartum period, that same capacity for change makes the brain more susceptible to disturbances. The window that should lead to learning and bonding, for some women, opens onto suffering instead — especially when society fails to support them, when it doesn't recognize this period as a stage in which women need protection and support from their families and institutions.

The brain changes during pregnancy and the postpartum period are more pronounced and rapid than those that take place during adolescence.

The epidemiological data are as alarming as the personal stories behind them. Roughly 1 in 5 women will experience perinatal depression. In developed countries, suicide linked to peripartum mental disorders is one of the leading causes of maternal death. Let me say that again, because it bears repeating: Suicide linked to peripartum mental disorders is one of the leading causes of maternal death. And what happens to a mother's mental health does not stay with her — it ripples out to the well-being of her baby, her family and society as a whole. Advancing maternal mental health is urgent, and the first step is to generate the high-quality data that will let us truly understand the brain transformation that accompanies pregnancy and the postpartum period — to describe what happens to mothers on the basis of science, not personal opinion, inherited prejudice or incomplete medical models.

It is a serious problem, but the solution is straightforward ‪—‬ especially now, in the age of artificial intelligence. The tools of modern data science are extraordinarily powerful, but they are hungry ‪—‬ they need large, high-quality, deeply characterized datasets to learn from and make predictions. In maternal brain health, those datasets do not yet exist. We have blood biobanks from pregnancy, neuroimaging from postpartum parents, questionnaires on bonding, records on breastfeeding — but they sit in separate silos, captured at different moments, never integrated. No resource follows the same women from before conception, through pregnancy, and years past birth, linking biofluids, neuroimaging, neuropsychological assessments, and the social conditions of their lives.

Building that resource should be a priority for anyone who cares about women's health. It is the kind of infrastructure that transformed other fields. Databases like the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative for Alzheimer's disease and the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study for adolescence turned scattered observations into predictive science. Motherhood deserves the same — not a footnote appended to the study of something else. It deserves its own chapter — its own public, longitudinal, well-characterized database, spanning from molecules to societies.

For the past nine years, my lab's efforts have focused on laying the groundwork for such a database, and we now have hundreds of participants assessed before pregnancy, during pregnancy, and in the postpartum period. But hundreds is not enough. To do this science properly, we need to scale from hundreds of women to thousands and to ensure, as much as possible, adequate geographic and social representation. My role within initiatives like ENIGMA-Neuroendocrinology and the Ann S. Bowers Women's Brain Health Initiative is to coordinate with other outstanding researchers to reach that goal with the highest quality and the greatest urgency we can manage.

None of this requires a scientific miracle. It requires a decision to treat the maternal brain as something worth studying with the same rigor and the same resources we devote to every other domain of biomedicine. For centuries, we drew the pregnant body without a head. We now have the tools to fill in what we left blank. What we need is the collective will, and the sustained funding, to finish the picture.

If you or someone you know needs help, the national suicide and crisis lifeline in the U.S. is available by calling or texting 988. There is also an online chat at 988lifeline.org.

Eighty-five percent of women experience pregnancy at some point in their lives. It enables the very existence of our species. Yet this first step in the process of nurturing the next generation has had little serious, rigorous study — until now.

Susana Carmona's A Mother’s Brain is a landmark in ending sexual bias in women's health. Among her many initiatives, she is building a unique longitudinal database tracking how mothers’ brains change from preconception to several years after childbirth.

Susana Carmona is the author of "A Mother's Brain: The New Science of the Neuro-Maternal Revolution" (The MIT Press). Carmona is the founder of Neuromaternal, a lab based in Madrid, and is a mother herself. She has led international research projects and published her findings in Science Advances and Nature Neuroscience, among many other publications. Her research has been referenced across popular media from the CBS sitcom "The Big Bang Theory" to the New York Times, the Wall Street Journal, the Washington Post, National Geographic, Smithsonian, and Mother Jones.

#6359. Bacteria and Nuclear Power Could Grow Ready-Made Homes on Mars Before Astronauts Arrive

As we gear up to eventually land a human on Mars, more and more ideas are coming out about how to prepare for that. A recent one from Pioneer Labs, a research institute founded by bioengineer Erika DeBenedictis to develop biological technologies for space exploration, is now available on arXiv, without any plans to release it in a paid journal as part of the âOpen Scienceâ policy of The Astera Institute, who funded the research. It details âMars Seedâ - a new architecture that is self-contained and can produce a full 870 sq meters of pressurized habitat using nothing but Martian inputs within roughly every four Earth years.

Mars Seed tackles plenty of in-situ resource utilization challenges all at once. One of the most notable is weight. According to the paper, the entire system weighs in at 20 metric tons - well below the threshold of Martian payloads for Starship or NASAâs proposed 25 ton Mars landers. And crucially, rather than relying on sugar or chemical inputs from Earth, the entire system wonât need any further input from our home planet once it is established on the Red one.

The plan starts off with a landing at a mid-latitude Martian site, with flat terrain and sub-surface water ice deposits. Immediately after landing, an autonomous rover sets about unloading the packageâs hardware and assembling a 40kW nuclear fission reactor modeled on the compact nuclear reactors NASA is already developing for Mars and Moon missions. About a month later, the reactor should be fully up and running, providing both electricity and âwasteâ heat that can be used to climate control a habitat.

Fraser interviews Dr. Congrui Jin about using bioreactors to grow Martian habitats.

Or in the case of this particular mission structure, to melt some ice. The system would put the heat from the nuclear reactor into a Rodriguez well - a type of ice-drilling technique that melts a pocket of underground ice and pumps the liquid water to the surface, which has already been proven in Antarctica.

Water is a crucial component in the entire systemâs operation. Once the first supply of it has been obtained from the âRodwellâ as itâs known, the system uses a scaled-up version of the urine-recycling system currently in place on the International Space Station (ISS) to recover around 90 percent of the water from each production batch of material.

But water isnât the only component input from Mars itself - another is dirt, or âregolithâ in the language of space exploration. The paper estimates the system will require around four tons of Martian soil deposited into its hoppers every day. This could be collected by autonomous mining machines, like NASAâs RASSOR. Approximately 800 kg of that dirt is then stirred into water-filled mixing tanks to dissolve out nutrients like phosphorus and nitrogen. But that still leaves the most deadly component of Martian soil - perchlorates.

Fraser interviews Dr. Michael Hecht, one of the main scientists behind the MOXIE experiment to create oxygen out of the atmosphere of Mars.

While these would kill a normal microorganism, Pioneer Labsâ speciality is designing biological systems for use in space exploration. So they simply evolved a hardy strain of the bacterium Cupriavidus necator, which they call sPL.001, which can thrive in the equivalent of a perchlorate-laced broth of Martian regolith simulant back on Earth. That bacterium is also the key engine in creating the bioplastics that are used to 3D print the radiation-shielded habitats.

Bacteria need food though, and shipping it from Earth would be prohibitively expensive. So thereâs one final input to the system from the Red Planet - its atmosphere. The first step in that process is an upgraded version of the MOXIE experiment that successfully showed an ability to split the carbon dioxide in Marsâ atmosphere into carbon monoxide and oxygen.

Typically, that system simply gets rid of the carbon monoxide to capture the oxygen for use in rocket fuel. But in Mars Seed, carbon monoxide is actually the prize. Using a technique inspired by an emerging field called âelectro-agriculture,â the system combines waste carbon monoxide gas with water to produce liquid acetic acid - the main ingredient in vinegar.

Fraser talks in detail about what we can find to live off of when we eventually do send humans to the Red Planet.

While a diet of straight vinegar might not sound appealing to a human, to a microbe it's nourishing enough. In four separate 1,000L fermentation tanks, the engineered microbes eat this vinegar, combined with oxygen, packing themselves with a bioplastic called polyhydroxybutyrate, with the polymer eventually making up 70% of their body weight. At that point, a high-speed centrifuge harvests the bacteria cells from the liquid broth, and the resulting paste is split into two separate assembly lines.

Half of the raw paste is mixed with Martian dirt and fed into a giant gantry 3D printer, which then extrudes a corrugated, arched outer protective shell. Rovers then work to pile around 2m of dirt onto the outer shell, creating a barrier to the cosmic rays and micrometeorites that plague the Martian surface.

The other half of the bacteria is subjected to a pressure bath of liquid carbon dioxide, again pulled straight from the atmosphere. This extracts the pure bioplastic, which is then melted and spun into an airtight, reinforced inner tent that is capable of holding a breathable atmosphere.

Interview with Dr. Erika DeBenedictis, the founder of Pioneer Labs. Credit - The New Biology YouTube Channel

So, in essence, this 20 ton system can be dropped on Mars, including a pair of helping rovers, and extract all of the necessary components to continually and consistently build atmosphere-tight, safe shelter for astronauts, at a rate of about 75 sq meters every 130 days. The paper notes that, comparing the system to directly launching 20 tons of pre-made plastic building materials from Earth, the break-even point of the stand-alone biofabrication facility is around 1,400 Martian days - which lines up nicely with the two orbital alignment cycles NASA is planning to utilize before sending human crews.

The main difference is that the biofabrication facility never stops producing those safe habitats, which clearly is a major advantage. Despite its promise, though, there are still plenty of engineering challenges to overcome before this system will be anywhere near launch ready. But, when that time comes, it appears that we might be able to literally grow safe habitats out of Martian water, air, and soil. And that is something any future mission planner will be thrilled to have as an option.

#6358. Two Overlooked “Forever Chemicals” Linked To More Than Double the Risk of Liver Cancer

Two little-studied “forever chemicals” have been linked to substantially higher odds of liver cancer in a new University of Southern California (USC) study. People with the highest blood concentrations of either chemical had roughly two to two-and-a-half times the odds of developing the disease compared with those with the lowest concentrations.

The association was especially strong among people genetically predisposed to fatty liver disease. Published in Environmental Health Perspectives, the findings suggest that inherited susceptibility may influence how environmental chemical exposures affect cancer risk.

Researchers analyzed blood samples from 223 people who later developed hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), the most common form of liver cancer, and 223 matched controls. The samples were collected an average of 7.8 years before diagnosis as part of the Multiethnic Cohort Study (MEC), which has tracked more than 215,000 participants in California and Hawaii since the 1990s.

Of the 12 per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) measured, two showed significant associations with liver cancer: perfluoroheptanoic acid (PFHpA) and perfluorononanoic acid (PFNA).

“The concerning thing about our results is that the strongest associations were not in the most studied legacy PFAS,” said lead author Jesse Goodrich, PhD, assistant professor at the Keck School of Medicine of USC. “They are among the newer PFAS, and we don’t have much information about their effect on human health.”

The researchers also examined whether inherited susceptibility to metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), commonly called fatty liver disease, influenced cancer risk. They found that the association between PFHpA exposure and liver cancer was considerably stronger among participants with high genetic susceptibility to MASLD. No statistically significant association was detected among those with low susceptibility.

“Our study shows that genetic differences in how the liver processes fats may play an important role in determining susceptibility,” Goodrich said. “You have this one-two hit: first, your genes and then PFAS impacting this pathway.”

PFAS exposure may disrupt liver fat metabolism, contributing to the fat accumulation associated with MASLD. Over time, the condition can progress to inflammation, scarring, and cancer. MASLD is an increasingly important driver of HCC, which has a five-year survival rate below 20%.

“PFAS have been linked to an increase in fat accumulation in your liver, and over time, that can actually increase the risk of liver cancer,” Goodrich said.

PFAS are found in products such as nonstick cookware, food packaging, stain-resistant fabrics, and firefighting foams. Many resist degradation and persist in the environment for decades. These chemicals have been detected in drinking water across roughly half of U.S. water systems, while an estimated 99% of the global population has detectable PFAS in their blood.

Most regulatory attention has focused on older compounds such as perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS). PFHpA was developed as an alternative to these chemicals, which were phased out of many applications because of health and environmental concerns.

“PFOA and PFOS have received much of the scientific and regulatory attention, however, they represent only a small part of the PFAS family,” said senior author Vaia Lida Chatzi, MD, PhD, professor at the Keck School of Medicine. “Our findings show why we need to look beyond those legacy compounds. We can miss important associations with liver health if we study only the chemicals we already know best.”

The PFHpA finding also supports results from an independent National Cancer Institute study published two months earlier. However, these observational studies cannot establish that PFAS exposure causes liver cancer.

Identifying people with both elevated PFAS exposure and high genetic susceptibility could eventually help guide earlier liver cancer screening. Reducing exposure may also offer a potential prevention strategy, although its effect on cancer risk remains uncertain.

“Our study actually provides something that is actionable,” Goodrich said. “You can make lifestyle and diet changes and there are certain types of water filters you can put in that can reduce exposure. And if you have the information on genetic susceptibility, that could also provide additional evidence for things that you could do to mitigate risk.”

The study is the first publication from a USC Norris Comprehensive Cancer Center research program supported by a $3.4 million federal grant to investigate PFAS and liver cancer.

“This first paper from our NIH-funded study is an important step. Drawing on the diverse Multiethnic Cohort, it adds to the evidence that some PFAS may be associated with liver cancer,” said senior author V. Wendy Setiawan, PhD, professor at USC. “We hope this work will help build the evidence needed to reduce harmful exposures and inform prevention efforts for diverse communities.”

The team plans to investigate additional environmental exposures to better understand how chemicals encountered throughout life may contribute to cancer.

Reference: “Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances, Hepatic Lipid Metabolism Genes, and Hepatocellular Carcinoma: Evidence of Gene–Environment Interactions in a Multiethnic Cohort” by Jesse A. Goodrich, Hongxu Wang, Adelynn Paik, Sihao Han, Brittney Baumert, Joseph Romano, Razieh Moghadam, Shiwen Li, Tanya L. Alderete, Syam S. Andra, Robert O. Wright, David V. Conti, Lida Chatzi and Veronica Wendy Setiawan, 6 November 2026, Environmental Health Perspectives. DOI: 10.1021/EHP.6c00546

#6357. LISA's Gravitational Wave Detections Could Reveal Exoplanets

LISA, the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna, is scheduled to be launched in 2035. The ESA is still developing the mission, but it's basic design is established. It will feature three separate spacecraft flying in an equilateral triangle formation. They'll be connected by laser interfometry, and LISA will use that interferometry to detect gravitational waves (GW).

GWs are ripples in spacetime that are the signatures of mergers between massive objects, either compact binaries containing stellar mass black holes, white dwarfs, and neutron stars, or between supermassive black holes (SMBH). Astronomy is concerned with light in all its wavelengths, but gravitational waves open another window on the Universe.

By detecting GWs from SMBH mergers, scientists study how galaxies merged and grew so massive. GWs from mergers between compact binaries can act as distance markers, helping cosmologists measure the expansion of the Universe. And the Universe was opaque to light in its first 380,000 years, so that time period is behind a curtain. But that curtain of opacity can't stop gravitational waves, so they can potentially bring those crucial years of the Universe's evolution into view.

But now researchers are saying that LISA may also be able to detect exoplanets.

This artist's impression shows gravitational waves from the merger of two compact objects. The presence of an exoplanet can leave a signature on these waves that LISA can detect. Image credit: NASA

âThe most common source for LISA is expected to be double white dwarf systems, which are binaries composed of white dwarfs in tight orbits,â said Casey McGrath, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Maryland and NASAâs Goddard Space Flight Center. âIf an exoplanet also orbits within one of these systems, its presence becomes imprinted on the gravitational wave signal in a way weâll be able to uncover.â

Two new papers outline LISA's planet-detection potential, and McGrath is involved in both. He's the sole author of "Receiving Exoplanet Messages with Gravitational-wave Carriers: The Gravitational-wave Radial Velocity Method," published in The Astrophysical Journal. It explains how LISA could detect exoplanets.

"Gravitational-wave (GW) radial velocity (RV) may offer a new method for detecting exoplanets, one that would primarily target planets orbiting GW-emitting, ultracompact, post-main-sequence stellar objects such as white dwarfs, neutron stars, and black holes," McGrath writes in the first paper.

The GWRV operates on the same principle as the RV exoplanet detection method does. In those instances, astronomers measure the tiny wobble a star experiences as an orbiting exoplanet tugs on it. Stars rotate, and the visible part of the star rotating toward the observer is blue-shifted, while the visible part of the star rotating away is red-shifted. The wobble creates doppler shifts in the red and blue light that astronomers measure with spectrographs.

In GWRV, an orbiting exoplanet creates a wobble in the center of mass of a compact binary. That creates a detectable doppler shift in the gravitational waves instead of in starlight. The method is more sensitive to high-mass, long-period planets than traditional RV, which more readily detects massive planets on short-period orbits around lower-mass stars like M dwarfs.

If the method works, it has some advantages over other exoplanet detection methods. "For one, GW observatories have potentially much farther reach into the Milky Way and beyond, since the GW amplitude is inversely proportional to the source distance," explains McGrath. "They will also inherently be probing post-main-sequence stellar systems, where EM observatories simply have not found as many exoplanets."

Exoplanets that go undetected in compact binaries can also cloud the GW signal. That can create misunderstandings as researchers try to understand and constrain the GWs. So detecting them also clarifies the GW signal from the compact binary.

This graphic shows how LISA works by detecting tiny changes in the distances between the spacecraft. Image Credit: By ESA / ATG Medialab, CC BY-SA IGO 3.0, CC BY-SA 3.0 igo, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/144582237 This graphic shows how LISA works by detecting tiny changes in the distances between the spacecraft. Image Credit: By ESA / ATG Medialab, CC BY-SA IGO 3.0, CC BY-SA 3.0 igo, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/144582237

This work is just an initial attempt to understand how it could all work. There's much more work to be done, as McGrath himself acknowledges. For one thing, the movement of LISA itself introduces some Doppler effect into the signal that has to be managed. Ground-based GW observatories don't move, and LISA will be the first one that does.

"Future, more complex and robust analyses will be needed to better understand the ability to detect exoplanets in GW signals," McGrath writes. "But hopefully this work can better shed light on the fundamental physics that can inform those studies."

If LISA does detect a signal in a GW that indicates a possible exoplanet, it will only be a candidate. That signal will have to be confirmed, and that will require observations in the electromagnetic regime. That's the subject of a second paper.

McGrath is also the lead author on another paper in the same journal that focuses on validating GW exoplanet candidates. It's titled "Multimessenger Exoplanets: Combining Infrared Excess and Astrometry with Gravitational-wave Detections of Double White Dwarf Exoplanets." It explains how the JWST can confirm GW exoplanet detections, possibly with help from Gaia or the Habitable Worlds Observatory.

âBy themselves, double white dwarfs will emit gravitational waves at a nearly continuous frequency," said Scott Noble, a theoretical astrophysicist at NASA Goddard and a coauthor on the second paper. "Add a sufficiently massive planet to the system, and its presence causes the binary to experience reflex motion, adding a Doppler modulation to the gravitational signal.â

LISA will see these as signals that bracket the primary GW signal from the DWD. These secondary signals are positioned in frequencies above and below the primary. So while the primary signal carries information about the DWD, the secondaries carry information about the exoplanet.

Every observatory, whether electromagnetic or gravitational, is built to detect signals at particular frequencies. LISA's frequency range means it will excel at detecting DWDs with short orbital periods. White dwarfs aren't rare, since they're the main evolutionary outcome for stars like the Sun, once they leave the main sequence. DWDs are rarer than single WDs, but astronomers still think that there are about 10 million DWDs with orbital periods of less than one hour in the Milky Way. Of those 10 million, researchers expect LISA to find about 10,000.

Astronomers think that LISA will find about 10,000 white dwarf doubles (DWDs) with short orbital periods. LISA should be able to detect exoplanets in DWDs, if they're there. Image Credit: Tod Strohmayer (GSFC), CXC, NASA, Illustration: Dana Berry (CXC)

LISA should be able to find the bracketed signals that exoplanets on circumbinary orbits around DWDs display. They would be candidates at first, and if those signals can be confirmed, they would be the first of those exoplanet types to be found.

"This population is unique: no such planets are currently known around DWDs, and only a handful of circumbinary planets around main-sequence stars and planets orbiting white dwarfs (WDs) have been identified," the authors write. "Independent EM confirmation will be essential, especially for the first GW-detected exoplanets, to validate this method."

Validation is critical, and it'll rely on electromagnetic confirmation. In their work, they use a representive known DWD (ZTF J2243+5242) to compute its detectability by LISA GWRV. "We then demonstrate two complementary EM techniquesâJWST infrared (IR) excess and Gaia or Habitable Worlds Observatory astrometryâthat could independently confirm a GW-detected planet in this fiducial system," the authors write.

An exoplanet orbiting a DWD produces more infrared than the stars themselves. The JWST is all about detecting infrared light, and it should have no problem detecting infrared excess out to a distance of about 500 light years. In their test case for a DWD at that distance, the JWST can detect an exoplanet with about five Jupiter masses, while LISA could detect one much smaller, with as little as 0.5 Jupiter masses, under perfect conditions.

âOnce LISA captures its first exoplanet detections, it will be critical for us to validate some of them,â said Mary Anne Limbach, an assistant research scientist at the University of Michigan and a co-author on the confirmation paper. âThese joint detections will allow us to establish that the gravitational signals correspond to genuine planets rather than false positives.â

The authors say we're about to enter a new phase of exoplanet detections once LISA is operational. The JWST's initial planned mission was for 5 to 10 years, but it may last 20. If it does, then it will overlap with LISA for several years, and it can be used to validate LISA exoplanet detections.

"A multimessenger exoplanet would be a historic discovery, and a DWD circumbinary would help to provide key insights into planetary and stellar evolution and into a part of the exoplanet census not yet probed," the authors write.

When the first gravitational wave was directly detected by LIGO/VIRGO in 2015, astronomers declared that a new window into the cosmos had been opened. LISA is prying that window open wider than ever, and as this work shows, the view might be even more detailed than thought. If it can detect exoplanets beyond the scope of traditional methods, then it'll give astronomers an even more expansive view of the cosmos than they anticipated.

#6356. Suqaar Digaag (Chicken and Vegetable Sauté)

It’s no exaggeration to say that xawaash is at the heart of Somali cuisine. It is Somali history on a plate—a culinary reminder of Somalia’s centuries of global trade, particularly along the Indian Ocean. Xawaash is what makes many Somali dishes taste distinctly Somali. While every household’s xawaash recipe is its own, typically seven core spices—cumin, coriander, black pepper, cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and turmeric—are toasted until their fragrance blooms, then blended into an earthy golden-brown powder. Xawaash stores very well and for a long time in an airtight container, though it’s at its peak shortly after it’s made. If you use it often, you can double or triple the recipe for a big batch.

Like all suqaar, this chicken suqaar features xawaash and bright peppers, but it skips the potato found in hilib (beef) suqaar. It has a hint of heat thanks to the black pepper and optional jalapeño. Suqaar is cooked covered to keep the meat juicy and moist. Serve with the flatbread of your choice (canjeero, muufo, or sabaayad) for a light lunch or over plenty of rice for a more filling dinner.

Toast 1 cup (100 g) whole cumin seeds, 1 cup (70 g) whole coriander seeds, ¼ cup (35 g) black peppercorns, 1 small-to-medium piece of cinnamon bark, 2 Tbsp. green cardamom pods, and 1½ tsp. whole cloves in a medium skillet over medium heat, stirring constantly so the spices don’t burn. The spices are toasted when they have a slightly darker color and become fragrant, 1–2 minutes. Transfer the toasted spices to a blender or spice grinder and blend until they become a fine powder. Transfer to a bowl and mix in ¼ cup (30 g) ground turmeric until it’s fully incorporated and the spice mix is golden brown. Allow to cool completely, then store in an airtight container.

In a medium bowl, combine the juice of ½ lemon, 1 tsp. xawaash, 1 tsp. fine sea salt, ½ tsp. paprika, and ⅛ tsp. ground black pepper. Add 1 lb. (450 g) boneless, skinless chicken thighs, cut into bite-sized pieces, and mix everything together to coat the chicken. Set aside.

In a large skillet over medium-high heat, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil until loose. Add 1 large yellow onion, halved and sliced, and cook, stirring occasionally, for 8 minutes, or until the onion is softened. Add 6 garlic cloves, minced, and 1 medium jalapeño, halved, and stir for another minute, then add the chicken in a single layer. Allow it to cook undisturbed for 5 minutes, then turn the pieces over and cook for 3 minutes more, until fully cooked through.

Add the remaining 1½ tsp. xawaash, ¾ cup (12 g) coarsely chopped cilantro leaves, 1 medium red bell pepper, sliced, and 1 medium yellow bell pepper, sliced, and stir to combine. Cover the skillet and turn the heat down to medium-low; cook until the peppers have softened, 10 to 15 minutes. Serve hot.

#6355. The Best Holiday Cocktails, According to Eater Editors

Don’t let cocktails fall by the wayside in the flurry of holiday dinner prep — these drinks make the party

In the endless iterating that goes into devising a menu for a holiday dinner, there’s one finishing touch that really makes or breaks the vibe: the drinks. The wine and beer will, of course, flow — at these festive events, a bottle of Champagne or sparkling rose is likely to make an appearance — and it’s easy enough to throw together a gin and tonic or screwdriver. But nothing makes a holiday gathering feel chic, totally put together, gloriously intentional, like a batch cocktail, made-to-order martini, or gussied-up punch.

Now, we all have our preferences when it comes to strength, spirit, and format. The host’s bandwidth is also a consideration; do you want to make a lot of one thing, or tailor your options to your guests’ preferences? Those questions are for you to answer, but our staff is here to help by providing this rundown of six tried, vetted, and loved drinks to make at your own celebration.

Below, find Eater editor-approved recipes for cocktails that will add the most festive of feelings to every holiday gathering.

Stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

I host a holiday potluck with a core group of friends in December, and one of my favorite potential additions is whatever punch that drinks columnist M. Carrie Allan is cooking up over at the Washington Post. A favorite from 2022 was a meringue-topped citrus punch, featuring blood orange, Aperol, and a dramatic meringue topping. Said topping adds undeniable flair and drama to the presentation, but if you’re daunted by the idea, the punch itself is still a festive, not-too-sweet drink to serve, celebrating winter citrus. —Missy Frederick, editorial director, dining

Meaghan Dorman’s modern classic is a favorite year-round, but there’s something about the holidays that calls for Scotch. No shade to the nog freaks, but the subtly spiced sour is a pleasant counterpoint to the onslaught of holiday food and beverage maximalism. No need to break out the single malt either, your dusty bottle of Dewars or Monkey Shoulder will do just fine. —Allison Hamlin, director of network development

The French 75 — the effervescent classic cocktail made with gin, Champagne, and lemon — is already one of my easy-drinking favorites, and I like it even better in punch form, accented with an aesthetically pleasing ice block of cheery lemon slices. What makes it 77 instead of 75? The substitution of St-Germain (or any elderflower liqueur) for simple syrup, adding just a tiny touch of herbal complexity. It’s perfect for New Year’s Eve, but just as refreshing at Thanksgiving or any other holiday table where you want something light and zesty. —Hilary Pollack, deputy editor

As the de facto cook for Thanksgiving, I like to keep the drinks options simple so I can focus on food prep. This cocktail recipe requires only two ingredients, doesn’t require pre-batching, and is easy enough for people to pour on their own. I also like how it uses Basque cider, which is drier than the typical ciders, so it’s not too sweet while still tapping into that cozy fall feeling —Rayna Rossitto, editor, branded content

I grew up guzzling Broguiere’s eggnog, but I love the more tropical combination of rich, creamy coconut milk, rum, and cinnamon in coquito; the Puerto Rican holiday cocktail was first described to me as “eggnog, if it went on vacation,” and I haven’t looked back since. This version is by bartender Shannon Ponche, and gets extra dressed up in spice for the holidays with the addition of a homemade cinnamon simple syrup, a woody, nutty oloroso sherry, and a splash of spiced Braulio. —Francky Knapp, staff writer

There are two schools of thought on a post-dinner drink: You could go for a bracing digestif to “aid digestion,” or you could indulge in a liquid dessert that swaddles you in sugar, fat, and everything nice. I’m notoriously bad at decision making, so I tend to split the difference with an eggy flip tinged with something bitter. Together, a whole egg and syrup (in this case honey syrup) build a comforting base, while an entire 1.5 ounces of cocktail bitters (as opposed to the usual dash or two) ensure you don’t entirely fall asleep in your glass. Angostura is a great option, delivering some classic holiday spice, but any style of cocktail bitters would probably work, as would an amaro. Dry shaking (shaking the liquid ingredients without ice) is key to achieving a frothy texture, and don’t forget the half-ounce of whiskey, which punches up the rest of the flavors. —Nick Mancall-Bitel, editor

Several members of my husband’s family are Manhattan drinkers, so I expect that my decision to serve the Grandfather cocktail during Thanksgiving appetizers will be a hit. It’s a riff on the classic drink with a hint of fall, courtesy of the addition of Applejack, an apple brandy. It’s smooth and well-balanced. It’s also quite boozy, so I’ll probably look for a slightly lower-proof option to tide us over after that initial round. I’ve had success with a bourbon and ginger ale bar (with various sodas and mixers) in the past, as well as Smitten Kitchen’s fall sangria; maybe this year we’ll go with her (okay, still pretty boozy) apple cider Old Fashioneds. —Missy Frederick, cities director

A factory worker experimented with a pressurized air system while on the job, and it resulted in a fatal injury.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The patient: A 35-year-old man in the Czech Republic

The symptoms: The man was injured while working in a factory. His co-workers learned he'd been hurt after he crawled from the ground floor to the first floor and shouted for help. He had severe abdominal pain and rectal bleeding, and he said he had been injured while conducting "a silly experiment" involving a pressurized air system. However, he did not describe exactly what had happened.

"He repeatedly stressed that the incident was his own fault," doctors later wrote in a report of his case.

What happened next: The man was flown by helicopter to a nearby hospital, but during the flight, he became unresponsive and showed signs of hemorrhagic shock — a type of shock caused by significant blood loss over a short period. Shock, broadly, is when organs and body tissues don't receive enough oxygen due to decreased blood flow; if untreated, it can lead to organ failure and death.

Medical attendants in the helicopter worked to revive the man, but he died before he could be admitted to the hospital. Because the fatal injury occurred at the man's workplace, the police ordered a medicolegal autopsy, which both identifies the cause of death and collects details for law enforcement agencies, as part of an inquest procedure.

The autopsy: The coroner examined the body and noted that the soft tissues of the man's face were swollen and abnormally distended from retained air. The man's anus and genital areas were similarly distended and densely coated with dried blood, with radial tears in the skin surrounding the anus.

Next, the coroner conducted an internal examination. The man's brain was swollen, and he had air bubbles in his brain and chest cavity. Blood had collected around his diaphragm (the large muscle that helps inflate and deflate the lungs). It had also accumulated in the wall between the heart chambers on the left side, in tubes leading to his lungs, and in the membranes covering his lungs and heart. Reservoirs of blood also pooled in the man's abdominal cavity, in the tube leading to his right kidney, and in his digestive organs.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The man's heart was "shrunken and empty," according to the report.

The autopsy also revealed foreign objects stuck between loops of the man's small intestine. These included three pieces of a black rubber pipe stopper and scraps of a plastic bag. His rectum — the final straight portion of the large intestine — had detached violently from his anus. It was surrounded by blood and marked with a laceration that was nearly circular, indicating that an "explosive rectal injury" had triggered hemorrhagic shock and caused the man's death, the coroner concluded.

Further investigation: Additional evidence from the factory and rubber fragments in the man's small intestine provided the police with further insight into his injuries; additional clues came from his internet search history, including photos of himself that he'd submitted to an amateur sex website.

The police concluded that the man had been performing autoerotic anal stimulation while at work, using a rubber inflatable pipe stopper measuring 2 to 3 inches (50 to 70 millimeters) in diameter, and an air gun, a handheld device for directing powerful jets of compressed air.

They suggested that the man likely attached the expandable pipe stopper to the muzzle of the air gun, which was in turn connected to the factory's air distribution system by a long, high-pressure hose. He then covered the pipe stopper with a plastic bag, inserted it into his rectal cavity, and pressed the air gun's trigger, causing "an unexpected abrupt inflation and explosive bursting of the pipe stopper within his rectum," the doctors wrote in the case report.

What makes the case unique: This case is the first recorded example of a person dying from a "rectal explosion during self-gratification," the doctors wrote. Piecing together the circumstances leading up to the man's injury was important for the hospital's doctors and law enforcement to understand how the fatality likely occurred, the authors said.

When performed responsibly and consensually, rectal insertion of foreign bodies typically does not cause significant injury, the authors added. However, "the introduction of some objects into the rectum might have unpredictable and even fatal effects."

For more intriguing medical cases, check out our Diagnostic Dilemma archives.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.
